concepts.definition: Physico-chemical separation method in which fine particles selectively attach to gas bubbles and rise to the froth layer. In beneficiation, it exploits differences in surface properties of minerals.
Industrial processing area focused on separating valuable minerals from gangue and improving the quality of mined raw materials. Flotation is one of the key methods used in this application.
Excess energy associated with atoms or molecules located at a phase boundary relative to the bulk. It governs interfacial phenomena such as wetting, spreading, and adhesion in flotation.
Measure of the strength and character of intermolecular interactions in a phase. In flotation, polarity controls wettability, association, solvation, and the nature of mineral surfaces.
Ability of a liquid to spread on and adhere to a solid surface. In flotation, wettability depends strongly on the polarity mismatch between the liquid and the mineral surface.
Surface area per unit mass of a particulate material. It increases as particle size decreases, making surface effects increasingly important in flotation.

Attractive forces between molecules that generate interfacial energy differences and drive wetting, spreading, and adhesion. These forces are described in the text as the fundamental basis of flotation phenomena.
Mechanism by which certain mineral particles preferentially adhere to injected air bubbles and are transported to the surface. This selectivity enables separation of minerals from suspension.

Chemical additive introduced into a flotation slurry to enhance selectivity, attachment strength, and separation efficiency. Such reagents may be water-soluble or sparingly soluble and act at the solidтАУliquidтАУgas interfaces.
Strongly polar liquid phase that serves as the continuous medium in flotation suspensions. Its interaction with mineral surfaces largely determines wetting behavior and separation selectivity.
Highly polar silicate mineral used as an example of a hydrophilic surface. Water readily spreads on quartz because of the relatively small polarity mismatch.
Low-polarity carbonaceous mineral used as an example of a hydrophobic surface in flotation theory. It is not readily wetted by water and therefore behaves differently from silicate minerals.
Nonpolar hydrocarbon material cited as an example of a surface with low polarity. It is poorly wetted by water but readily interacts with nonpolar liquids such as hydrocarbon oils.

Particle-size regime in which surface phenomena dominate the behavior of solids in suspension. Flotation is especially effective for these fine particles, typically below about tenths of a millimeter.

Flotation variant used to recover dissolved ions from true solutions by forming complexes with surface-active species that attach to gas bubbles and rise into the froth. It is especially effective for dilute metal-bearing solutions.
Flotation method that generates hydrogen and oxygen microbubbles by electrolysis of water. The small, controllable bubble size improves capture of fine particles or dissolved species.
Flotation scheme in which gangue minerals are transferred to the froth while valuable minerals remain in the pulp. It is used when the waste phase is easier to float than the target mineral.
Flotation mode designed to separate multiple valuable minerals into individual concentrates. It relies on finely tuned reagent chemistry and differences in surface selectivity.
Agitated aqueous mineral suspension used as the working medium for flotation. Air bubbles are introduced into the pulp, where selective attachment determines recovery into froth or tailings.

Dilute-solution regime in which ion flotation is particularly advantageous for preconcentrating trace species. It is typical for hydrometallurgical streams, analytical samples, and wastewater treatment.

State reached when spontaneous interfacial and wetting processes lower the system free energy to the minimum allowed under the given conditions. In flotation theory, it represents the endpoint of surface-energy-driven rearrangement.
Tendency of a surface or particle to resist wetting by water and preferentially interact with a gas phase. In flotation, higher hydrophobicity promotes bubble attachment and froth recovery.
Tendency of a surface to be readily wetted by water. Hydrophilic particles are less likely to attach to air bubbles and therefore tend to remain in the pulp.
Diatomic gas formed during water electrolysis and used as a bubble phase in electroflotation. Its bubbles can serve as attachment sites for particles or complexes being floated.
Diatomic gas formed during water electrolysis and used as a bubble-forming phase in electroflotation. It can be used together with or separately from hydrogen to influence flotation behavior.
Metal extraction and purification domain based on aqueous solutions and leachates. Ion flotation is used here to recover dilute metal ions from process streams.

High-temperature metallurgical domain in which flotation may be used for feed preparation or purification of associated mineral streams. It is listed in the text as one of the areas where flotation is applied.
Chemical analysis domain where ion flotation can preconcentrate trace analytes before measurement. The method is especially useful when the analyte concentration is very low.

Industrial and municipal treatment domain focused on removing suspended solids, microorganisms, and dissolved contaminants from effluents. Flotation is used there as a clarification and separation method.
Gas-treatment domain in which flotation-based capture can remove bacteria and solid particles from air streams. The text cites it as one of the broader application areas of flotation.
Industrial sector where flotation is used for separation and purification of raw materials, intermediates, and products. The method is valued for surface-selective separation in complex mixtures.
Industrial sector where flotation is used to improve raw-material quality by removing unwanted mineral impurities. It is mentioned in the text as an application area of flotation.
Earth-science domain where flotation can aid mineral separation, sample preparation, and analysis of geological materials. The text lists it among the areas of flotation application.
Biomedical domain where flotation can be used to separate cells, microorganisms, or particulate matter. The text cites medicine as one of the non-mining application areas of flotation.
Life-science domain where flotation methods can separate biological particles, cells, or bacteria. It is listed as one of the broader application areas in the text.
Agricultural processing domain where flotation can separate seeds or remove unwanted particulate matter. The text mentions it as one of the areas where flotation is applied.

Process KPI describing the amount of oil reagent consumed per unit of ore or concentrate. In early flotation, reducing oil consumption was a primary driver of technological development and industrial adoption.
Legal exclusivity over a process or apparatus that restricts technology diffusion and industrial competition. In the text, the basic patent slowed the development of flotation until its cancellation.

Early flotation method in which crushed ore is mixed with mineral oil so that selected mineral particles become oil-wet, agglomerate, and rise to the surface. It is especially associated with sulfide minerals and is limited by high oil consumption.

Flotation variant in which sufficiently hydrophobic fine particles float on the water surface without added oil. The method is inherently unstable and low in productivity when compared with froth flotation.

Modern flotation scheme in which air bubbles, collectors, and frothers are used to transport hydrophobic particles into a stable froth layer. It enabled economically viable and selective separation of fine and polymetallic ores.

Historical flotation process for lead-zinc tailings in which pulp was treated with hot sulfuric acid or sodium bisulfite to generate carbon dioxide bubbles. The bubbles attached to zinc sulfide particles and carried them to the surface.
Flotation method in which reduced pressure above the pulp releases dissolved gas as bubbles. The generated bubbles facilitate attachment and lifting of hydrophobic particles or oil-coated aggregates.

Mechanism in which one phase preferentially wets certain mineral surfaces while other phases do not. In oil and film flotation, selective wetting controls whether particles aggregate, remain in pulp, or float.

Mechanism by which mineral oil wets mineral surfaces and causes fine particles to stick together into larger agglomerates. This increases apparent particle size and promotes surface rise during separation.
Nonpolar organic liquid used as the wetting phase in oil flotation. It selectively wets sulfide particles, promotes agglomeration, and helps them rise to the pulp surface.
Gas phase used as bubble-forming medium in froth flotation. Air bubbles provide attachment sites for hydrophobic particles and are essential for efficient flotation separation.
Gaseous phase generated during boiling of flotation pulp. In early oil flotation, steam bubbles contributed to lifting oil-wet particles to the surface.
Gas generated in the Potter-Delprat process and used as a flotation bubble phase. Its bubbles attach to mineral particles and promote their transport to the froth layer.

Strong mineral acid used in flotation-related processing to acidify pulp and generate carbon dioxide bubbles in the Potter-Delprat process. It can also alter surface chemistry and mineral liberation behavior.
Reducing salt used as a cheaper alternative to sulfuric acid in historical flotation practice. In the Potter-Delprat process it helped generate gas bubbles for lifting sulfide particles.
Mineral class whose surfaces are often naturally amenable to oil wetting and collector adsorption. Sulfide minerals are central feedstocks for early oil flotation and later froth flotation processes.
Sulfur-containing flotation collector widely used to hydrophobize sulfide minerals. Water-soluble xanthates became one of the key reagents enabling selective froth flotation.
Unsaturated fatty acid used as a flotation reagent, especially in early industrial formulations. It acts through surface adsorption and hydrophobization of selected particles.
Water-soluble salt of fatty acids used as a flotation collector. Such soaps adsorb on mineral surfaces and increase hydrophobicity, supporting selective separation in froth flotation.
Reagent class designed to adsorb on target mineral surfaces and increase their hydrophobicity. Collectors are central to selective flotation because they control particle-bubble attachment.
Reagent class that stabilizes bubble size and froth structure in flotation pulp. Frothers improve bubble dispersion, froth persistence, and the selectivity of particle recovery.
Reagent class used to adjust pulp chemistry, surface state, and selectivity between minerals. Regulators are essential in selective flotation of polymetallic ores.

Patent record describing the first oil flotation concept, where crushed ore was mixed with mineral oil to agglomerate sulfide particles. It is a key historical source for the origin of flotation technology.
Patent record proposing boiling pulp in oil flotation to reduce oil demand and use gas bubbles for lifting graphite particles. It marks an early attempt to introduce a gas phase into flotation.

Patent record for film flotation, an early oil-free flotation concept based on the tendency of hydrophobic fine particles to float at the water surface. It is historically important even though it had limited practical use.
Patent record describing vacuum-assisted oil flotation and the use of gas bubbles generated by water electrolysis. It is associated with the transition toward gas-phase-assisted flotation.

Foundational patent family associated with Mineral Separation Ltd. that promoted air suction, low oil usage, oleic acid, and continuous flotation operation. It strongly influenced the commercialization of froth flotation.

Patent record for a flotation apparatus that complemented the basic patent and helped establish the first complete industrial froth flotation scheme. It supported controlled air introduction and continuous operation.
Patent record associated with the introduction of water-soluble xanthate collectors for sulfide flotation. It is a key source for modern selective collector chemistry.
Patent record describing the use of soluble fatty-acid soaps as flotation reagents. It represents an important source for collector development in froth flotation.
Measure of charge separation in a molecule or molecular fragment. In water, high dipole moments strengthen intermolecular interactions and contribute to liquid association and structuring.
Specific intermolecular interaction responsible for the strong association of water molecules. It is a key factor in the transient structural ordering of water relevant to flotation behavior.

Formation of a bound water layer on a mineral surface during contact with aqueous media. The hydration layer modifies interfacial properties and reduces the probability of air-bubble attachment in flotation.
Ability of a mineral surface to become hydrated in water. Higher hydratability increases the formation of a stable hydration layer and generally lowers flotation response.
Gaseous species dissolved in water that can alter its structure and interfacial behavior. In flotation systems, dissolved gases influence wetting, adsorption, coagulation, and bubble formation.

External physical field that can modify the structure of water and the behavior of dispersed mineral systems. The text links magnetic-field treatment to changes in wetting, adsorption, and coagulation during flotation.

High-frequency acoustic field used as an external physical factor acting on water and suspension structure. It can alter interfacial phenomena relevant to wetting and particle aggregation in flotation systems.
Interfacial accumulation of ions or molecules on a solid or liquid surface. In flotation, adsorption controls reagent attachment to minerals and strongly affects selectivity and recovery.
Aggregation of dispersed particles into larger clusters or flocs. In flotation pulp, coagulation changes suspension stability and can either promote or hinder bubble-particle capture.

Attractive interaction between molecules of the same phase, responsible for the internal integrity of a liquid or solid. In wetting and flotation theory, cohesion competes with adhesion and helps determine whether a liquid spreads on a mineral surface.

Attractive interaction between two different phases at their interface, such as water and a mineral surface. Adhesion governs liquid spreading, bubble attachment, and the strength of reagent fixation on mineral particles.
Energy per unit area required to separate a liquid column into two parts and overcome internal molecular attraction. It is used as a quantitative measure of cohesive forces in wetting analysis.

Energy per unit area required to separate two contacting phases at an interface, such as a liquid and a mineral surface. In flotation, it is a key indicator of how strongly water or an apolar reagent can bind to a mineral surface.

Angle formed at the three-phase contact line that quantifies the degree of wetting of a solid by a liquid. In flotation, a larger contact angle corresponds to lower wettability and higher hydrophobicity, favoring bubble attachment.

Interfacial force per unit length, or equivalently excess free energy per unit area, acting at a phase boundary. Surface tension controls droplet shape, spreading, and the equilibrium wetting state described by the Young equation.

Interfacial process in which a liquid spreads on or partially covers a solid surface. In mineral processing, wetting is governed by the balance between adhesion and cohesion and determines whether a particle behaves hydrophilically or hydrophobically.

Surface treatment or reagent-assisted process used to reduce the wettability of mineral particles by water. In flotation, hydrophobization increases the contact angle and promotes attachment of particles to air bubbles.

Non-equilibrium behavior in which the observed contact angle depends on the history and direction of wetting or dewetting. It becomes more pronounced on rough or chemically heterogeneous surfaces and influences bubble attachment in flotation.

Time-dependent form of wetting hysteresis caused by delayed motion of the contact line, often due to surface roughness or adsorption layers. In flotation, it can stabilize the three-phase contact perimeter and improve bubble retention on particles.

Dependence of the measured contact angle on whether a surface is wet from the dry state or from the immersed state. It reflects metastable interfacial states and incomplete relaxation of the wetting perimeter.

A chemical bonding mechanism based on electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions in a crystal lattice. In mineral surfaces, ionic bonds create strong polar sites that increase surface free energy and favor interaction with water.

A bonding mechanism formed by shared electron pairs between atoms. On mineral surfaces, covalent bonding contributes to high bond strength and strongly affects the surface's interaction with polar liquids.

A bond type intermediate between ionic and covalent bonding, with unequal electron sharing and partial charge separation. Such bonds generate polar mineral surfaces with elevated surface energy and strong affinity for water.

Weak intermolecular forces that act between atoms and molecules without forming classical chemical bonds. In mineralogy and flotation, they are characteristic of apolar surfaces and contribute to low wettability and hydrophobic behavior.

A nonmetallic element used in the text as an example of a crystal whose cleavage exposes weak intermolecular interactions. Its surface properties help illustrate why some minerals are naturally hydrophobic.

Lead sulfide mineral used as an example of a sulfide surface that is initially relatively hydrophilic after fresh fracture. Its interaction with dissolved oxygen can subsequently change surface wettability and flotation response.

A structured interfacial water layer formed adjacent to a mineral surface by adsorption and hydrogen-bond-mediated ordering. It differs from bulk water by higher viscosity, reduced diffusion, and a strong influence on bubble attachment in flotation.

A degradation process in which dissolved oxygen reacts with a mineral surface, especially sulfide minerals, forming oxidized layers or species. This typically increases hydrophilicity and reduces flotation performance by weakening bubble attachment.

Thermodynamic quantity describing the energy change associated with wetting a mineral surface by water. In flotation, it reflects the strength of water attachment to the surface and is linked to hydrophilicity and bubble-detachment resistance.

Energy released when ions or surface species become hydrated by water molecules. In mineral dissolution, hydration energy competes with crystal lattice energy and governs whether minerals partially dissolve in pulp.

Energy required to overcome the electrostatic cohesion of a crystal lattice and separate it into ions or molecules. In aqueous mineral systems, it is the opposing term to hydration energy and controls dissolution tendency.

Measure of the ionic character of a polar bond on a mineral surface. Higher ionicity increases interaction with water and reduces natural floatability, while lower ionicity corresponds to greater covalency and poorer wettability.

Inorganic sulfide compound used as a sulfidizing reagent in flotation of oxidized nonferrous-metal minerals. Because of its high ionic character, it interacts strongly with water and can facilitate conversion of oxide surfaces into sulfide-like flotation-active surfaces.

Ionic species released from partial dissolution of minerals into the liquid phase of flotation pulp. These ions are always present to some extent and can interact with mineral surfaces and flotation reagents, altering selectivity and reagent consumption.

Equilibrium amount of a substance that can dissolve in a liquid under given temperature and composition. In flotation systems, solubility controls ion release from minerals and the formation of dissolved species that affect surface chemistry and reagent interactions.
Effective size of an ion in a crystal or solution environment. In the text, ionic radius is linked to trends in lattice stability and solubility, including the solubility of silver halides.
Ability of water or pulp to conduct electric current through dissolved ions. The slice notes that purified distilled water has very low conductivity, while dissolved salts increase conductivity.

Process-water condition caused mainly by dissolved calcium and magnesium salts. In flotation, high hardness can precipitate collectors such as soaps and fatty acids and can also alter mineral surface behavior, reducing selectivity.
Acidity/alkalinity parameter of the aqueous pulp. In the slice, sulfide oxidation forms acidic species and lowers pulp pH, which in turn changes mineral surface chemistry and flotation response.

Interfacial charge structure formed at the boundary between a mineral and the liquid phase due to preferential ion dissolution and adsorption. It governs surface potential, electrostatic interactions, and many flotation-relevant wetting and reagent effects.

Treatment method used to reduce the concentration of hardness ions, mainly calcium and magnesium, in process water. In flotation, softening is applied to prevent reagent precipitation and to restore selectivity when hard water interferes with collector action.

Chemical pretreatment that converts oxidized mineral surfaces into sulfide-like, flotation-active surfaces. It is used especially for oxidized nonferrous-metal minerals and is often carried out with sulfidizing reagents such as barium sulfide.

Failure mode in which hardness ions, especially calcium and magnesium, react with soaps or fatty acids to form insoluble precipitates. This consumes flotation reagents, worsens selectivity, and can require water softening before flotation.

The electrokinetic potential difference that appears at the slipping plane between a moving mineral particle and the surrounding liquid. In flotation pulp, it is strongly affected by electrolyte concentration and by adsorption of dissolved ions and reagents on the mineral surface.

The total interfacial potential difference between the inner and outer parts of the electrical double layer at the mineralтАУliquid boundary. Unlike zeta potential, it is defined at the interface itself and is less sensitive to particle motion.

Nonuniformity of a mineral surface in composition, free surface energy, and adsorption activity across different crystal faces and defect sites. This heterogeneity causes some surface regions to react and adsorb reagents more readily than others, which is important for flotation selectivity.

Material class with electrical conductivity intermediate between metals and insulators, typically sensitive to temperature, impurity content, and crystal defects. In the slice, semiconductors are discussed as minerals whose electronic structure strongly influences adsorption and interaction with flotation reagents.

Material class characterized by very high electrical conductivity and the absence of an energy gap between occupied and conducting electronic states. The text contrasts metals with semiconductors because their conductivity decreases with heating and impurity addition typically reduces conductivity.

Material class with extremely low electrical conductivity and a wide forbidden energy gap. The slice uses insulators as the reference class opposite to semiconductors when discussing energy-band structure and charge transport.

Energy interval between the valence band and the conduction band in a solid, representing the energy required to promote an electron into a conducting state. In the slice, the band gap distinguishes semiconductors from insulators and governs thermal activation of conductivity.

Thermodynamic/electronic energy level describing the chemical potential of electrons and holes in a solid. The slice uses the Fermi level to explain how electron and hole populations distribute in semiconductors and how this affects reactivity.

Rate at which electrical conductivity changes with temperature. The text highlights the positive coefficient of semiconductors, meaning their conductivity rises rapidly as temperature increases, unlike metals.

Impurity species that can donate extra electrons to a semiconductor lattice. In the slice, donor impurities convert a semiconductor into an n-type material with electron conductivity and influence adsorption behavior through electronic structure changes.

Impurity species that creates electron vacancies in a semiconductor lattice by accepting electrons. In the slice, acceptor impurities produce p-type semiconductors with hole conductivity and alter mineral reactivity toward flotation reagents.

Semiconductor whose dominant charge carriers are electrons, typically formed by donor doping or donor-like defects. The slice notes that such materials arise when impurities contribute excess electrons to the crystal lattice.

Semiconductor whose dominant charge carriers are holes, typically formed by acceptor doping. The slice explains that these materials conduct by motion of electron vacancies created in the valence structure.

Ideal semiconductor containing no foreign dopants, where electron and hole concentrations are equal and conductivity is governed by thermally generated carriers. The slice describes this as the limiting case of a perfect crystal without impurities or lattice disruptions.

Quantum-physical framework used to describe allowed and forbidden electronic energy states in solids. In the slice, it explains why semiconductors, metals, and insulators differ in conductivity and how temperature or impurities shift charge-carrier populations.

Electrical potential generated in a material when it is subjected to a temperature gradient. In mineral semiconductors, it is used together with conductivity measurements to estimate electron and hole concentrations and to infer adsorption behavior toward flotation reagents.

Analytical technique that uses labeled atoms or isotopes to track the spatial distribution of a reagent or element on a mineral surface. In flotation studies, it reveals strongly nonuniform reagent adsorption and surface heterogeneity.

Imaging method based on recording the spatial distribution of radiation through or from a specimen. In the slice, it is used to visualize the uneven distribution of flotation reagents on mineral polished sections.

High-resolution autoradiographic imaging technique used to localize labeled species on individual mineral particles. It makes it possible to observe reagent adsorption patterns directly on flotation-size grains and on particles recovered from flotation products.

Fine-scale geometric nonuniformity of a mineral surface, including protrusions, depressions, microcracks, and grain-boundary features. It strongly affects reagent interaction, local wetting, and adsorption in flotation systems.

Nonuniform distribution of anodic and cathodic activity across a mineral surface. This heterogeneity creates spatially different adsorption and redox conditions, which changes the interaction of sulfides with collectors such as xanthates.

Mechanism in which atoms or ions of similar size and compatible charge replace one another in a crystal lattice while preserving the overall structure. In minerals, this alters lattice energy, hardness, solubility, and flotation response.

Crystalline material phase formed when different atoms or ions occupy equivalent lattice positions through isomorphic substitution. Solid solutions are common in minerals and often explain deviations between ideal and actual chemical composition.
Effective size of an atom in a crystal or bonding environment. In the slice, closeness of atomic or ionic radii is a key criterion for isomorphic substitution in mineral lattices.

Charge-related chemical characteristic of an ion that determines how it can substitute into a crystal lattice and interact with other species. The text uses differences in valency to distinguish isovalent and heterovalent isomorphism.

Inorganic iron(III) sulfate formed during sulfide oxidation in aqueous systems. It acts as an aggressive oxidizing medium that accelerates sulfide-to-sulfate conversion and generates acidity that changes mineral surface chemistry.
Copper sulfate species formed during oxidation of copper sulfides in pulp. It is part of the secondary chemistry that modifies sulfide surfaces and can influence subsequent flotation behavior.
Reduced sulfur gas released in reactions between sulfides and acidified aqueous media. In the slice, it appears as a product accompanying sulfide conversion to sulfates during acid attack.

Iron sulfide mineral discussed as one of the sulfides whose flotation response is altered by copper sulfate treatment. Its surface chemistry can be modified to change hydrophobicity and collector interaction.

Iron sulfide mineral used as an example of a sulfide phase whose flotation properties can change after interaction with copper sulfate. It is relevant to sulfide activation and surface oxidation chemistry.
Copper sulfide mineral mentioned as weakly affected by copper sulfate treatment in the slice. It is a sulfide feed mineral whose surface reactivity determines flotation response.
Zinc sulfide mineral whose flotation properties can be significantly altered by copper sulfate activation. It is a key sulfide mineral in selective flotation circuits.
Copper iron sulfide mineral referenced as weakly affected by copper sulfate treatment. Its surface state strongly influences collector adsorption and flotation behavior.

Reversible sorption mechanism in which reagents bind to mineral or bubble surfaces through weak intermolecular interactions rather than electron transfer. In flotation, it produces a comparatively small heat effect and is easily removed by washing or dilution.

Specific sorption mechanism in which the adsorbate and mineral surface form a chemically bonded interfacial layer via electron transfer or electron sharing. In flotation, chemisorption is stronger and more selective than physical adsorption and can persist after washing.

Component of intermolecular attraction arising from the interaction of permanent dipoles. It contributes to van der Waals forces and affects how polar reagents interact with mineral and aqueous surfaces.

Component of intermolecular attraction in which a permanent dipole induces a dipole in a neighboring molecule or surface fragment. It is one of the contributions to weak adsorption forces relevant to flotation systems.

Component of intermolecular attraction caused by instantaneous fluctuations of electron density and the resulting transient dipoles. It is a key part of van der Waals interactions on apolar mineral surfaces.

A bulk interfacial reaction that proceeds at the mineral surface and is described in the slice as the volume analogue of chemisorption. It can follow chemisorption, produce autonomous surface phases, and form mosaic multilayer coatings on the mineral surface.

A form of adsorption in which whole electrolyte molecules are taken up by the solid surface with equivalent adsorption of cations and anions. In this regime electroneutrality at the phase boundary is preserved and no electrical double layer is formed.

A class of adsorption in which ions from an electrolyte are selectively taken up by a solid surface. In the slice, it is contrasted with molecular adsorption and includes exchange adsorption and specific adsorption.

Selective adsorption in which ions of one sign are taken up from solution while ions of the same sign already on the surface are displaced in an equivalent amount. This preserves electroneutrality of both the solution and the interface and does not change the net surface charge.

A selective adsorption process in which certain ions are preferentially bound to the mineral surface and generate a potential difference at the phase boundary. This adsorption is responsible for the formation of the electrical double layer and is important for flotation-relevant surface charging.

An ion that adsorbs specifically on a mineral surface and determines the interfacial electrical potential. Such ions may be present in the crystal lattice or may substitute for lattice ions if their size and charge are compatible.

A positively charged aqueous species noted in the slice as being adsorbed more strongly than alkali-metal ions. Hydrogen ions influence surface charging, acidity, and the adsorption behavior of mineral surfaces in electrolyte solutions.

A monovalent anion that the slice identifies as adsorbing more strongly than other inorganic anions. Hydroxide ions are important in controlling surface charge, hydration, and flotation behavior in alkaline media.

An amphiphilic chemical substance that preferentially adsorbs at phase boundaries and lowers interfacial free energy. In flotation, surfactants include frothers and related reagents that stabilize the waterтАУair interface and control bubble formation and particle attachment.

A state of an interfacial system in which the electrokinetic potential is zero because counterions have shifted from the diffuse layer into the compact part of the electrical double layer. In flotation, this condition is associated with reduced electrostatic repulsion and altered wettability of mineral surfaces.

A flotation suppression mechanism in which an ion common to the mineral lattice is adsorbed or incorporated at the surface and decreases floatability. It can modify the surface layer, hinder collector action, and is used intentionally in some selective flotation schemes.

A densely packed interfacial layer of adsorbed, oriented molecules formed when the surface becomes saturated with surfactant species. In flotation, this layer reduces surface energy, can be rigidified by hydration of polar groups, and is important for froth stabilization.

Ability of a substance to adsorb at an interface and reduce interfacial free energy. In the slice, surface activity governs the foaming performance of frothers and the dependence of interfacial behavior on hydrophobic radical length.
Resistance of a foam or froth to collapse, drainage, and bubble coalescence. In flotation, higher froth stability helps retain mineralized bubbles and improves separation efficiency.

Aggregation of reagent molecules in solution driven by intermolecular attraction, especially dispersion forces, when hydrophobic chains become long enough to overcome polar-group hydration. In the slice, molecular association lowers solubility and reduces foaming efficiency.

Nonpolar hydrocarbon-based flotation reagent used to hydrophobize mineral surfaces by physical adsorption and wetting. The slice describes petroleum-derived apolar collectors such as kerosene, mineral oils, and heavy petroleum fractions.

Hydrocarbon class containing one or more aromatic rings. In the slice, aromatic enrichment of petroleum fractions is associated with stronger flotation effects and improved hydrophobization performance for apolar collectors.

Ability of a molecule or molecular fragment to form an induced dipole under an external electric field. In flotation, higher polarizability strengthens the attraction of apolar hydrocarbon collectors to ionically bonded mineral surfaces and improves fixation.

Resistance of a fluid to flow, which reflects the intensity of intermolecular interactions and the molecular architecture of the hydrocarbon phase. In the slice, viscosity is used as a practical criterion for the hydrophobizing effectiveness and retention strength of apolar collectors on mineral surfaces.

Geometric property in which all atoms of a molecular framework lie in one plane. For aromatic hydrocarbons, complanarity contributes to more stable adsorption and stronger fixation on mineral surfaces than in comparable aliphatic structures.

Flotation collector reagent containing polar or ionizable groups that can adsorb on mineral surfaces and impart hydrophobicity. In the text, ionogenic collectors are contrasted with apolar collectors as more expensive but capable of preconditioning mineral surfaces for subsequent hydrophobization.

Non-aromatic hydrocarbon class with chain or non-aromatic cyclic structure. In flotation, aliphatic hydrocarbons are used as apolar collectors, but they generally adsorb less stably on mineral surfaces than aromatic hydrocarbons of comparable composition.

Economic indicator describing the cost of flotation collectors per unit mass or process unit. The slice states that apolar collectors are several times cheaper than ionogenic reagents, making collector cost a key driver for reagent selection and process economics.

Carbonaceous sedimentary material that can exhibit high natural hydrophobicity and respond well to apolar collectors. In the slice, coal is cited among minerals/materials that can be floated by hydrophobic surface interactions.
A crystalline carbon material with very low wettability and strong natural hydrophobicity. The slice uses diamond as an example of a mineral that can be readily acted on by apolar collectors.
Molybdenum sulfide mineral with inherently hydrophobic basal surfaces. It is listed in the slice among minerals with the highest natural hydrophobic properties.

Calcium fluoride mineral commonly recovered by flotation with cationic or other selective collectors. The slice mentions fluorite as a target mineral in separation schemes involving alkyl sulfate and other reagents.
Barium sulfate mineral used as a flotation target in selective separation circuits. The slice cites barite recovery from scheelite concentrates as an application example.
Calcium tungstate mineral commonly processed in tungsten ores. In the slice, scheelite is mentioned in the context of barite separation and tungsten flotation circuits.

Tin oxide mineral that can appear in flotation concentrate and tailings separation schemes. The slice mentions cassiterite as a mineral that can remain in the chamber product when fluorite is floated.

Phosphate-bearing mineral raw material processed in flotation circuits. The slice cites phosphorites as a target of cationic collectors and as a source of separation problems with quartz and silicates.

A group of silicate minerals used as examples of non-valuable or separating phases in flotation of quartz-bearing feeds. The slice mentions garnet in conjunction with quartz separation by cationic collectors.
Aluminosilicate mineral cited as a flotation target in quartz separation schemes. It is one of the industrial mineral examples mentioned for cationic collector applications.
Complex borosilicate mineral mentioned as a flotation target in separations from quartz. The slice lists it among minerals recovered or rejected using cationic collectors.
Beryllium-bearing silicate mineral used as an example of a material separable by cationic collectors. The slice mentions beryl among minerals recovered in flotation circuits with amine-type reagents.
Lithium aluminosilicate mineral important in lithium ore beneficiation. The slice lists spodumene among minerals effectively floated with cationic collectors.
Hydrophobic magnesium silicate mineral commonly removed from ores by flotation. The slice notes separation of talc from mica as a practical cationic-collector application.
Layered aluminosilicate mineral used as a target or gangue phase in flotation separations. The slice mentions its separation from talc and its flotation behavior with cationic reagents.
Rock-forming aluminosilicate mineral that is commonly separated from quartz, kaolin, and mica by flotation. The slice cites feldspar in multiple cationic-collector separation examples.
Chromium-bearing spinel mineral used as a flotation separation target. The slice mentions chromite separation from olivine using cationic collectors.
Magnesium-iron silicate mineral mentioned as a companion or gangue phase in chromite flotation. It is cited in the slice as a mineral separable from chromite by cationic collectors.
Iron oxide mineral commonly recovered by reverse or direct flotation routes. The slice lists hematite among minerals effectively floated by cationic collectors.
Titanium-iron oxide mineral used as a flotation target in heavy-mineral processing. The slice cites ilmenite among minerals recovered with cationic reagents.
Oxide mineral class cited as a flotation target in the slice. It is included among minerals that can be separated using cationic collectors.
Iron carbonate mineral referenced as a flotation target in the slice. It appears in the list of minerals amenable to cationic collector flotation.

Flotation reagent class whose active species carry positive charge in pulp and adsorb on negatively charged or specifically reactive mineral surfaces. In the slice, cationic collectors are used for quartz, silicates, oxidized zinc minerals, phosphorites, and many industrial minerals, but their use is limited by higher cost and toxicity.

Amines converted to their hydrochloride salts, used as water-soluble cationic flotation collectors. The slice describes such reagents as a mixture of C13-C16 aliphatic primary amine hydrochlorides with effective use in quartz, silicate, and iron-ore flotation.

Permanently charged cationic surfactant/collector class derived from quaternary ammonium compounds. In the slice, these reagents are noted for their pH-stable cationic behavior and applicability in relatively alkaline flotation conditions.

Anionic flotation reagent class used as a collector in mineral separation. The slice notes its use in separating barite from scheelite concentrates and in fluorite recovery under mildly acidic conditions.
Modified petroleum-derived flotation reagent obtained by sulfation/sulfonation of a kerosene fraction. The slice states that it is used, together with other collectors, in coal flotation.
A petroleum-hydrocarbon-based anionic collector class used in non-sulfide ore flotation. The text notes that it is insensitive to hard water and is commonly used together with apolar oils.

A hydroxamate-type collector family that forms complexes with Ti, Nb, Ta, and Sn. It is used in flotation of pyrochlore, loparite, perovskite, and cassiterite ores and is valued for relatively simple synthesis and high selectivity.

A salt form of primary amine collectors used to improve handling and flotation performance when free amines are poorly soluble in water. The text notes that cationic collectors are often applied as acetate and hydrochloride salts.

A pulp-industry byproduct composed mainly of higher fatty acids and resin acids. It is used as an effective collector for non-sulfide minerals and oxides and can replace oleic acid in several flotation circuits.

The saponified form of tall oil used as a collector in flotation. It is especially effective for non-sulfide minerals and oxide ores, including apatite, barite, scheelite, and certain iron-, manganese-, and tin-bearing ores.

A collector obtained by oxidizing kerosene with air oxygen at elevated temperature in the presence of a catalyst. Its collecting action is attributed to organic acids formed during oxidation and it is used in coal flotation.

A mixture of saturated normal monocarboxylic acids produced by catalytic oxidation of solid petroleum paraffins. In flotation they are usually applied as sodium soaps and may be combined with other anionic collectors.

A water-soluble soap collector derived from oleic acid. It is a standard carboxyl-type collector in non-sulfide mineral flotation, but its consumption increases sharply in the presence of calcium ions due to insoluble calcium oleate formation.

A class of carboxyl collectors with cyclic hydrocarbon radicals, used similarly to oleic acid in flotation. The text presents them as another technically important reagent family for non-sulfide minerals.
A phosphate mineral commonly recovered by flotation using fatty-acid-type collectors. It is cited in the text as one of the non-sulfide minerals effectively floated by tall oil and related reagents.
A niobium-bearing mineral processed with hydroxamic-acid collectors. The text mentions it as a target mineral for the IM-50 family because of its ability to form complexes with Nb and related metals.
A complex rare-metal mineral whose flotation can be improved by hydroxamic-acid collectors. It is listed among the ores for which the IM-50 reagent family is considered promising.
A calcium titanate mineral referenced as a target for hydroxamic-acid flotation chemistry. Its surface interactions with complexing collectors are important in selective rare-metal ore processing.

Iron-bearing raw material processed by flotation to improve concentrate quality or remove silicate gangue. The text cites iron ores as one of the non-sulfide ore groups floated by fatty-acid-type collectors.
Manganese-bearing ore processed by flotation in non-sulfide mineral circuits. It is named in the text as a practical target for tall oil, tall oil soap, and related carboxyl collectors.

Tin-bearing ore processed by flotation, often using carboxyl collectors and related reagents. The text lists tin ores among the industrial mineral feeds amenable to tall oil and fatty-acid collectors.

Self-assembly of surfactant molecules into micelles above a critical concentration. In the slice, micelle formation is noted for alkyl sulfonates and alkyl sulfates and is relevant to collector solubility and froth behavior.

Water-soluble sodium salts of naphthenic acids used as flotation reagents. In the slice, they are described as a soap-like collector class that can replace oleic acid and sodium oleate in some cases, but typically at higher consumption.

A flotation collector family based on carboxylic acids and their salts, including oleic acid, oleates, and naphthenates. These reagents adsorb on mineral surfaces, hydrophobize particles, and are strongly affected by pH, water hardness, and micelle formation.

A heated flotation-pulp regime used to improve handling of long-chain carboxylic collectors that are solid or poorly dispersible at room temperature. In the slice, temperatures around 40тАУ60 ┬░C or higher are recommended for such reagents to enable dosing and flotation performance.

A class of anionic flotation reagents whose hydrophilic group contains oxygen-based functionality and whose hydrophobizing ion is an anion. In the slice, this class is presented as the main collector family for non-sulfide minerals, but with lower selectivity than sulfhydryl collectors.

A less common subgroup of oxyhydryl flotation collectors whose solidophilic group is based on sulfate-type anions. The text contrasts these reagents with carboxyl collectors and notes that they are used much less frequently in practice.

A sulfur-containing sulfhydryl collector family used in flotation, especially for sulfide ores. In the slice, dithiophosphates are used as a performance benchmark, and organic acids/m soaps are stated to be substantially weaker collectors than this class.

Weak organic acids of the aliphatic series, characterized in the slice by dissociation constants on the order of 10^-4 to 10^-5. In flotation, they form poorly performing carboxyl-type collectors and hydrolyze strongly in water, especially as alkali-metal salts.

A sulfur-containing flotation collector family used primarily for sulfide minerals. These reagents adsorb on sulfide surfaces and promote hydrophobicity, making them a central reagent class in sulfide ore flotation.

A dry, powder-form dithiophosphate collector family prepared from phosphorus pentasulfide and aliphatic alcohols followed by neutralization. In flotation practice, these reagents are water-soluble collectors without frothing action and are used for selective sulfide flotation.

A dithiophosphate collector family derived from phenols, especially cresols. The text notes that these reagents can act both as collectors and frothers, but their use requires caution because of toxicity and burn hazards.

A widely used water-soluble dithiophosphate collector, described in the text as the most common alcohol aerofloat. It has no frothing properties and is applied in alkaline pulps for copper minerals and sphalerite to minimize pyrite contamination.

A sulfur-containing collector family structurally related to xanthates and considered promising for sulfide ores. In the slice, dialkyldithiocarbamates are described as colorless, slightly water-soluble liquids with a density close to 1 g/cm3.

An insoluble, oil-like disulfide formed by oxidation of xanthate ions. Dixanthogenide can form on sulfide mineral surfaces and contribute to hydrophobization, including via chemisorption or physical fixation on heterogeneous surface sites.

An electrochemical surface process in which adsorbed xanthate ions are oxidized to dixanthogenide under oxidizing conditions in flotation pulp. This mechanism is important on conductive sulfide minerals and strongly affects collector fixation and hydrophobic layer formation.

A sulfurizing reagent used as a precursor in the synthesis of dithiophosphates from alcohols or phenols. In the text, it is the key starting material for producing aerofloat-type collectors before neutralization to the active salt form.

Water-soluble xanthate salts of alkali metals used as flotation collectors. They dissolve readily in water, can be precisely dosed into pulp, and are especially effective for sulfide-mineral flotation.

Xanthate salts of heavy metals that are practically insoluble in water and more hydrophobic than alkali-metal xanthates. Their low aqueous solubility and higher affinity for apolar media are associated with strong collector behavior and surface fixation on sulfide minerals.

Degradation process in which xanthates hydrolyze in aqueous media to alcohol, alkali, and carbon disulfide. It is accelerated by moisture, elevated temperature, and acidic conditions, reducing collector stability and requiring dry, sealed storage.

Volatile sulfur-containing reagent used as a key precursor in xanthate synthesis from alcohols and alkali. It also appears as a hydrolysis/decomposition product of xanthates, making it central to xanthate chemistry and storage stability.

Strong alkali used in the preparation of xanthates from alcohol and carbon disulfide. It provides the alkaline medium required for xanthate formation and, when present as free alkali, can promote xanthate decomposition during storage.

A water-soluble alkali-metal xanthate collector used in sulfide flotation. In the slice, it is compared with sodium oleate and shown to be weaker on oxidized sulfide surfaces, reflecting the strong dependence of xanthate fixation on surface oxidation state and hydration.

An inorganic oxyanion formed during oxidation of sulfide minerals. In flotation systems, sulfate-ion formation is associated with surface oxidation, dissolution of oxidized species, and changes in surface hydration and collector adsorption behavior.

Synergistic flotation effect arising when two collectors are used together instead of separately. The combination can increase recovery and flotation rate while reducing total reagent consumption, especially when a stronger and a weaker collector are paired.

Process KPI expressing the fraction of valuable mineral transferred into the froth concentrate. In the slice, recovery is used to compare the effect of individual collectors and their combinations on galena flotation.

Operational KPI describing the amount of flotation reagent required per unit of ore or concentrate. Lower reagent consumption is one of the main economic advantages of using collector combinations in flotation practice.

Structural property of a collector molecule that controls hydrophobization, adsorption kinetics, and water solubility. In the slice, shorter or longer hydrocarbon chains change the effectiveness of xanthates and the rate at which flotation equilibrium is reached.

Low-molecular xanthate collector used in sulfide flotation. In the slice, it is one of the reagents tested alone and in combination with dithiophosphate, where mixtures improved galena recovery relative to the single reagent.

Higher-chain xanthate collector used for sulfide mineral flotation. The slice shows that its performance can be further improved by combining it with dithiophosphate, although the synergy depends on reagent ratio and mineral surface state.

Dithiophosphate collector reagent used together with xanthates in galena flotation tests. The slice notes that, by itself, it is a relatively weak collector for lead sulfide, but it can enhance flotation when combined with xanthates.

A flotation conditioning strategy in which coarse and fine particles are treated with different collector concentrations before flotation. The slice states that this approach accelerates adsorption-layer formation, improves flotation performance, and reduces collector consumption.

Structural characteristic of a collector hydrocarbon tail in which the carbon chain contains branches rather than a linear arrangement. In flotation collectors, branching changes dispersion interactions, adsorption-layer stability, and the ability to disrupt hydrated surface layers, which can alter collecting strength.

The lowest-member xanthate collector in the homologous series discussed in the slice. It is used as a reference reagent when evaluating how hydrocarbon chain length affects collector strength, water interaction, and flotation efficiency.

A straight-chain xanthate collector used as an intermediate homologue in the chain-length comparison described in the slice. Its flotation strength is discussed relative to methyl, ethyl, butyl, and amyl xanthates.

A branched-chain xanthate collector mentioned in the slice as being stronger than the corresponding normal propyl xanthate in some cases. It illustrates how chain branching can improve collector action by more effectively disrupting hydrated surface layers near the mineral surface.

A flotation collector class that does not dissociate into ions in the pulp and often has limited solubility and dispersibility in water. In the slice, such collectors are described as interacting with mineral surfaces slowly, frequently as droplets, because their transport and wetting behavior are controlled by physical dispersion rather than ionic adsorption.

The minimum contact time between an air bubble and a mineral particle required for attachment to occur. In flotation, it is used as a practical measure of how quickly a critical adsorption layer forms and whether the particle will report to the froth under given reagent conditions.

The amount of reagent fixed per unit mineral surface area, often discussed relative to an idealized monomolecular layer. The slice states that flotation can be effective at densities well below complete monolayer coverage, but that performance improves as coverage becomes sufficiently dense and more uniformly distributed.

Degree to which a collector is distributed evenly across the mineral surface rather than localized on only a subset of active sites. In the slice, more uniform surface coverage is associated with better flotation results at the same overall reagent loading.

A flotation reagent class whose active species are anions and which adsorb on mineral surfaces via electrostatic attraction, chemisorption, or specific surface reactions. In the slice, this class includes xanthates and related reagents that are central to sulfide and oxide flotation.

A mineral class containing carbonate groups in the crystal lattice. Such minerals are typically strongly hydrated and show relatively low natural floatability compared with sulfide minerals because their surfaces interact strongly with water dipoles.

A mineral class containing sulfate groups in the lattice. These minerals generally have polar, water-active surfaces and, like carbonates, tend to have lower natural floatability than corresponding sulfide minerals.

Interfacial mechanism in which electrons move between the mineral surface and species in the pulp, including collector anions. In flotation, the direction and favorability of electron transfer are controlled by the mineral's electronic structure and Fermi level, and they determine collector fixation and surface activation.

Equilibrium constant describing the dissolution or precipitation tendency of a sparingly soluble compound. In flotation, it is used to judge whether a collector-metal reaction product can form a stable surface phase on the mineral and thereby affect collector fixation.

A limited oxidation state of a sulfide surface that creates chemically active sites while preserving enough sulfide character for flotation. In the slice, such slight oxidation is described as a necessary prerequisite for successful xanthate flotation, whereas excessive oxidation suppresses recovery.

An inorganic oxidizing salt used in flotation as a suppressing regulator for sulfide minerals. In the slice, it is cited as a treatment that increases hydrophilicity of galena surfaces and prevents stable bubble attachment.

The ion of an anionic flotation collector that carries the hydrophobic hydrocarbon fragment and adsorbs on the mineral surface. In the text, this role is assigned to the collector anion, while the counterion remains in the bulk liquid and does not participate in hydrophobization.

The polar functional part of a collector molecule responsible for chemically binding the reagent to the mineral surface. Its structure controls selectivity, chemical activity, and the strength of collector fixation in flotation.

A chemically bound surface phase formed on a mineral during interaction with flotation reagents. Such surface compounds are typically monomolecular, highly specific, and can be more strongly attached than simple physically adsorbed layers.

A three-dimensional layer of reaction products or adsorbed substances formed on a mineral surface. The text treats such films as independent phases that can change surface composition, wettability, and flotation response, and can sometimes be mechanically removed to expose a fresh surface.

The degree to which a collector or surface process acts preferentially on one mineral phase over others. In the slice, selectivity is governed by the solidophilic group and by the specificity and strength of surface bonding.

Net electrical charge or charge distribution at a mineralтАУliquid interface. In flotation, surface charge governs electrostatic attraction and repulsion, affects the structure of hydrated layers, and strongly influences bubble attachment to particles.

Refractory transition metal used in the slice as an example of a surface that can strongly chemisorb oxygen. It serves to illustrate that chemisorbed surface species may be bound with energies comparable to the cohesion of the substrate.

A gaseous carbon oxide mentioned as the form in which chemisorbed oxygen on coal can be removed under room-temperature conditions. In the slice, it appears as a product associated with the desorption of strongly bound surface oxygen species.

A flotation scheme in which inorganic electrolytes influence froth formation and particle recovery, especially for coal, naturally hydrophobic minerals, and soluble salts. The method relies on electrolyte-induced changes in interfacial water structure and bubble stability.

A mechanism in which ions are depleted from the near-surface layer and shift into the bulk solution rather than accumulating at the interface. In the slice, this produces an oriented hydration layer with elevated surface tension that stabilizes bubbles.

The merging of colliding gas bubbles into larger bubbles, which reduces bubble dispersion and destabilizes froth. The text describes frothers as suppressing this process, while excess apolar substances can intensify it.

A dispersion mechanism in which a reagent is broken into finer droplets or more uniformly distributed in water, improving its collecting action. The slice notes this effect for fatty acids and pine oil in flotation pulp.

Pressure difference associated with curvature of the bubble surface, which controls the force required to detach a bubble from a mineral particle. Frothers reduce this pressure indirectly by lowering interfacial free energy.

A nonpolar aromatic hydrocarbon used in the slice as an example of an apolar additive that can induce stable froth when combined with a polar liquid. It illustrates the positive effect of small amounts of apolar compounds on foaming.
A low-molecular alcohol used in the slice as an example of a liquid that does not form stable froth on its own. Its foaming behavior changes when an apolar hydrocarbon such as benzene is added.

A natural frothing reagent used in flotation and cited in the slice as a material whose collecting action can be improved by peptization of dispersed collector species. It is a common flotation frother with surface-active behavior.

A soluble calcium sulfate mineral present in ores and coal that can affect foaming behavior in flotation pulps. Its dissolved ions contribute to electrolyte effects on bubble stabilization and froth formation.

A common soluble salt mentioned as an impurity that influences foaming in flotation systems. Dissolved sodium chloride modifies electrolyte concentration and can alter hydration-layer structure and bubble stability.

Industrial synthesis route used to obtain alcohol-based flotation reagents from unsaturated hydrocarbons. In the slice, it is the production method for IM-68, derived from hydrocarbons present in cracking gasoline.

Frother reagent composed mainly of aliphatic C6-C8 alcohols with a predominantly branched structure. It is used directly or as a 1тАУ5% aqueous emulsion stabilized by alkyl sulfates or nonionic surfactants, and is applied in iron ore flotation.

term.primary: Monobutyl Ethers of Lower Polyethylene Glycols

concepts.definition: A frother reagent family consisting of monobutyl ethers of lower polyethylene glycols. The text describes these reagents as effective foaming agents for collective flotation of polymetallic ores.

A byproduct mixture containing octyl alcohols, alcohols with more than eight carbon atoms, acetals, aldehydes, and a small amount of butyl alcohol. Its main active component is 2-ethylhexanol, and the mixture is used in coal flotation.
A low-cost frothing reagent mixture of saturated and unsaturated C4-C8 alcohols, produced as a byproduct of synthetic rubber manufacture. It is poorly soluble in water and is used in coal flotation.
A cyclic alcohol used as a frother in selective flotation of polymetallic ores. The slice notes that it forms a brittle foam and has practically no collector properties.
A non-toxic phthalic acid ester used as a flotation reagent and presented as a replacement for toxic cresol. It is applied in flotation of polymetallic copper-bearing ores.

A complex reagent mixture in which 60тАУ80% of the components are dioxane and pyran alcohols. It is obtained during rectification of dimethyldioxane in isoprene production and is used in flotation of ores and coals because of its low cost and availability.

A frother composed of monobutyl ethers of polypropylene glycols. It is produced by reacting propylene oxide with the corresponding alcohol and is used in flotation of some copper-molybdenum ores, where it shows very strong frothing action.

Polyethylene glycol ether surfactants based on mono- and dinonylphenols. The slice describes OP-7 and OP-10 as good dispersants of collectors in flotation of non-sulfide minerals and as frothers used in iron ore flotation.
A secondary alcohol widely used as a high-efficiency frother in ore and coal flotation. The text emphasizes its high selectivity and its positive effect on concentrate quality and recovery.

Flotation application focused on upgrading iron-bearing ores by controlling froth properties and reagent selectivity. The slice explicitly mentions several frothers and dispersants used in iron ore flotation circuits.
Flotation application used for coal cleaning and recovery of carbonaceous material. The slice identifies several low-cost frothers and byproduct reagents as suitable for coal flotation.

Flotation process used to recover multiple valuable minerals from complex polymetallic feeds. The text refers to this application when discussing combined frothers, selective frothers, and collectorтАУfrother interactions.
Specialized flotation application for copper-molybdenum ores. The slice notes that the OP-SCB frother reagent is useful in some copper-molybdenum flotation circuits.

An inorganic cyanide reagent used in flotation as a depressant and complexing agent. In the slice, it binds dissolved copper ions, lowers their concentration in solution, and thereby promotes desorption of copper xanthate from mineral surfaces.

An inorganic cyanide depressant and complexing reagent used in flotation. It acts similarly to sodium cyanide by binding dissolved copper ions and shifting surface equilibrium away from collector fixation.

The anionic form of cyanide present in alkaline solution. In flotation pulp it complexes copper ions, and its speciation is strongly controlled by pH because it is converted to hydrocyanic acid in acidic media.

A weakly dissociated acid formed by hydrolysis/protonation of cyanide in water. In the slice, its formation at lower pH removes free cyanide ions from solution and deactivates the depressing action of cyanides.

Acid-base transformation in aqueous pulp where cyanide ions are converted into hydrocyanic acid and hydroxide is generated. This shifts cyanide speciation with pH and reduces the concentration of flotation-active CN- at lower pH values.

An inorganic sulfide depressant used in flotation. The slice describes it as a reagent that suppresses many sulfide minerals and sulfidized oxidized minerals by introducing sulfide and hydrosulfide species into the pulp.
A divalent sulfur anion present in sulfide-reagent solutions and pulp. In the slice, it acts as a potential-determining ion for sulfide minerals and helps displace collector ions from the surface.

The singly charged sulfur anion generated in sodium sulfide solutions. It is described as strongly surface-active on sulfide minerals and capable of displacing collector ions, thereby depressing flotation.

A hydrophilic lead-containing surface phase formed on galena under alkaline conditions. Its formation replaces xanthate on the mineral surface and reduces floatability by increasing surface hydration.

A sparingly soluble lead salt that can form on galena surfaces during oxidative or chromate-related suppression. It contributes to hydrophilic surface films and creates conditions for further exchange with chromate ions.

A poorly soluble lead chromate phase that can form on galena in the presence of dichromate/chromate ions. In the slice, it is part of the hydrophilic surface film responsible for depressing galena flotation.

A mixed lead surface compound produced during chromate suppression of galena. The slice describes these species as more hydrophilic surface products that occupy uncovered areas and lower the mineral's floatability.

A hydrophilic zinc-containing precipitate formed in alkaline pulp from zinc sulfate-containing systems. In the slice, its fine particles adhere to sphalerite and suppress flotation by coating the mineral surface.

An inorganic reducing/suppressing reagent used in sulfide flotation. In the slice, it is noted to have a suppressing action similar to cyanide-related reagents, although with somewhat poorer technological results.

An inorganic sulfur-containing reagent used as a depressant in flotation. The text states that its mechanism is analogous to cyanide in suppressing certain sulfide minerals, but it gives inferior process performance.

An alkaline reagent mentioned as having a suppressing effect similar to cyanide in selective flotation. It can also dissolve zinc hydroxide, thereby altering depression behavior in zinc sulfide flotation circuits.

An inorganic zinc salt used in flotation as a suppressing reagent, especially for zinc sulfide minerals. In the slice, it is used together with cyanide to intensify depression of sphalerite and reduce cyanide consumption.

A sparingly soluble zinc cyanide compound formed when cyanide reacts with zinc sulfate in pulp. The text describes its selective precipitation on sphalerite surfaces as one possible reason for zinc mineral depression.

A precious metal mentioned in the context of cyanide flotation suppression. Cyanides can dissolve gold and thereby lower gold recovery into the froth product, which is an important practical limitation.
Selective flotation process for lead-zinc polymetallic ores. The slice discusses cyanide and zinc salt regimes for depressing sphalerite, pyrite, and some copper sulfides during this application.

Selective flotation route for copper-zinc polymetallic ores. In the slice, cyanide-based and cyanide-free suppressing regimes are discussed for improving separation of copper minerals from zinc sulfides.

Flotation application for sulfide molybdenum ores containing molybdenite together with other sulfides. The slice notes that sodium sulfide can depress the accompanying sulfides while leaving molybdenite recoverable.

A safety and environmental constraint associated with cyanide use in flotation. The slice emphasizes that cyanides require restricted handling because of their acute toxicity, release of HCN in acidic media, and impact on plant safety and reagent selection.

An alkaline pulp condition required for safe and effective cyanide use in flotation. The slice states that free alkali shifts cyanide hydrolysis to the left, suppressing HCN release and improving reagent efficiency.

An alkaline silicate reagent widely used as a depressant and regulator in flotation. It hydrophilizes quartz and many silicate minerals, and under some conditions can also desorb collectors from carbonate and non-sulfide mineral surfaces.

Strongly hydrated colloidal entities formed from hydrolyzed silicate species in sodium silicate solutions. Their adsorption on mineral surfaces is described as a key factor in suppressing flotation by increasing hydrophilicity and weakening collector action.

An alkaline inorganic reagent used together with sodium silicate to increase depressant selectivity in flotation. It raises pulp alkalinity and helps condition mineral surfaces before subsequent separation.

A class of polyvalent-metal salts used in combination with sodium silicate to improve selective depression. In the slice, they are reported to enhance the separation of closely behaving minerals such as calcite and fluorite, and scheelite from calcite or apatite.

An inorganic electrolyte containing the sulfate ion. The text notes that it suppresses flotation of sulfate minerals such as barite, celestine, and anglesite because it shares a common ion with the mineral lattice.
An inorganic electrolyte containing the sulfate ion. It is cited together with sodium sulfate as a reagent that depresses flotation of sulfate minerals by the common-ion effect.

A calcium carbonate mineral frequently used as a reference gangue phase in selective flotation. In the slice, it is one of the minerals whose separation from fluorite or scheelite is improved by sodium silicate-based depression schemes.

A strontium sulfate mineral whose flotation is suppressed by sulfate-containing electrolytes through the common-ion effect. It is listed together with barite and anglesite as a sulfate mineral affected by sodium and potassium sulfates.

A lead sulfate mineral whose flotation is suppressed by sulfate electrolytes via the common-ion effect. The slice groups it with barite and celestine as a sulfate-bearing mineral sensitive to sulfate salts and sulfuric acid.

A copper carbonate mineral mentioned as being activated by very small doses of sodium silicate in flotation. It is relevant as an oxide/carbonate copper mineral whose surface chemistry can change markedly under regulator treatment.

A lead carbonate mineral noted as becoming activatable by low sodium silicate dosages in flotation. It is cited alongside malachite and apatite as a mineral whose surface response to silicate regulators can be nonmonotonic.

A strongly hydrophilizing phosphate reagent used as a depressant in flotation. It belongs to the class of phosphates that suppress the flotation of nearly all minerals by intensively hydrating the surface.
A polyphosphate reagent with strong hydrophilizing and depressing action in flotation. It is used as part of the phosphate regulator family that suppresses the flotation of many minerals.
A polyphosphate reagent that strongly hydrophilizes mineral surfaces and depresses flotation. The slice groups it with other phosphate regulators as an effective inhibitor of many mineral systems.

A nonionic polymeric organic depressant used in flotation. It selectively suppresses certain mineral surfaces by adsorption and hydrophilization, and belongs to the traditional class of high-molecular organic reagents.
A nonionic carbohydrate polymer used as an organic depressant in flotation. It is part of the classical high-molecular selective depressant family and acts by modifying surface wettability.

A plant-derived tannin reagent used as a high-molecular organic depressant in flotation. It is listed among selective reagents that became important after the second world war for targeted mineral suppression.

A protein-based organic depressant used in flotation. It belongs to the historical class of high-molecular selective reagents that can suppress specific minerals by adsorption and surface hydrophilization.

A nonionic cellulose derivative used as a polymeric organic depressant. The slice lists it among nonionic reagents that contain hydroxyl or carbonyl polar groups and act selectively on mineral flotation.
An anionic cellulose derivative used as a selective organic depressant. It contains carboxyl groups and is employed to hydrophilize and suppress flotation of specific mineral surfaces.
An anionic polymeric organic depressant derived from lignin sulfonation. In flotation it is used as a selective inhibitor that modifies surface charge and wettability of certain minerals.

A class of high-molecular organic reagents that suppress flotation without carrying ionizable groups. The text identifies this class as containing hydroxyl- and carbonyl-bearing polymers such as starch and oxyethyl cellulose.

A class of high-molecular organic reagents that suppress flotation through anionic polar groups such as carboxylate or sulfonate functionalities. In the slice, carboxymethyl cellulose and lignosulfonates are given as examples.

A cationic polymer containing amino groups that can adsorb on mineral surfaces and act as an organic depressant. In flotation, it suppresses recovery by blocking collector adsorption and increasing surface hydrophilicity.

A cationic biopolymer with amino-containing polar groups used as an organic depressant. It binds to mineral surfaces through strong interfacial interactions and can hinder subsequent collector attachment.
Cationic polymeric reagents containing pyridine-based polar groups. In flotation, they belong to the class of organic depressants that can adsorb on mineral surfaces and reduce floatability.

An amphoteric polymer containing both anionic and cationic polar groups, sometimes with additional nonionic polar functionality. In flotation it behaves as an organic depressant that strongly hydrophilizes mineral surfaces.
A protein-based amphoteric organic depressant used in flotation systems. Its polar functional groups adsorb on mineral surfaces and contribute to hydrophilization and suppression of collector action.

A class of polymeric organic depressants containing cationic polar groups such as amines or pyridinium groups. These reagents adsorb on mineral surfaces, can partly resist desorption, and suppress flotation by increasing hydrophilicity and preventing collector fixation.

A class of organic depressants that contain both anionic and cationic polar groups. They adsorb strongly on mineral surfaces, often behaving similarly to cationic depressants, and suppress flotation by hydrophilizing the interface and blocking collector adsorption.

A surface-treatment process that increases the affinity of a mineral surface for water. In flotation, hydrophilization is a key suppressing action because it reduces collector attachment and weakens bubble-particle adhesion.

Removal of adsorbed collector molecules from the mineral surface by depressants, washing, or competitive interfacial interactions. It decreases surface hydrophobicity and is one of the main causes of flotation suppression described in the slice.

An alkaline reagent widely used in flotation as a low-cost pH regulator and pyrite depressant. It is commonly dosed as milk of lime, and its use shifts pulp chemistry toward conditions that suppress pyrite flotation and alter surface hydration.

Operational KPI describing the mass of lime required per unit mass of ore processed. In flotation practice it is a major cost and control parameter, with the text citing typical consumption on the order of 1.5тАУ2 kg/t.

Selective flotation application focused on recovering pyrite from oxidized or alkaline-conditioned ores. The slice describes oxygen conditioning and acid treatment as ways to restore pyrite floatability after strong alkaline suppression.

Fundamental flotation mechanism in which a mineral particle attaches to or nucleates on a gas bubble to form a stable particle-bubble aggregate. This aggregate rises to the froth layer and constitutes the elementary act of flotation.

A mixed iron sulfide-sulfate surface compound formed on pyrite during interaction with oxygen, water, and acidic treatment. It is a flotation-active surface phase that can react with sulfhydryl collectors and is relevant to activation of oxidized pyritic ores.

Formation of a gas bubble from dissolved gas preferentially at a solid surface rather than in the bulk liquid. In flotation, this surface-assisted nucleation is energetically easier on hydrophobic mineral particles and becomes more probable when pressure is reduced or the solution is near gas saturation.

A flotation attachment route in which a small bubble first forms on the mineral surface, then a larger bubble contacts and coalesces with it, and the merged bubble finally carries the particle into the froth. This sequence lowers the energetic barrier for attachment compared with direct collision-driven sticking.

Threshold thickness of the water film separating a particle and a bubble at which the hydration layer becomes unstable and attachment accelerates sharply. Below this critical distance, the free energy of the film decreases rapidly and bubble-particle contact becomes effectively spontaneous.

Fluid-flow interaction between a mineral particle and a gas bubble that governs their approach, collision probability, and the relative motion in the narrow gap before attachment. In flotation, this interaction can either deflect fine particles around the bubble or promote near-contact conditions that allow adhesion to occur.
