The removal of liquid from the thin water layer separating a mineral particle from a bubble surface. This drainage step is required for attachment in flotation and becomes faster when the particle surface is more hydrophobic or when collision conditions more effectively disrupt the hydration layer.

The minimum bubble-nucleus radius at which a gas embryo becomes stable rather than redissolving into the liquid. It is controlled by capillary pressure and the balance between internal bubble pressure and the external gas pressure during flotation gas release.

State of an aqueous system in which the dissolved gas concentration exceeds equilibrium at the current pressure. In flotation by gas release, higher supersaturation increases the probability of bubble nucleation on mineral particles but can reduce selectivity if pressure drop is too abrupt.

Growth mechanism in which a newly formed gas nucleus increases in size by diffusion of dissolved gases from the surrounding solution into the bubble. In flotation, this growth can turn an initially too-small nucleus into a bubble capable of lifting mineral particles into the froth.

Mechanism of aggregation between dissimilar dispersed phases, here most relevant to the attachment of very fine mineral particles to bubbles when direct three-phase contact is difficult. In flotation, heterocoagulation becomes important for ultrafine particles and can substitute for ordinary collision-driven attachment.

Threshold particle diameter at which the balance between buoyancy, detaching forces, and attachment strength determines whether a mineral grain can remain on a bubble and float. In the cited analysis, this critical size depends on bubble radius, particle density, and the acceleration of detachment forces.

Composite aggregate formed by coalesced mineral particles and gas bubbles in flotation pulp. Such aggregates can arise under strong hydrophobicity, adequate aeration, and weak agitation, and they behave as a distinct floating material phase during separation.

A flotation regime in which mineral particles are transferred to the froth as aeroflocs, i.e. aggregates of particles and multiple bubbles. The text describes it as a high-efficiency mode that is favored by adequate gas release, weak agitation, fine bubble dispersion, and prior removal of excess collector from the pulp.

A flotation method based on the release of dissolved gases when pressure is reduced, generating bubbles in situ. It is highlighted as especially effective for fine suspensions because bubble nucleation and particle capture are promoted without relying only on particle-bubble collisions.

Aggregation of mineral particles into flocs or loose clusters, distinct from coagulation by the role of surface layers and interparticle bridging. In flotation pulp, flocculation changes suspension stability and can modify the probability of bubble attachment and transport of particles to the froth.

The maximum particle size that can still be effectively recovered by flotation under given hydrodynamic and reagent conditions. The text notes that increasing this limit has strong industrial value because it improves throughput in grinding and downstream separation and allows coarser concentrates to be produced.
Formation of a fine-slime layer on a larger mineral particle surface. Such coatings block direct bubble attachment, increase hydrophilicity, and suppress flotation of the underlying mineral.

Adsorption of fine slime particles onto air bubbles, creating a hydrophilic shell around the gas phase. This reduces attachment of normally floatable particles to the bubble surface and lowers flotation efficiency.
Carryover of fine particles into the froth with water and bubbles without true particle-bubble attachment. It contaminates concentrate with gangue and is especially important for very fine slimes.

Flotation approach in which coarse hydrophobic or hydrophobized particles are added as carriers for fine mineral particles. The fines adhere to the carrier surface and become easier to float as larger aggregates.
Pre-flotation removal of fine slime fractions from pulp. Desliming reduces collector loss, lowers gangue entrainment, and improves selectivity for the remaining coarse fraction.

A reagent class that disperses fine particles and prevents the formation of slime coatings on minerals and bubbles. In flotation practice, peptizers are used to reduce harmful aggregation and improve separation selectivity.
Fine-grained hydrophilic aluminosilicate material commonly present as slime gangue in flotation pulps. Clays can adsorb collectors, form slime coatings, and suppress flotation of valuable minerals.

Random thermal motion of very fine particles suspended in liquid. In flotation pulps, it increases collision opportunities for ultrafine particles and becomes significant when gravitational settling is weak.

A separation method in which a chosen reagent flocculates only specific fine particles while others remain dispersed. In the slice, it is used for fine slimes to enlarge the recoverable object before subsequent decantation or flotation.

A synthetic water-soluble polymer used as a flocculant in fine-particle processing. In the slice, it is one of the flocculants evaluated for selective flocculation, but it is less selective than hydrolyzed polyacrylonitrile for some sulfide minerals.

A hydrolyzed synthetic polymer used as a selective flocculant. The slice reports that, among tested flocculants, it showed sufficiently selective action for some sulfide minerals, making it suitable for fine-slime selective flocculation.

A fine-grained iron ore feed rich in siliceous and iron-oxide components. In the slice, finely ground taconite is used as an example of an ore beneficiated by selective flocculation before downstream flotation.

A kinetic parameter describing the intrinsic flotation rate of a mineral under fixed conditions. In the cited model, its value is independent of how much material was floated earlier, which makes it useful for comparing flotation behavior across time intervals.

An empirical exponent in flotation rate equations such as d╬╡/dt = K(1тИТ╬╡)^n. It reflects the apparent order of the flotation-rate change and is used to fit non-ideal kinetics where the rate varies during the process.

An experimental method in which flotation is carried out in successive fractions to obtain time-resolved recovery data. The resulting curves are used to estimate specific flotation-rate coefficients and diagnose changes in kinetics during the process.

A flotation regime with excess bubbles and an available bubble surface that is not yet significantly blocked by attached particles. Under these conditions, the attachment of new particles is not hindered by prior mineralization of the bubbles.

The fraction of a bubble surface covered by attached mineral particles. The slice notes that flotation kinetics begin to change when occupancy becomes critical, with reported thresholds around 20тАУ50% of the bubble surface.
An enrichment mechanism in flotation froth caused by preferential removal of gangue particles from the froth phase. It improves concentrate grade after the initial particle-bubble transfer.

A froth failure mode in which the foam breaks too easily and may produce splashing or spray above the froth surface. The slice links this state to excessive frother concentration and to poor froth handling during flotation.

The velocity at which pulp moves through flotation chambers. It affects the balance between flotation rate and residence time, and excessive velocity can reduce overall recovery despite faster transport.
The time that pulp or particles remain in a flotation cell. It is a key process condition because it controls how long minerals can contact reagents and bubbles before leaving the machine.

Drainage-driven contraction of a foam structure in which liquid redistributes and flows out of the inter-bubble films and channels. In flotation froths, syneresis accelerates thinning of separating water layers and contributes to bubble coalescence and froth decay.

Water-soluble or partly soluble organic froth-stabilizing additive cited as an example of the first group of foam stabilizers. It can modify adsorption layers at the gasтАУliquid interface and influence foam stability in flotation systems.

Surface-active natural compound cited as an example of a reagent that forms colloidal or semi-colloidal solutions in water. In flotation, saponins adsorb on bubble surfaces and can form rigid adsorption structures that increase froth stability.

Poorly water-soluble apolar hydrocarbon liquid used as a flotation reagent and froth modifier. In the slice, kerosene is described as a representative of the third group of reagents that can destabilize or suppress certain foams by coating bubble surfaces.

Degree to which flotation froth is loaded with attached mineral particles and mineral films on bubble surfaces. Higher froth mineralization generally indicates stronger particle-bubble attachment and is an important indicator of froth structure and concentrate quality.
Post-flotation operation that collapses separated froth after it leaves the cell. It is used to release entrained water and gangue and to obtain a handleable concentrate or tailings stream.

Controlled spraying of water onto the froth surface to increase drainage between bubbles and remove attached gangue particles. In flotation practice, it improves concentrate grade by weakening the adhesion of waste particles to the froth.

An apparatus in which pulp aeration, selective mineralization of bubbles, froth formation, froth retention, and froth discharge are carried out. Flotation machines are designed to maximize recovery and selectivity while minimizing energy use.

Mechanical device used to remove the upper layers of flotation froth from the cell surface. It is used to selectively withdraw concentrate-bearing froth or, in some circuits, to remove the entire froth layer including lower, coarser mineral-rich strata.
Electrical energy consumed per unit mass or volume of pulp processed. In flotation machine design, this KPI should be minimized to improve process economics and reduce operating cost.

Bubble-based separation method in which surface-active ions or molecules adsorb on rising bubbles and are transported into the froth. It is used to remove organic contaminants, including detergent-like compounds, from aqueous streams.

Synthetic anionic surfactant family cited as a wastewater contaminant removed by foam fractionation. These compounds are persistent detergent species that adsorb strongly at bubble interfaces and can be concentrated into froth.

Hybrid separation process in which hydrophobic compounds are concentrated in an organic liquid layer covering an aerated aqueous solution. It combines flotation and liquid-liquid extraction while typically consuming less extractant than conventional extraction.

Recovery route in which dissolved metal species are first converted into fine, sparingly soluble precipitates and then floated by gas bubbles. The method is used for metal recovery from water and can achieve high extraction levels when the precipitate has suitable surface properties.

Two-step flotation route in which metals are first precipitated and then rendered floatable with collectors. It is applied to metal-bearing wastewaters and allows selective recovery after staged precipitation by pH control.

Rotating aeration element in a flotation machine that disperses air into fine bubbles and creates local turbulence and pressure drops. It is central to bubble formation, cavitation, and mixing in the pulp.

Formation and collapse of vapor or gas cavities in low-pressure zones of a rapidly moving liquid, especially near impeller blades. In flotation, cavitation contributes to air breakup, bubble generation, and intensified gas release from the pulp.

Operating regime of the pulp characterized by fine-scale turbulent eddies that increase bubble-particle collision frequency and promote gas release. It is described as favorable for bubble mineralization while still allowing selective attachment.

Aeration method in which an air stream is broken into fine bubbles by mechanical action of the liquid flow and rotating aerators. The process is enhanced by turbulence and cavitation, increasing the gas-liquid interfacial area for flotation.

Electrochemical decomposition of water into hydrogen and oxygen at the cathode and anode under an applied electric field. In electroflotation, it serves as the bubble-generation route for pulp aeration and determines bubble size and gas yield under controlled current passage.

The additional voltage beyond the thermodynamic decomposition voltage required to initiate electrolysis at real electrodes. In electroflotation, it depends on electrode material, temperature, and surface roughness, and it governs the practical energy cost and onset of gas bubble generation.

State of flotation pulp characterized by bubble size, bubble number, and the uniformity of their distribution. The text states that pulp aeration controls flotation rate, technological performance, and, to some extent, reagent consumption.

Characteristic size of gas bubbles dispersed in flotation pulp. The slice notes that mechanical flotation machines at optimal frother dosage typically produce bubbles of about 0.4тАУ0.8 mm, whereas pneumatic machines produce larger bubbles of about 2тАУ3 mm.
Statistical distribution of bubble sizes in flotation pulp. The text describes it as a curve with a pronounced maximum, analogous to the size distribution of ground ore particles.
Amount of air dispersed and retained in flotation pulp. In the slice, it is used together with air-flow rate and distribution uniformity to evaluate aeration quality and process efficiency.
Degree to which air bubbles are evenly distributed throughout the pulp volume. The text identifies this as a key component of aeration quality, beyond the simple amount of air supplied.

Time that introduced air remains within the flotation pulp before escaping. The slice notes that better dispersion and greater resistance to bubble rise can increase this time, reaching values up to about 20 s.
Volume of the pulp region containing dispersed air bubbles. The text states that machine productivity under otherwise equal conditions is directly proportional to this volume.

Operational indicator describing the volume of air introduced into the flotation machine per unit time or per unit pulp volume. The slice treats it as a common but incomplete measure of aeration because it does not capture bubble dispersion, distribution, or residence time.

Sampling method in which special devices are used to take pulp samples from multiple points across the machine volume, followed by statistical processing. It is described as a more informative way to quantify average air content and air-distribution uniformity than simple air-flow measurement.

Imaging method used to determine bubble-size characteristics in flotation pulp. The text mentions its use with a periscope or a transparent water-filled tube, while also noting possible errors from sampling and bubble coalescence.

Flotation machine in which an impeller mechanically sucks in and disperses air into the pulp. The slice identifies this as one of the principal machine classes and notes that it typically produces fine bubbles under optimal frother dosage.
Flotation machine combining mechanical impeller aeration with pneumatic air supply. The text classifies it as a hybrid design that uses both mechanical mixing and forced air introduction.

Flotation machine in which pulp is aerated by blowing air directly into it rather than by impeller suction. The slice notes that these machines are typically of trough type and generally produce larger bubbles than mechanical machines.

Flotation machine in which gas bubbles are generated by reducing pressure above the pulp and releasing dissolved gas. The text lists this as a distinct machine class based on pressure decrease in the pulp system.
Flotation machine in which bubbles are generated by electrolysis of water. The slice classifies electroflotation as a separate machine family based on bubble generation by electric current.

Flotation machine with a single elongated chamber in which pulp flows longitudinally from feed to tailings discharge. The text notes that froth is removed along the side edges and that the pulp level is uniform along the trough.

Flotation machine in which a long chamber is divided by partitions that do not reach the bottom or pulp surface, creating separate compartments with aeration devices. The pulp level is maintained uniformly across the chamber system.

Flotation machine composed of separate chambers, often coupled together, with devices for regulating the pulp level in each chamber. The slice describes this as a common design for mechanical and pneumomechanical flotation machines.

Single-chamber flotation machine installed between a grinding mill and a classifier. The text notes that it is used to float coarse-ground pulp and recover liberated mineral grains directly from the grinding circuit.
Pneumatic flotation machine with a chamber in the form of a column. The slice lists it as one of the main machine configurations used for air introduction and separation.

A flotation machine design in which a grid or similar distributor creates a particle-rich, upward-moving fluidized zone above the impeller. Repeated bubbleтАУparticle contacts in this 'boiling' layer increase flotation rate and allow recovery of coarser particles than conventional cells.

A gas-lift transport device that uses injected air to raise pulp or slurry through a vertical channel. In flotation machines, it is used to circulate pulp and assist bubble generation and particle transport in the working zone.

A hybrid flotation machine combining mechanical impeller aeration with an airlift circulation loop. The design is used to intensify pulp circulation, stabilize the particle-rich fluidized zone, and improve bubble mineralization and overall flotation efficiency.

Flotation machine design that uses a finger-type impeller and a stator to disperse compressed air into pulp. The configuration promotes intense local turbulence, fine bubble generation, and self-discharge of froth without a separate froth skimmer.

Experimental flotation machine that uses vibration-assisted aeration to disperse air and release dissolved gases in the pulp. The vibrating disk creates zones of reduced pressure and enhanced circulation, improving bubble formation and flotation activity.

Widely used chamber-type flotation machine with a rod rotor-stator aeration system. It provides high pulp aeration at low specific energy consumption and can operate with low pulp depth while maintaining effective froth removal.

Flotation machine family characterized by alternative impeller geometries, including inclined-disk designs. In the slice, the design evolution is associated with stronger pulp mixing, better aeration, and a reduced specific energy consumption.

Throughput normalized to the occupied floor area of a flotation machine or flotation section. It is used to compare equipment layouts and machine designs where compactness and plant footprint are important economic factors.

Industrial flotation application focused on recovering potassium salts from ore feeds. The slice notes that flotation machines of this type are used in potash processing because they provide effective aeration and froth handling for coarse and granular feeds.

A flotation aerator that creates a low-pressure axial zone inside a small chamber while pulp is introduced tangentially to form a fast swirling flow. Air is dispersed by turbulent pulsations and by gas release from solution, making this design relevant for high-intensity pneumomechanical flotation.

A rotating truncated-cone aerator with surface protrusions that pumps pulp upward along the cone surface and disperses compressed air through turbulent pulsations and pressure drops. The design promotes fine bubble formation and intense wall-layer turbulence, and is presented as a promising flotation aeration scheme.

A deep trough-type pneumatic flotation machine with vertical air tubes and a tall pulp column that increases aeration by repeated pressure reduction during upward circulation. It produces very fine bubbles, a high aerated fraction, and a froth overflow suited to high-throughput separation.

A flotation-based separation mode in which the entire feed pulp is introduced onto a froth layer and particles are partitioned by their ability to remain in the froth or drain back through it. Separation occurs mainly through secondary concentration in the froth phase, often with froth washing to improve selectivity.

A flotation machine designed for froth-separation operation, where pulp is fed onto a stable froth layer and hydrophobic particles are retained while hydrophilic particles drain away. Such machines typically include froth-washing capability and are used for coarse particle recovery and fine slime removal.

A jet-type aerator that mixes compressed air with injected water under pressure and discharges the resulting emulsion into the pulp. The design creates strong local dispersion and abundant fine bubbles, and is highlighted in the Apatit flotation machine.

A pneumatic flotation machine that uses jet nozzles and ejector action to disperse air into the pulp. This design intensifies aeration by high-velocity fluid injection and is relevant for high-activity bubble generation in industrial flotation circuits.

Mineral beneficiation application focused on recovering apatite from ore using flotation. The slice identifies this application as one where high-aeration machines with jet-type aerators can produce a large, easily mobile froth fraction.

A potash ore material composed mainly of sylvite and halite, used here as a feed for froth-separation circuits. The text notes that deep froth-separation machines are particularly effective for removing fine clay slimes from sylvinite pulp and for handling coarse potash particles.

A flotation machine in which aerated pulp or water is first pressurized to form a gas-supersaturated liquid and then discharged into a chamber at near-atmospheric pressure. The pressure drop triggers gas release as fine bubbles, making the machine suitable for fine dispersed suspensions and wastewater treatment.

An electroflotation apparatus in which the liquid passes directly through the electrode zone while bubbles are generated by water electrolysis. This configuration is used mainly for low-throughput purification of liquids and wastewater, where continuous flow and in situ gas generation are advantageous.

A semi-submerged rotating drum installed along the overflow edge of a flotation cell to pick up the lower layers of froth and discharge them into a launder. It reduces the back-mixing of floated particles into the pulp, increases recovery, and can improve concentrate density.

A dosing device used to supply flotation reagents accurately and uniformly into the process pulp. Uniform reagent feeding is important for stable flotation performance, reproducible selectivity, and controlled reagent consumption.

A conditioning vessel where pulp is mixed with reagents before or during flotation to ensure sufficient contact time and surface conditioning. Contact tanks help stabilize reagent adsorption and improve process consistency.

A special-purpose flotation machine designed to recover coarse valuable mineral particles using hydraulic trap features that retain or concentrate heavier grains. It is used where standard cells are less effective for coarse particle capture.

Design constraint for trough-type flotation machines specifying that the length of a single trough should not exceed 10 m. It reflects practical limits of pulp transport and machine layout in industrial flotation circuits.

Dosing equipment used to supply powdered flotation reagents such as lime. In the text, this feeder class is treated as a small-scale analogue of feeders for fine crushed solids and is now used less often because lime is commonly introduced as milk of lime.

Dosing equipment for mobile liquid flotation reagents such as oleic acid, xanthate solutions, and soaps. The text notes that this group includes several constructions, selected according to reagent flow properties and dosing accuracy requirements.

Dosing equipment for relatively viscous flotation reagents such as oils. The text describes a feeder design in which the reagent film is carried by a rotating wheel and removed by scrapers for delivery into the process.

A feeder for dry powdered reagents that uses a slowly moving conveyor belt as the hopper bottom. The discharge rate is controlled by a gate opening, allowing continuous dosing of reagent powder into the process.

A dry-reagent feeder in which material is discharged from a cylindrical hopper onto a slowly rotating plate. A fixed scraper meters the powder into a chute, and the feed rate is adjusted by scraper position and plate clearance.

A liquid-reagent feeder that uses a periodically lifted and tilted skip cup to fill from a reservoir and pour into the process. The text emphasizes its reliability and widespread industrial use for reagent dosing.

A liquid-reagent dosing device with freely suspended cups mounted on a rotating disk. The cups fill in the reagent bath and empty into a chute when they are mechanically tilted, enabling adjustable feed delivery.

A high-accuracy reagent feeder that doses a fixed portion of solution each cycle from a measuring chamber. The text describes it as suitable for automatic regulation based on feed rate and ore composition.

A membrane-type reagent feeder designed for oxidizing or easily crystallizing solutions such as liquid glass, sulfate solutions, and cyanide-containing liquors. The text highlights its sealed operation without air contact and its suitability for contaminated reagents.

A feeder intended for clean reagent solutions such as xanthates or sodium sulfide, in which reagent is introduced from below and exits through an upper outlet. Flow is regulated by periodically opening and closing valves or nipples.

A feeder for viscous reagents such as oils, where a partially immersed rotating pulley carries a thin reagent film that is then scraped off into a chute. The text presents it as a practical design for stable dosing of oily reagents.

A high-capacity liquid-reagent feeder derived from a skip-feeder design and intended for large reagent flow rates. The text states that its discharge is controlled by bucket inclination and that it is used for large-scale reagent dosing in flotation plants.

Degree to which reagent concentration, solids density, and particle size are uniformly distributed throughout the pulp. In contact tanks, high homogeneity indicates effective mixing and is critical for stable reagent conditioning and flotation performance.
Mass concentration of the solid phase in a flotation pulp. It controls viscosity, mixing intensity requirements, and the effectiveness of reagent contact with mineral surfaces.
Particle-size distribution of the solid phase in an ore or pulp. It strongly affects mixing, slime formation, conditioning behavior, and the flotation response of the feed.

Mass-transfer mechanism by which reagents move through the thin liquid film adjacent to a mineral surface. In flotation conditioning, it governs how quickly reagents reach the surface and become fixed or desorbed.

Mechanism in which mixing or particle motion removes oxidized or contaminated surface layers and exposes fresh mineral surface. In flotation, surface renewal can restore reagent interaction and improve collector attachment.

Chemical alteration of primary mineral surfaces by reacting with dissolved salts or metal-bearing solutions, leading to new surface films of different composition. Such changes can substantially modify flotation properties by changing wettability and collector affinity.

Carbonate mineral often present as gangue in flotation feeds. It is important because its presence can make separation of fluorite, phosphate, and other industrial minerals significantly more difficult.
Copper sulfide mineral that can form as a secondary surface phase during mineral alteration. In flotation, it is relevant because it can coat primary sulfides and change their collector response.
Silver sulfide mineral mentioned as a secondary surface phase in ore alteration. It is relevant to flotation because its formation on other sulfides can modify surface chemistry and hydrophobicity.
Copper carbonate mineral included among oxidized copper minerals. It is important in flotation as an example of a hydrophilic oxidized phase that requires specialized collectors or activation.
Zinc carbonate mineral that belongs to the class of oxidized zinc ores. It is commonly difficult to float and often requires activation or sulfidization.
Lead molybdate mineral listed among oxidized lead-bearing minerals. Its flotation behavior is governed by the chemistry of its polar surface and its response to suitable collectors.
Aluminum oxide mineral included in the group of oxides and silicates. In flotation classification, it represents a strongly polar mineral surface with low natural floatability.

Hydroxide mineral of aluminum that belongs to the oxide/mineral class with strong water affinity. It is significant in flotation because its surface typically requires intensive conditioning or selective reagents.
Titanium dioxide mineral used as an example of an oxide mineral in flotation classification. Its surface properties make it relevant to selective separation from silicate gangue.
Aluminosilicate mineral included among silicates and aluminosilicates in flotation classification. It is relevant as a mineral with polar surfaces and difficult natural floatability.
Manganese dioxide mineral listed among oxide minerals. It is a representative strongly polar mineral whose flotation response is typically controlled by collector chemistry and surface activation.
Clay mineral that frequently appears as fine hydrophilic gangue. In flotation circuits it contributes to slime formation, reagent consumption, and poor selectivity.

Hydrated copper silicate mineral included among oxidized copper-bearing minerals. It is important in flotation because its surface is strongly hydrated and often requires special treatment for recovery.
Historical term for zinc silicate/carbonate minerals occurring as oxidized zinc ore. In flotation, calamine is significant because it is difficult to recover without activation or sulfidization.
Native metal included in the classification of flotation feed materials. It is relevant as an example of a naturally occurring metal phase that may occur with sulfides and other ore constituents.
Native metal included among naturally occurring metals in flotation classification. It is relevant as a noble metal phase associated with complex ore assemblages.

A hydrated borate mineral occurring in evaporite assemblages and mentioned in the slice as one of the readily water-soluble flotation feed minerals. Its flotation behavior is governed by high solubility and strong interaction with aqueous media.

A hydrated calcium borate mineral listed in the slice among highly water-soluble evaporite-type minerals. It is relevant to flotation of soluble salts, where medium composition strongly affects separation behavior.

Sodium chloride mineral and a classical highly water-soluble evaporite. In flotation of soluble salts, halite is a representative phase whose behavior depends strongly on the composition of the mother liquor.
Potassium chloride mineral and a common potash ore component with high solubility in water. The slice cites sylvite among minerals floated in saturated brines and other concentrated salt media.

A hydrated potassium-magnesium salt mineral occurring in potash deposits. It is included in the slice as a readily soluble mineral whose flotation is controlled by brine composition and salt concentration.

A potassium-magnesium sulfate mineral from evaporite and potash ores. In the slice it serves as an example of a highly soluble salt mineral floated in saturated mother liquors, where the medium composition is critical.

Size-reduction operation applied before flotation to break intergrowths and bring particles to a floatable size range. It controls liberation of valuable minerals, but excessive comminution creates slimes and raises energy consumption.

Separation of ground material into size fractions during comminution circuits. In flotation preparation, classification is used to remove fine slimes and return coarse fractions to grinding for better liberation control.

Excessive comminution that produces too many ultrafine particles and slimes, often after the ore has already reached adequate liberation. It reduces flotation selectivity, increases reagent consumption, and complicates downstream solid-liquid separation.

Fraction of mineral grains that are freed from intergrowths after comminution. It is a key determinant of flotation separability because insufficient liberation leaves composite particles that respond ambiguously to reagents.

Highly concentrated aqueous salt medium in equilibrium with dissolved solids. In the slice, flotation of soluble salts in mother liquors is described as strongly dependent on solution composition and may involve partial mineral transformations during separation.

Saline process water enriched in chloride, sulfate, sodium, magnesium, and calcium ions. In flotation, seawater can strongly affect reagent performance, especially for fatty acids and soaps, while cationic collectors are typically less sensitive to hardness salts.

A major inorganic anion in natural waters and process liquors. Chloride contributes to ionic strength and solution composition, which can alter flotation behavior indirectly through changes in interfacial chemistry and reagent activity.
A common carbonate-system anion in natural waters. It participates in pH buffering and can therefore influence mineral solubility and flotation conditions through changes in pulp alkalinity.

A divalent carbonate-system anion present in natural waters and alkaline pulps. Carbonate ions affect buffering capacity, mineral solubility, and the formation of surface precipitates or reaction films during flotation.

A common monovalent cation in natural and industrial waters. Sodium ions contribute to electrolyte composition and are part of the background ionic environment that influences flotation, especially in saline or recycled water systems.

A common monovalent cation in process and natural waters. Potassium ions contribute to ionic strength and are part of the background water chemistry that can affect reagent behavior and surface charging in flotation.

A hardness ion that strongly affects flotation chemistry. Calcium ions can precipitate fatty acids as insoluble calcium soaps and can also interact with other reagents, reducing selectivity and increasing reagent consumption.
A hardness ion commonly present in natural and seawater. Magnesium ions influence flotation by changing water hardness, reagent solubility, and the stability of interfacial films on mineral surfaces.

Natural organic acids present in bog waters and stagnant ponds. In flotation systems, humic acids act as colloidal organic impurities that can modify surface chemistry, adsorb on minerals, and interfere with reagent performance.

Insoluble iron-containing precipitates formed when iron ions are removed from solution by alkali addition. In flotation, iron hydroxides are used to suppress unwanted iron-ion activation and to reduce the adverse influence of dissolved iron species on reagent selectivity.

Dissolved silica species present in natural waters and process liquors. Silicic acid and related siliceous species can appear as colloidal impurities and influence flotation by modifying pulp chemistry and the behavior of mineral surfaces.

A conditioning step in which pulp is intentionally saturated with air, especially oxygen, before flotation. It is used when dissolved oxygen improves flotation behavior or when controlled oxidation is needed to optimize recovery and froth formation.

A staged reagent-introduction strategy in which a collector or regulator is fed into the process in several portions rather than all at once. In flotation this improves contact with freshly exposed mineral surfaces, allows dosing into different machine zones, and can reduce reagent consumption while improving selectivity.

A process failure in which concentrated sodium silicate solutions deposit on pipe walls and progressively block reagent lines. It increases maintenance burden, disrupts dosing accuracy, and is a practical limitation on using highly concentrated liquid-glass solutions.

An operating constraint requiring that process waters be cleaned and returned to circulation instead of being discharged. In flotation it reduces fresh-water demand, but it also forces the process regime to tolerate dissolved salts and other recycled-water impurities.

Economic KPI describing the total cost of processing one ton of ore, including reagents, energy, labor, depreciation, and related operating expenses. The slice uses this metric to compare flotation plants and shows that higher throughput lowers unit cost.

Operational KPI expressing the amount of process water consumed per unit mass of ore. In flotation it is a major operating-cost and water-balance parameter, and full water recycle lowers it from several cubic meters per ton to near 1.0тАУ1.5 m3/t.

Investment KPI describing the upfront cost of buildings, machinery, and plant infrastructure required to build flotation capacity. In the slice it is discussed per unit annual ore throughput and is one of the key economic measures of plant design.

The first flotation operation in a scheme, used to separate a target group of minerals from the feed. In polymetallic flowsheets, several main flotations may be used sequentially for different valuable components.
A repeat flotation operation applied to primary concentrates or concentrate-branch products to raise concentrate grade. It removes entrained gangue and improves the quality of the final concentrate.
A flotation operation applied to tailings or tail-branch products to recover residual floatable mineral and reduce losses to tailings. It serves as a cleanup step after primary flotation.

A flotation scheme in which several valuable components are recovered together into a single bulk concentrate. It is used when joint recovery is easier than immediate separation of individual minerals.

A flotation scheme in which valuable minerals are recovered one after another, typically starting with the easiest-to-float component. It is used when different minerals can be separated directly by differences in floatability.

A scheme in which several valuable minerals are first recovered together as a bulk concentrate and then separated from each other after additional conditioning or regrinding. It is especially useful for finely intergrown ores.
A flotation flowsheet organized as alternating grinding and flotation stages. This arrangement extracts liberated mineral particles progressively as intergrowths are broken down.
Additional grinding applied to concentrates, tailings, or intermediate products after an initial flotation pass. It is used to increase liberation before further flotation or separation.

A processing configuration in which intermediate products are returned to the initial flotation cycles for reprocessing. It is preferred when the recycle stream does not negatively affect pulp conditions or separation efficiency.

A processing configuration in which intermediate products are treated in a dedicated flotation loop rather than being returned to the main circuit. It is used when recycle streams contain excess slimes, reagents, or dilution that would impair the main process.

An industrial control system used to monitor, regulate, and optimize flotation-plant operations through centralized continuous measurement, local automatic control loops, and automated decision logic. In the slice, it is described as the basis for stable process control, measurement processing, and control of technological units and mechanisms.

The mineralogical and petrographic makeup of a coal or ore feed, including the relative proportions of mineral matter and petrographic constituents. In the slice, it is a key factor controlling flotation behavior together with surface oxidation and gangue inclusion characteristics.

The extent to which particle surfaces have been oxidized before or during flotation. The slice states that surface oxidation strongly influences coal floatability by changing hydrophobicity and the response to collectors and frothers.

A flotation mechanism in which apolar collector droplets attach to the surface of floatable particles rather than acting only through dissolved species. In coal flotation, it is described as the main mode of action of apolar collectors.

Dispersion of apolar flotation reagents into fine droplets in the pulp, often assisted by surface-active substances. In the slice, emulsification improves the distribution and collecting action of oils and other apolar reagents in coal flotation.

An operational and safety requirement that toxic flotation reagents be stored separately in dedicated rooms and handled separately during crushing, dissolution, and dosing. The slice highlights this as a strict safety rule for cyanides and sodium sulfide in flotation plants.

A flotation reagent fraction obtained from natural gas condensate with a boiling cut above 200 ┬░C. It is a nonpolar hydrocarbon mixture composed mainly of paraffinic, naphthenic, and aromatic components and is used as an apolar collector in coal flotation.

A family of apolar aromatized flotation reagents with elevated collecting activity. They are used in coal flotation as alternatives to kerosene and can reduce reagent consumption due to stronger selective wetting of hydrophobic coal surfaces.
A petroleum-derived apolar hydrocarbon reagent used in coal flotation as a collector. It acts primarily through selective wetting and droplet fixation on hydrophobic carbonaceous particles.

A flotation reagent obtained as an oxidation product of acetaldehyde and a byproduct of acetic acid and acetic anhydride production. It belongs to the group of surface-active frothing reagents used in coal flotation.

A sedimentation and thickening unit used to concentrate slurry and remove clarified water from process streams. In flotation circuits it is used for water recovery and for handling fine slimes before or after flotation.

A centrifugal hydraulic classifier used to separate slurry into coarse and fine fractions by particle size and density. In flotation preparation circuits it is applied for classification and slime removal prior to conditioning and flotation.

Mineral beneficiation application aimed at recovering graphite from flake, dense-crystalline, and cryptocrystalline ores. The process relies on graphite's natural hydrophobicity and is strongly affected by surface oxidation, impurities, and the presence of fine liberated flakes.

Beneficiation application for recovering native sulfur from sulfur-bearing ores. The process is used to produce sulfur concentrate for downstream autoclave melting, while rejecting gangue and minimizing contamination by slimes and carbonate minerals.

Beneficiation application for separating talc from associated magnesite, chlorite, chromite, and oxidized talc-containing feeds. It exploits talc's high natural hydrophobicity and often requires combined frother and apolar collector action.

Inorganic phosphate reagent used in flotation as a regulator and slime-dispersing agent. In sulfur ore processing it helps peptize fine slimes, suppress bitumen-bearing gangue, and improve concentrate grade and sulfur recovery.
Thermal processing step in which sulfur concentrate is melted in an autoclave after flotation. It is used to obtain lump sulfur while enabling recycle of smelting tailings back to flotation.

Special flotation process in which quartz, calcite, and similar minerals are separated in a liquid sulfur medium. Water droplets act as carrier and collecting phase for mineral particles, making the process distinct from conventional aqueous flotation.

Hydrophobic organic mixture present in some ores and gangue rocks. In flotation it can impart unintended floatability to waste material, contaminate concentrates, and require suppression by dispersing regulators.
Mass fraction of non-combustible mineral residue in coal, graphite, sulfur concentrates, and related products. It is a key quality indicator for beneficiation performance and product marketability.

Operational KPI expressing ore throughput or concentrate output per worker over a given time period. In flotation plants it reflects automation level, process stability, and overall production efficiency.

Mineral beneficiation domain focused on recovering gold, silver, and platinum-group metals from ores and placers. In the slice, it is used as a processing route both for direct noble-metal recovery and for preconcentration before cyanidation or smelting.

Hydrometallurgical extraction method that dissolves gold and some associated noble-metal species with cyanide solutions. The slice describes flotation as being combined with cyanidation either before or after flotation, and also notes that cyanidation can remove cyanide-sensitive gold-bearing fractions from ore.

Physical beneficiation method based on density differences between mineral particles. In the slice, it is used ahead of flotation to recover coarse gold particles and reduce the load on subsequent flotation circuits.

Separation method that exploits differences in magnetic susceptibility of ore components. The slice mentions it as a common pre-flotation operation in gold-bearing ore preparation, used together with crushing, grinding, and classification.

Magnesium carbonate mineral that may remain in talc-flotation tailings and can be recovered as a separate product. In the slice, magnesite is floated from talc tailings using fatty-acid-type collectors to obtain a marketable concentrate.
Highly hydrophobic talc variety with platy morphology. The slice states that it floats readily with pine oil, indicating stronger natural floatability than fibrous talc.

Talc variety with fibrous morphology and lower natural hydrophobicity than sheet talc. The slice notes that its flotation requires cationic collectors, showing that mineral habit can strongly affect collector choice.

Iron arsenic sulfide mineral commonly associated with gold in sulfide ores. The slice mentions it as one of the host sulfides in which fine gold is disseminated and from which gold can be recovered by flotation.

Pyrite containing dispersed gold inclusions or gold-bearing surface phases. In the slice, auriferous pyrite is important because flotation after cyanidation can recover gold associated with this sulfide mineral.

Strong alkali used to raise pulp pH in flotation circuits. The slice notes that increasing pH with sodium hydroxide strongly suppresses gold flotation, reflecting the sensitivity of surface chemistry and collector fixation to alkalinity.

Sulfur-containing organic collector family used in noble-metal flotation. The slice lists mercaptans among the reagents that can recover clean gold surfaces together with xanthates, dithiophosphates, and fatty-acid soaps.

Group of noble metals including platinum, palladium, rhodium, iridium, osmium, and ruthenium. The slice treats them as noble-metal constituents of ores, often occurring in sulfide forms or as fine inclusions in other sulfide minerals.

Mineral class containing telluride compounds of noble metals such as gold and silver. In the slice, telluride minerals are described as highly hydrophobic and readily floatable with apolar collectors, making them difficult to depress.

Iron sulfide mineral that oxidizes rapidly in flotation pulp and often occurs together with copper sulfides and pyrite in sulfide ores. Its surface state is highly sensitive to dissolved oxygen and pH, which strongly affects collector response and separation behavior.

Soluble sulfur oxyanion formed during oxidation of sulfide minerals in aqueous pulp. Its presence indicates partial sulfide oxidation and accompanies changes in pulp chemistry that can alter flotation behavior.

Amount of oxygen dissolved in the flotation pulp liquid phase. It controls the rate of sulfide oxidation and can be intentionally raised by pre-aeration to improve selective separation of sulfides with different oxidation kinetics.

Mechanism in which one sulfide mineral oxidizes faster than another, creating differences in surface chemistry and floatability. In the slice, this effect is used to facilitate separation of copper and iron sulfides by controlled oxygen exposure before flotation.

Ore feed dominated by copper sulfide minerals such as chalcopyrite, chalcocite, bornite and covellite, often with pyrite as an associated phase. In the slice, these ores are treated as the main industrial copper feedstock whose flotation response depends strongly on oxidation state, liberation and slime content.

Disseminated copper ore in which chalcopyrite and pyrite are the principal sulfide minerals, often accompanied by molybdenite and gold. The slice describes it as a feed typically processed by collective copper-molybdenum flotation and subsequent selective separation.

Copper-bearing sandstone ore characterized by fine disseminations of chalcocite and bornite and comparatively low pyrite content. The slice notes that this ore type can yield rich copper concentrates, especially when staged flotation and separate sands/slimes treatment are used.

Flotation pulp condition with lowered pH. In the slice, acidic medium restores floatability of suppressed pyrite by removing iron hydroxide films and is used to modify sulfide surface chemistry during reactivation.

A flotation flowsheet in which coarse sand fractions and fine slime fractions are conditioned and floated separately. The slice presents this scheme as especially effective for disseminated copper ores with aggregated sulfide intergrowths and strong slime effects.

Thermal pretreatment of a copper-molybdenum concentrate carried out with lime at elevated temperature. It strips xanthate-like surface coatings from chalcopyrite and pyrite, oxidizes the sulfide surfaces, and loads them with calcium species to suppress their flotation before molybdenite recovery.

A thermal conditioning step in which sulfide minerals lose flotation activity while molybdenite retains its floatability. In the slice, it is applied to dewatered chamber product before a final molybdenite flotation stage.

Inorganic oxidizing/complexing reagent used as a depressant in sulfide separation circuits. The slice notes its use for suppressing copper sulfides and pyrite in molybdenum and copper-molybdenum flotation schemes.

Bulk flotation concentrate containing chalcopyrite, pyrite, and molybdenite that requires subsequent selective separation. It is the intermediate product on which oxidative roasting, depressant treatment, and molybdenite flotation are carried out.

Ore type dominated by sulfide minerals, often with fine intergrowths of copper sulfides and pyrite. Such ores are difficult to beneficiate and typically require either direct selective flotation or collective flotation followed by regrinding and separation.

Highly alkaline pulp condition used to depress pyrite with lime in copper-pyrite and related sulfide flotation schemes. At this pH, pyrite is driven to tailings or suppressed in the collective concentrate before later reactivation or separate recovery.

Moderately alkaline pulp condition used to float pyrite after partial neutralization of excess lime. In the slice, this regime supports pyrite recovery with increased butyl xanthate dosage or collective flotation of copper sulfides and pyrite.

Classic selective flotation scheme for lead-zinc ores in which sphalerite is depressed with cyanide, or cyanide plus zinc sulfate, in alkaline medium. Lead is floated first; the suppressed ZnS is then activated with copper sulfate and floated in a second stage.

Selective lead-zinc flotation method that uses sodium sulfite, sodium thiosulfate, or sulfur dioxide together with zinc sulfate to depress sphalerite. It avoids cyanide-based drawbacks, but its applicability is more limited across ore types.

Selective flotation method for lead-zinc ores based on depression of zinc sulfide with sodium sulfide. It is a narrower special-case route than cyanide-based schemes and is applied only to certain ore compositions.

Selective separation route for collective sulfide concentrates in which sodium sulfide is used to desorb collectors from mineral surfaces before Pb-Zn separation. The desorbed collector is removed from the process together with the desorbent by filtration, decantation, or thickening.

Porous carbon adsorbent added to flotation pulp to capture dissolved gold from solution and reduce metal losses. In cyanide-based lead-zinc flotation, it is used to suppress gold dissolution losses and can then report to the lead concentrate.
Gaseous reagent used in some lead-zinc flotation schemes together with zinc sulfate to suppress sphalerite. It acts as a non-cyanide depressant option in selective flotation of zinc-bearing sulfides.

A selective flotation regime in which chromate or dichromate reagents are used to suppress galena and other lead-bearing sulfides. It is applied when lead is the dominant valuable component and the objective is to prevent lead from reporting to the froth.

A flotation separation method for lead-containing sulfide ores in which galena is depressed by a combination of ferrous sulfate and sulfite ions. The method is notable because it suppresses even copper-activated galena that is resistant to chromate-based depression, while allowing chalcopyrite to float.

An iron(II) sulfate reagent used in flotation as a depressant or conditioning additive. In the slice, it is combined with sulfite ions to suppress galena, including copper-activated galena, during selective lead separation.

An inorganic oxyanion used in flotation reagent systems as a reducing and depressing species. In the slice, sulfite ions are paired with ferrous sulfate to suppress galena and improve leadтАУcopper selectivity.

The principal nickel-bearing sulfide mineral in many copper-nickel ores. Its flotation behavior is intermediate between chalcopyrite and pyrrhotite, and it is often strongly affected by lime, copper-sulfate activation, and the degree of intergrowth with other sulfides.

A beneficiation domain focused on separating copper and nickel sulfide minerals, typically chalcopyrite, pentlandite, and pyrrhotite. The process often combines collective flotation, staged selection, magnetic separation, and reagent schemes tailored to differences in oxidation and activation behavior.

A solidified metallurgical product composed mainly of copper and nickel sulfides. In the slice, it is the feed for flotation separation into a copper-sulfide froth product and a nickel-sulfide chamber product.

A pyrometallurgical separation application used to divide copper and nickel sulfide phases in solidified matte. The process replaces older metallurgical separation routes and is carried out after crushing and grinding in alkaline pulp with xanthate and frother.
The main industrial bismuth sulfide mineral discussed in the slice. It floats readily with sulfhydryl collectors over a wide pH range and is part of the bismuth-ore separation problem.
A bismuth-bearing lead sulfide mineral with flotation behavior similar to bismuthinite. It is relevant in the selective separation of bismuth minerals from associated sulfides.
The elemental metallic phase of bismuth, mentioned in the slice as a flotation-recoverable component in bismuth-bearing ores. Its flotation response is close to that of bismuth sulfide minerals.
A strong mineral acid used in hydrometallurgical treatment of bismuth-bearing flotation products. In the slice it is applied for leaching bismuth from low-grade concentrates before cementation.

A water-soluble molybdenum compound formed after oxidative roasting and leaching of molybdenum-containing flotation products. It is the soluble intermediate from which molybdenum is subsequently recovered.
An insoluble molybdenum-bearing precipitate obtained after separating sodium molybdate from the leach residue. In the slice it is the recoverable solid form used for further metallurgical processing.

A hydrometallurgical recovery method in which dissolved metal is precipitated from solution by a more active reducing phase. In the slice it is used after hydrochloric-acid leaching to recover bismuth from solution.
The principal antimony sulfide mineral in the slice. It is readily floated after activation with heavy-metal salts and can also be floated by apolar collectors when unactivated.
The main mercury sulfide mineral, described as highly floatable with sulfhydryl collectors and, in the unoxidized state, even with frother alone. It is a key feed mineral in mercury-ore flotation.

The elemental metallic phase of mercury, noted in the slice as recoverable by flotation from metallurgical products. Its flotation behavior is similar to native gold and depends strongly on pulp chemistry and oxygen content.

A water-soluble ammonium salt used in selective sulfide flotation as a protective reagent for pyrite. In the slice it helps separate arsenopyrite and pyrite by allowing pyrite to float while arsenopyrite is depressed by lime.
A heavy-metal salt used for activation of stibnite before sulfhydryl-collector flotation. In the slice it belongs to the class of heavy-metal activators that improve antimony mineral recovery.
An oxidizing reagent used to pre-oxidize sulfide concentrates before selective flotation. In the slice it is especially effective in combination with dichromate for separating cinnabar from stibnite.

A beneficiation application focused on selective recovery of bismuthinite, native bismuth, and related bismuth sulfides. The slice describes it as a sulfide flotation problem with subsequent acid leaching and cementation when concentrate quality is insufficient.
A beneficiation application for stibnite-bearing ores. The slice notes activation by heavy-metal salts, depression by cyanides, and selective separation from mercury sulfide and other sulfides.

A beneficiation application for cinnabar-bearing ores and related mercury-containing products. The slice emphasizes the strong sensitivity of mercury recovery to oxidation state, oxygen concentration, and depressant addition.

term.primary: Oxidized and Mixed Nonferrous Ore Flotation

concepts.definition: A flotation application covering oxidized and mixed copper, lead, and zinc ores. The slice presents sulfidization followed by sulfhydryl-collector flotation as the principal route for these hard-to-float feeds.

A combined hydrometallurgical-flotation route for difficult oxidized and mixed copper ores. The ore is first sulfuric-acid leached, dissolved copper is then cemented, and the remaining material is floated under acid-resistant reagent conditions.

Hydrometallurgical treatment in which oxidized metal-bearing minerals are contacted with sulfuric acid to dissolve the target metal into solution. In the slice, it is used as the first stage of the Mostovich process before cementation and flotation.

An oxidized lead mineral of the apatite group, typically containing arsenate and chloride. In the slice it appears among difficult-to-float lead minerals that may require sulfidization or other special conditioning before flotation.

A lead-bearing iron arsenate-sulfate mineral occurring in oxidized lead ores. The slice describes it as difficult to float and only partially responsive to sulfidization, making it a problematic lead mineral in flotation practice.
A lead-containing jarosite-group mineral that is not amenable to sulfidization and does not float with xanthate collectors. It represents a strongly refractory oxidized lead phase in the text.
A zinc silicate mineral occurring in oxidized zinc ores. The slice lists it among zinc minerals recovered by cationic collectors after sulfidization or other activation treatments.

A calcium molybdate mineral included in the group of polar non-sulfide minerals. It is relevant in flotation because such minerals are generally water-active and require anionic collectors and selective regulators.

An organic acid used in flotation as a depressant/regulator, especially for suppressing fluorite in barite-fluorite separation schemes. It modifies surface chemistry and weakens flotation response of the target mineral.

A carbonate-fluorite ore feed in which calcite and fluorite are closely associated and therefore difficult to separate selectively. The text treats it as a beneficiation problem requiring calcite depression by liquid glass-based and auxiliary reagent schemes.

An inorganic fluorosilicate reagent used in fluorite ore flotation as part of calcite-depressing reagent systems. It is combined with acidified sodium silicate and heavy-metal salts to reduce carbonate flotation response.

A strong mineral acid used to create an acidic conditioning medium for staged flotation of carbonatized phosphorite ores. At sufficient dosage it promotes carbonate flotation first and is later replaced by alkaline conditions for phosphate mineral recovery.
A nonionic surfactant/dispersant used in apatite flotation of sliming or metamorphosed ores. It improves reagent dispersion and selectivity and allows flotation to proceed at reduced temperature.
An iron-bearing phyllosilicate gangue mineral common in phosphorite ores. It can interfere with selective flotation and is sometimes removed by washing or combined flotation schemes.

The main phosphate-bearing mineral phase in apatite and many phosphorite ores. Its flotation behavior is governed by surface substitution chemistry and by interactions with carboxylate, sulfo-, and phosphoric-group collectors.
A sodium-potassium aluminosilicate mineral associated with Kola apatite ores. The text notes that it can be recovered as a separate concentrate from apatite tailings by reverse flotation.
A calcium titanium silicate mineral present as a useful component in apatite-bearing ores. It is mentioned among the associated minerals in the Kola ore system.
A sodium iron silicate pyroxene occurring with apatite ores. It is listed as one of the useful ore components in the beneficiation circuit.
An iron-titanium oxide mineral found in apatite ore associations. The text identifies it as one of the coexisting components present alongside apatite and nepheline.
A phosphorite feed with elevated carbonate content that is especially difficult to beneficiate by flotation. The text describes staged acid/alkaline flotation as an effective route for such ores.

A beneficiation application for phosphorite ores in which phosphate-bearing material is separated from quartz, carbonates, glauconite, and other gangue minerals. The text describes both direct anionic flotation and reverse cationic flotation routes, including staged schemes for carbonatized feeds.

A high-temperature pre-treatment used to modify mineral surface chemistry before flotation. In the text, roasting activates phosphate minerals and removes carbonates, improving selectivity in phosphorite beneficiation.
A bibliographic source on flotation machine design and classification, cited in the reference list as a foundational work on flotation apparatus and aeration systems.
A bibliographic source on selective flotation theory and practice, cited as a key reference for mineral separation selectivity and reagent strategy.
A bibliographic source on ore beneficiation testing and evaluation, cited in the reference list as a methodological foundation for flotation response assessment.

term.primary: Beneficiation of Precious Metal Ores and Placers (1971)

concepts.definition: A bibliographic source on flotation and related beneficiation routes for precious-metal ores and placers, cited as an applied reference for noble-metal processing.
A bibliographic source on foam separation, cited as a reference for bubble-based separation processes closely related to flotation.
A bibliographic source on coal flotation technology, cited as a practical reference for coal beneficiation circuits, frothers, and apolar collectors.

term.primary: Gases and Reagents on Minerals in Flotation (1950)

concepts.definition: A bibliographic source on the interaction of gases and reagents with minerals in flotation, cited as an early theoretical foundation for interfacial effects.

term.primary: Irregular Reagent Distribution in Sulfide Flotation (1958)

concepts.definition: A bibliographic source on nonuniform reagent distribution in sulfide flotation, cited for work on adsorption heterogeneity and collector localization.

term.primary: Rare Metal Ores and Placer Beneficiation (1967)

concepts.definition: A bibliographic source on beneficiation of rare-metal ores and placers, cited as an applied reference for complex mineral feeds and rare-metal flotation practice.

term.primary: Flocculation and Foam Formation in Flotation (1950)

concepts.definition: A bibliographic source on the significance of flocculation and foam formation in flotation, cited for early ideas on suspension structure and froth behavior.
A bibliographic source on flotation kinetics, cited as a reference for rate laws, time dependence, and kinetic modeling of flotation processes.
A bibliographic source on manganese ore flotation, cited as an applied reference for oxide and non-sulfide mineral beneficiation.
A bibliographic handbook source covering ore beneficiation methods and practice, cited as a general reference for flotation and related separation operations.
A bibliographic source on the natural floatability of minerals from the standpoint of structural characteristics, cited for links between crystal structure and flotation response.

term.primary: Improving Collector Efficiency in Ore Flotation (1971)

concepts.definition: A bibliographic source on improving collector efficiency in ore flotation, cited as a practical reference for reagent performance optimization.

term.primary: Chemistry of Surface Phenomena in Flotation (1977)

concepts.definition: A bibliographic source on the chemistry of surface phenomena in flotation, cited as a theoretical reference for adsorption, wetting, and interfacial reactions.
A bibliographic source on electrochemical technology in beneficiation and hydrometallurgy, cited for electrochemical aspects of flotation and mineral processing.
A bibliographic source on the relationship between semiconductor mineral properties and flotation reagent action, cited for electronic-structure effects on flotation behavior.
A bibliographic source on new developments in flotation kinetics, cited as a reference for advances in kinetic measurement and modeling.
A bibliographic source on non-sulfide mineral flotation, cited as a foundational reference for oxide, silicate, and other non-sulfide ore systems.
A bibliographic source on modifier and regulator reagents in flotation, cited for depressants, activators, and pH-regulating additives.

A monograph on flotation-based mineral beneficiation covering flotation schemes, machine design, reagent regimes, and practical applications to sulfide and non-sulfide ores. The publication serves as a foundational source for flotation process classification and industrial practice.

A set of production and economic indicators used to evaluate flotation processes and plant performance. Typical components include unit beneficiation cost, energy consumption, water consumption, throughput, and labor productivity, which together determine process efficiency and operating cost.

Bibliographic source for the ╤Г╤З╨╡╨▒╨╜╨╛╨╡ ╨┐╨╛╤Б╨╛╨▒╨╕╨╡ on precious-metals metallurgy published by M╨Ш╨б╨╕╨б in 2007. It provides the theoretical and technological framework for extraction, processing, and refining of noble metals.

Industrial and academic field focused on extraction, beneficiation, hydrometallurgy, pyrometallurgy, and refining of noble metals such as gold, silver, platinum, and platinoids. In the slice, it is presented as the subject of the textbook and includes processing of ores and intermediate products.
A group of chemically stable metals with high resistance to oxidation and other chemical attack. In the slice, this group includes gold, silver, platinum, and the platinum-group metals.
Resistance of a metal to chemical interaction with surrounding media, especially oxidation and formation of oxygen compounds. The slice identifies this as a defining property of noble metals.
Concentration of an element in natural materials or the Earth's crust. The slice gives very low mass fractions for noble metals, linking their scarcity to high economic value.
A platinum-group noble metal listed among the platinoids in the slice. It is characterized by high chemical resistance and very low natural abundance.
A platinum-group noble metal listed among the platinoids in the slice. It is one of the rarest noble metals and is noted in the text as highly chemically stable.
A platinum-group noble metal listed among the platinoids in the slice. It belongs to the highly chemically resistant metals used to define the noble-metals group.
A platinum-group noble metal listed among the platinoids in the slice. It is a rare, chemically stable metal with very low natural abundance.
A platinum-group noble metal listed among the platinoids in the slice. It is part of the rare noble-metal set distinguished by high chemical stability and scarcity.

Ability of a material to transfer heat through the lattice or electron system. In noble metals, high thermal conductivity is one of the key reasons for their use in thermal contacts, heaters, and precision technical components.

Ability of a metal to undergo plastic deformation under compressive stress without cracking. The slice emphasizes the exceptional malleability of gold, silver, and platinum, which allows them to be rolled into thin foil and formed into technical and decorative products.

Ability of a material to sustain large tensile deformation before fracture. In the text, gold, silver, and platinum are highlighted as highly ductile metals that can be drawn into fine wire for electrical, medical, and jewelry applications.

Resistance of a material to localized plastic deformation and indentation. The slice notes exceptionally high hardness for osmium, iridium, ruthenium, and rhodium, with the first three approaching quenched steel in hardness.

Temperature at which a solid transforms into the liquid state. The noble metals are contrasted in the slice by widely varying melting points, from relatively low for silver and gold to extremely high for osmium and iridium.

Temperature at which a liquid transitions to vapor under given pressure. The text uses boiling point to characterize the thermal robustness of noble metals, especially the high-temperature stability of osmium, iridium, and related platinum-group metals.
Mass per unit volume of a material. The slice uses density to distinguish the heavy and light platinum-metal subgroups and to compare noble metals as a family of very dense materials.

Ability of a surface to reflect incident radiation, especially visible or thermal radiation. In the slice, high reflectivity is listed among the functional properties that make noble metals attractive for technical and decorative applications.

Ability of a material to accelerate chemical reactions without being consumed. Noble metals and their alloys are noted in the slice as important catalysts because of their chemical stability and strong surface reactivity in selected environments.

Response of a material to an applied magnetic field, including susceptibility and magnetic ordering effects. The slice lists specific magnetic properties among the special functional characteristics that broaden noble-metal applications.

Electrochemical potential of a redox couple measured under standard conditions. The slice gives standard electrode potentials for gold, platinum, palladium, and silver as a quantitative measure of noble-metal chemical stability and electron affinity.

Resistance of a material to chemical degradation in aggressive environments. The text identifies corrosion resistance as a major reason for the widespread use of noble metals and their alloys in industrial and household products.

Highly aggressive acid mixture of nitric and hydrochloric acids used to dissolve gold. In the slice it is the reference solvent demonstrating the exceptional chemical resistance of gold and, to a lesser extent, other noble metals.

Alloy or solid solution containing mercury as one component. The slice notes that noble metals readily form amalgams when their surfaces are free of oxide films, making amalgamation an important metallurgical interaction for gold, silver, and platinum-group metals.

Manufacturing domain focused on ornaments and precious-metal products. The slice cites noble-metal alloys as a main material basis for jewelry because of their color, workability, chemical stability, and market value.

Medical-technical field concerned with fabrication of dental prostheses and related restorative components. The slice explicitly mentions gold-based alloys as standard materials for this application because of their chemical inertness, formability, and biocompatibility.

Technical application in switching and current-transfer components where stable electrical performance and corrosion resistance are critical. The slice notes gold and related noble-metal alloys as preferred materials for reliable contacts.

Industrial and laboratory application in which noble metals act as active catalyst phases. The slice lists catalysts among the major uses of noble metals because of their surface activity combined with high chemical stability.

Manufacturing domain for diagnostic and surgical tools requiring corrosion resistance and long service life. The slice identifies noble metals and their alloys as suitable materials for these devices.

Surface-protection application in which a noble metal layer is applied to another substrate to improve durability. The slice includes anticorrosion coatings among the principal technical uses of noble metals.

Gold-bearing ore hosted in bedrock formations, typically in veins and primary rock masses. It commonly contains gold together with sulfides, quartz, and other gangue minerals, and is a major feed for gravity, flotation, and cyanidation routes.

Secondary ore material formed by weathering and redistribution of primary deposits, where liberated gold particles are concentrated in sediments. Placer ores are usually easier and cheaper to mine and can contain free gold with relatively low cutoff grades.

Mass concentration of gold in ore, usually expressed in grams per ton. It is the key technical indicator used to assess ore quality and to compare the economic attractiveness of placer and lode deposits.

Minimum gold content required for profitable mining and processing under a given deposit and technology regime. The threshold depends strongly on ore type, mining method, and recovery cost, and is much lower for placers than for many primary gold ores.

Historical extraction method in which gold, silver, or platinum is selectively dissolved into mercury to form an amalgam. After washing, squeezing, and mercury distillation, a crude precious-metal product is obtained and the mercury is regenerated.

Pressure oxidation pretreatment used to decompose sulfide minerals before further precious-metal recovery. It is applied when fine or submicroscopic gold is locked in sulfides and must be liberated before cyanidation.

Thermal pretreatment in a chlorine-bearing atmosphere used to transform refractory silver-bearing minerals into forms more amenable to downstream extraction. In the slice, it is required before cyanidation of argentojarosite-containing ores.

Gold telluride mineral and one of the most common chemically bound forms of gold in ore. It is significantly more refractory than native gold and often requires oxidation or fine grinding for efficient gold recovery.

Silver chloride mineral occurring mainly in oxidized silver ores. It is relatively easy to recover by cyanidation and amalgamation because of its high reactivity compared with refractory silver sulfosalts.
Silver-antimony sulfosalt mineral forming refractory silver ore bodies. It is less amenable to direct cyanidation than simple silver sulfides and commonly requires more intensive pretreatment.

Silver-antimony sulfosalt mineral of refractory silver ores. Its complex sulfosalt structure makes direct cyanidation difficult, so it is usually considered in specialized silver beneficiation schemes.
Silver-arsenic sulfosalt mineral occurring in significant silver deposits. It is a refractory silver phase whose extraction is more difficult than that of silver chloride or argentite.
Silver-antimony mineral belonging to the class of refractory silver-bearing sulfosalts. It can form substantial ore bodies but is difficult to extract by direct cyanidation.
Complex silver-copper sulfosalt mineral. It is a refractory silver-bearing phase that does not undergo direct cyanidation without pretreatment such as roasting.
Copper-silver antimony sulfosalt mineral occurring in polymetallic silver ores. Like polybasite, it is generally refractory to direct cyanidation and is processed with specialized pretreatments.

Secondary silver-bearing iron sulfate mineral typical of oxidized ores and iron-cap zones. It is difficult to recover by flotation and becomes amenable to cyanidation only after chlorinating roast pretreatment.
Silver telluride mineral occurring in silver and gold-silver ores. It represents a chemically bound, refractory form of silver that is more complex to process than native silver or silver chloride.
Platinum-group mineral rich in copper and iron. It is one of the natural platinum-bearing phases occurring in placer and primary PGM deposits.
Natural platinum-bearing mineral containing nickel and iron as alloying components. It is part of the native platinum group and reflects compositional variability in placer platinum concentrates.
Platinum-group sulfide mineral containing platinum, palladium, and nickel. It is a naturally occurring PGM phase relevant to ore beneficiation and precious-metal concentration.
Native platinum mineral with elevated palladium content. It belongs to the compositional family of platinum-group native alloys found in placer deposits.
Native platinum mineral enriched in iridium. It is one of the compositional varieties of platinum-group native alloys described in placer platinum concentrates.

Naturally occurring platinum alloy mineral found in placer and primary deposits. Its composition can vary widely in Fe, Ni, Pd, Ir, and other platinum-group metals, and it is recovered by gravity and related methods.
Natural iridium-rich metallic mineral occurring in platinum-group placer concentrates. It is an extremely dense and refractory PGM phase associated with other native platinum alloys.
