Platinum-group alloy mineral enriched in iridium and osmium, often with minor Ru, Pt, and Pd. It is one of the classic native PGM minerals recovered from placer concentrates.
Osmium-rich platinum-group alloy mineral containing substantial iridium and minor Ru, Rh, and Pt. It is a native PGM phase characteristic of heavy-mineral concentrates.
A specific osmium-iridium-ruthenium platinum-group alloy mineral from placer platinum assemblages. It is a dense native PGM phase associated with other iridosmine-group minerals.

Solid-liquid separation method used to remove leach residue or concentrate solids from a pregnant solution or slurry. In hydrometallurgical flowsheets it is applied after leaching and before downstream metal recovery, and it directly affects solution clarity and metal losses.

Leaching route in which finely ground ore is mixed with a reagent solution in stirred tanks so that valuable components dissolve into the liquid phase. It is the main industrial option for fine fractions that cannot be processed efficiently by percolation.

Leaching method in which a solution flows through a coarse ore bed or sand fraction and dissolves target components during passage. It is used for materials that remain permeable to liquid flow and is typically less suitable for fine slimes.

Pre-treatment operation used to remove soluble impurities from ore or concentrate before subsequent leaching or precipitation steps. By reducing the burden of dissolved contaminants, it improves downstream selectivity and lowers reagent consumption.

Conditioning and solid-removal operation used to separate suspended particles from a process solution before metal precipitation or recovery. It improves solution quality, prevents contamination of downstream products, and reduces interference with cementation or adsorption recovery.

A gravity separation method in which a pulsating water flow stratifies particles by density and size on a screen or bed. Heavier grains move downward and are recovered as concentrate, while lighter grains report to tailings.

A device for gravity concentration that creates a pulsating liquid flow through a particle bed to stratify material by density. In the slice, it is used for gold and platinum-bearing feeds over a broad particle-size range.

A simple jigging machine that produces periodic water pulses by means of a hydraulic valve or similar oscillating mechanism. It is used to create the pulsating stratification field required for gravity separation of heavy minerals.

A gravity separation apparatus with an inclined, riffled deck that oscillates to separate particles by density and size. Heavy grains migrate to the concentrate side, while lighter particles are washed to tailings by the water flow.

A sluice-type gravity concentrator with a compliant lining that promotes retention of heavy particles during flow. It is used for coarse gold recovery where selective trapping of dense grains is required.

A rotating gravity concentration device that separates heavy and light particles using centrifugal and hydrodynamic effects inside a drum. In the slice, it is listed among wet gravity apparatus for gold and platinum recovery.

A hydrocyclone with a short conical section used in wet gravity separation to classify and concentrate dense particles. The reduced cone length intensifies centrifugal stratification and makes the unit suitable for fine heavy-mineral recovery.

A gravity separation method in which particles are treated in a dense suspension medium so that minerals with different effective densities segregate. The technique is used when ordinary water-based gravity separation is insufficient due to narrow density contrasts.

The rate at which a particle moves downward through a liquid under gravity or an imposed flow field. In gravity concentration, differences in settling velocity between dense and light minerals are the basis of stratification and separation.

An inclined gravity-concentration device in which slurry flows as a thin film over a channel with riffles, traps, or a soft lining. Heavy particles settle and are retained near the bottom while lighter gangue is carried away, making the unit suitable for gold-bearing sands and fine placer material.

A sluice equipped with vibration on the deck to improve particle stratification and wash-off of accumulated concentrate. Vibration increases separation efficiency for gold-bearing ores compared with a stationary sluice, especially when fine heavy particles must be retained on the deck.

A continuous sluice in which a moving rubber belt with a rough or ribbed surface carries the slurry counter-current to the belt motion. It provides continuous concentrate removal, higher throughput than stationary sluices, and is used mainly for concentrate cleanup and some sulfide ores.

A compact gravity concentrator used in milling-classifier circuits to recover free gold and associated heavy minerals with low water demand. It is typically built as an inverted pyramid or cone, where coarse particles are retained near the inlet or on a screen while finer material settles into the chamber for discharge as concentrate.

Integrated mining and beneficiation method in which all operations are concentrated on a floating dredge. It is used mainly for placer deposits, where excavation, transport, primary concentration, and tailings disposal are carried out in one continuous process.

Beneficiation domain focused on recovering gold from placer deposits by gravity-based and dredging-based routes. The process emphasizes recovery of fine liberated gold particles from sand and gravel feeds with low energy and labor intensity.

Rough concentrate obtained in the first stage of gravity beneficiation of placer ores. It is typically low in gold grade and requires further upgrading on sluices, jigging machines, or shaking tables before final refining.

Amalgamation carried out simultaneously with grinding inside the milling apparatus. It allows freshly exposed gold surfaces to contact mercury immediately, before they become coated with sulfides, gangue, or oxidation films.

Amalgamation performed outside the grinding device, usually on sluices or in dedicated amalgamators. It processes already ground material and is more sensitive to surface contamination of gold particles than internal amalgamation.
Heavy grinding mill with rotating runners that crush and abrade ore on a hardened bed. In the slice, it is used for internal amalgamation so that mercury contacts gold during comminution.
Small rotating cylindrical apparatus used for internal amalgamation of rich concentrates or small batches. It combines mixing, limited grinding, and mercury contact in a closed drum.
Inclined sluice lined with amalgamated copper sheets for external amalgamation. Pulp flows over the mercury-bearing surface, where gold particles wet and adhere to the amalgam layer.

Formation of stable, non-coalescing mercury droplets under the influence of oils, carbonaceous matter, graphite, and mechanical agitation. It reduces mercury wetting of gold, increases mercury losses with tailings, and is harmful to amalgamation efficiency.

Diffusion-controlled penetration of mercury into gold during the second stage of amalgamation. This process leads to goldтАУmercury solid solutions and intermetallic phases that determine the final structure and brittleness of the amalgam.

Product of gold amalgamation consisting of mercury with dissolved gold and dispersed solid phases. It may contain gold in solution, goldтАУmercury intermetallic compounds, and residual solid particles, and can become brittle when contaminated with copper or iron.

Hydroxide precipitate formed from dissolved copper after lime addition. In amalgamation practice, it removes copper from the pulp and helps prevent copper contamination of mercury, improving the quality of the amalgam.

A specialized gold-recovery device in which pulp moves through a zigzag path past amalgamated plates to increase contact time and rubbing action against mercury-bearing surfaces. The design is used to capture very fine free gold that is difficult to recover in ordinary sluices.

A modified amalgamation route in which ore or concentrate is treated with zinc amalgam in an acidic medium. Hydrogen evolved from the zinc-acid reaction activates noble-metal surfaces, improves wetting by mercury, and increases gold or platinum recovery into the amalgam phase.

A mercury-based alloy containing zinc, used as an activating amalgam in enhanced gold recovery. In acidic contact with pulp it generates hydrogen and provides a chemically active mercury surface that improves amalgamation of noble-metal particles.

A sealed high-temperature vessel used to heat semi-dry amalgam and distill off mercury for reuse. The remaining noble-metal sponge or powder is then recovered for melting, while mercury vapor is condensed and returned to the process.

A condensation unit used downstream of a mercury retort to cool and liquefy mercury vapor. Water cooling enables mercury recovery and recirculation while limiting vapor losses during amalgam decomposition.

Surface-activation mechanism in which hydrogen generated in an acidic zinc-amalgam system removes passivating films and increases the wettability of noble-metal particles by mercury. This improves amalgamation kinetics and recovery, especially for platinum-bearing materials.

A safety and environmental constraint associated with the handling and thermal distillation of mercury-containing amalgams. Toxic vapor emissions require closed equipment, controlled heating, and strict exposure limits in order to avoid occupational poisoning and environmental release.

A cyanide reagent used for gold leaching as a cheaper alternative to sodium cyanide. The slice notes that it is often supplied as a fused salt mixture (cyanplav) and typically requires a higher consumption rate than NaCN for comparable cyanidation performance.

Process-condition parameter describing the free cyanide content in cyanidation liquors. In the slice, it has an optimum range because too little cyanide slows gold dissolution, while excess cyanide increases reagent loss and can suppress overall extraction by intensifying side reactions.

Equilibrium amount of oxygen that can dissolve in water or cyanide solution under given conditions. The slice gives oxygen solubility as a key limiting factor in cyanidation kinetics, because sufficient dissolved oxygen is required to sustain gold oxidation and complex formation.

Cathodic mechanism in cyanidation where dissolved oxygen accepts electrons and enables the anodic dissolution of gold. The slice treats oxygen as the practical depolarizer that, together with cyanide, makes electrochemical leaching of noble metals thermodynamically feasible.

Formation of highly stable metal-cyanide complexes in solution, which lowers the activity of dissolved metal ions and drives further dissolution of the metal surface. In the slice, this mechanism is central to gold and silver cyanidation through formation of dicyano complexes.

Electrochemical dissolution mechanism in which a gold particle and an attached sulfide or impurity phase act as a short-circuited microgalvanic cell. The resulting anodic gold oxidation and cathodic oxygen reduction accelerate metal dissolution in cyanide solution.

Stable complex anion formed when Au+ is bound by two cyanide ions in cyanide leaching solutions. It is the dissolved gold species that represents the thermodynamic endpoint of gold cyanidation in alkaline media.

Stable complex anion formed by silver ion binding with cyanide in alkaline cyanidation solutions. The slice describes this species as the dissolved form of silver that is analogous to dicyanoaurate during silver leaching.

Hydrometallurgical dissolution process in which one or more components are selectively transferred from a solid feed into a liquid solvent. In the slice, leaching is the general framework for cyanide dissolution of noble metals and for diffusion-controlled mass transfer from finely ground ore particles.

Bulk liquid motion that transports dissolved species and homogenizes concentration in the solution. In leaching systems it is generated by stirring, percolation through the ore bed, or temperature gradients and rapidly replenishes solvent near the dissolving particle.

Dissolution regime in which mass transfer through the thin saturated boundary layer around a particle is slower than the surface chemical reaction and therefore limits the overall rate. The slice describes this as the controlling mechanism for noble-metal leaching, with the diffusion layer acting as the main resistance to dissolution.

Mass-transfer parameter governing the rate at which dissolved species move through the liquid phase. In the slice, it directly controls gold dissolution kinetics in cyanidation and increases with temperature while decreasing as solution viscosity rises.
Thickness of the stagnant boundary layer adjacent to a dissolving solid. A larger diffusion layer increases mass-transfer resistance and lowers the dissolution rate of metals during leaching.

Loss of active cyanide from leaching solutions through mechanical carryover, leakage, splashing, incomplete washing, hydrolysis to HCN, and formation of non-productive complex compounds. It increases reagent consumption and operating cost in cyanidation circuits.

Sulfur-containing reaction products that can form when cyanide solutions interact with ore or concentrate components during leaching. Their formation consumes cyanide and contributes to chemical losses and downstream process complications.
Iron oxide mineral that is described as practically inert toward cyanide solutions in gold leaching. It is therefore a non-problematic gangue component in cyanidation compared with sulfide minerals.
Hydrated iron oxyhydroxide mineral that is described as practically inert toward cyanide solutions. It is listed among the iron minerals that do not significantly interfere with gold cyanidation.

A hexacyanoferrate(II) complex anion formed in alkaline cyanide solutions when iron(II)-bearing species react with excess cyanide. It is a key intermediate in the formation of blue iron-cyanide precipitates and reflects side chemistry that consumes cyanide in pulp.

An insoluble iron(II) cyanide precipitate that forms when ferrous hydroxide reacts with cyanide in alkaline solution. In cyanidation circuits, it represents a transient iron-cyanide phase that can further dissolve in excess cyanide to form ferrocyanide.

A deep-blue ferric hexacyanoferrate precipitate formed by oxidation of ferrocyanide or by direct reaction between Fe3+ and ferrocyanide species. Its appearance in cyanide solutions indicates insufficient protective alkali and unwanted iron-cyanide side reactions.

A sparingly soluble ferric hydroxy-sulfate phase formed during hydrolysis of ferric sulfate in wet oxidizing conditions. It is an intermediate product in sulfide oxidation and can subsequently transform into ferric hydroxide, contributing to cyanide consumption and pulp contamination.

A family of sulfur-rich anions formed during partial oxidation and rearrangement of sulfide species in cyanide pulp. Their presence indicates complex sulfide-side chemistry and contributes to nonproductive consumption of oxidants and cyanide.

A family of sulfur oxyanions generated during oxidation of sulfide minerals in cyanide systems. They are part of the complex sulfur speciation in pulp and reflect advanced oxidation pathways beyond simple sulfate and thiosulfate formation.

High-temperature pretreatment in an oxidizing atmosphere used to decompose refractory sulfide minerals before cyanidation. In the slice, it is applied to arsenopyrite-bearing ores to remove arsenic as volatile trioxide and improve downstream gold extraction.

A cyanide-processing strategy that uses weak cyanide solutions to suppress excessive interaction with copper minerals while still recovering gold. It is mentioned as a practical route for copper-bearing gold ores when conventional cyanidation becomes uneconomic due to cyanide loss.

Lead monoxide used as a cheaper lead reagent in cyanidation of rapidly oxidizing sulfide ores. In alkaline pulp it forms plumbite species and helps convert harmful sulfide and thio-salts into insoluble lead sulfide, reducing cyanide losses.

Insoluble lead sulfide phase formed when lead reagents bind sulfide species in cyanide pulp. Its precipitation is used to remove reactive sulfide ions and related antimony/arsenic sulfide species from solution chemistry.

A soluble lead-bearing anion formed in alkaline solutions from lead compounds such as litharge. It reacts with sulfide, thio-antimonate, and thio-arsenate species to precipitate lead sulfide and drive harmful sulfur species into less active forms.

A sulfurтАУcarbonтАУnitrogen anion formed in cyanide solutions during oxidation of sulfides and reaction of cyanide with elemental sulfur. Its formation consumes cyanide, but the slice notes that lead treatment can rapidly convert more harmful sulfide species into thiocyanate.

Soluble copperтАУcyanide complex formed when metallic copper or copper minerals dissolve in cyanide pulp. Its accumulation causes major cyanide consumption and slows gold dissolution in copper-bearing ores.

Mixed copper complex containing both cyanide and thiocyanate ligands. It forms from copper cyanide species in the presence of thiocyanate and reflects advanced side chemistry that increases reagent loss during cyanidation.
Volatile arsenic oxide produced during oxidative roasting of arsenopyrite-bearing ores. Removal of arsenic as this phase is used to prepare refractory gold ores for cyanidation.

Formation of dense, thin reaction films from arsenic- and antimony-bearing decomposition products on gold and silver surfaces. These films hinder solvent access, suppress dissolution kinetics, and reduce cyanidation recovery.

Percolation leaching of crushed ore stacked on an impermeable pad and irrigated from above with a lixiviant, typically cyanide solution in gold processing. The method is widely used for low-grade ores because it is simple, low-cost, and suitable for large tonnages with slow solution percolation.

In-situ leaching carried out directly in an ore body or abandoned workings by injecting solution and recovering pregnant liquor through wells. It is limited by solution losses through fractures and by the risk of contaminating surface or groundwater.

Loss of dissolving capacity of cyanide liquors caused by accumulation of impurities and surface-active species during repeated use. Once sufficient contaminants have built up, the activity cannot be fully restored by simply adding more free cyanide.

Restoration of cyanide liquor activity by partial bleed-and-replace of the process solution or by decomposition of impurity-metal complexes to recover active cyanide. It is used to counteract solution fatigue and reduce reagent losses in recycling circuits.
Mercury telluride mineral that may occur in gold-bearing ores. In cyanidation, it behaves similarly to other mercury minerals and can contribute mercury species to solution chemistry.

Oxide of divalent mercury that dissolves readily in cyanide solutions to form cyano-complexes. It is one of the mercury-bearing species relevant to cyanide leaching of amalgamation tailings and mixed ore products.

Monovalent mercury oxide that only partially transfers to solution in cyanide media, leaving elemental mercury as a residue. It is important because mercury-bearing residues can affect downstream cyanidation chemistry.

Soluble copper-cyanide complex anion formed in cyanide liquors when copper dissolves from ore or concentrate. Its accumulation consumes cyanide and suppresses precious-metal dissolution by shifting solution chemistry toward copper complexation.

Stable zinc-cyanide complex anion present in spent or impurity-rich cyanide liquors. It can adsorb at metal surfaces, participate in double-layer screening, and contribute to cyanide solution fatigue.

Soluble mercury-cyanide complex formed by dissolution of mercury-bearing minerals or metallic mercury in cyanide solutions. It represents the chemically stabilized dissolved form of mercury under cyanidation conditions.

The fraction of gold transferred from the ore feed into the pregnant solution or final product during leaching and recovery operations. In the slice, it is used to compare heap, tank percolation, and agitated cyanidation, where poor classification and clays reduce recovery while fine grinding and aeration improve it.

Characteristic linear size of ore particles after crushing or grinding. In the slice, particle size controls permeability, percolation rate, and gold liberation: coarse porous ore can be heap-leached, while finer grinding accelerates cyanidation in agitated systems.

Velocity at which leach solution passes through a packed ore bed or tank charge. The slice uses it as a feasibility criterion for tank percolation, with low values indicating that the material is uneconomical to treat by percolation.

Fraction of clayey or silty fine material in a feed. In the slice, higher clay content slows solution filtration, increases retained moisture, lengthens leaching time, and lowers gold recovery in percolation circuits.

Pre-leach conditioning in which moist ore fines are granulated into porous, permeable lumps. In the slice, agglomeration is done with cement, cyanide, and alkali in a drum granulator to improve heap/tank permeability, shorten cyanidation time, and allow gold to contact lixiviant during handling.

A rotating device used to agglomerate ore by rolling moistened feed with binders and process reagents. In the slice, it produces porous pellets from clayey or poorly classified ores before cyanide leaching.

A rotating feed distributor with radial tubes and flattened nozzles that spreads slurry over a circular area. In the slice, it is used to load percolation tanks uniformly and relies on jet reaction for rotation, similar to a Segner wheel.

A vessel with a false bottom used for percolation leaching of gold-bearing sand or crushed ore. The tank supports uniform bed loading, drainage of pregnant solution, and controlled solution irrigation from above or below.

An operating mode in which leach solution is introduced from the bottom of the ore bed or tank. In the slice, this reduces solution dilution, shortens drainage time, and improves the uniformity of percolation through the packed material.

A pulp-thickening vessel with a central rotating rake mechanism that accelerates settling of suspended solids and withdraws clarified overflow. In cyanidation flowsheets it is used before leaching to reduce slurry volume, lower pumping and mixing demand, and improve process stability.

An agitated vessel used to contact ore pulp with leaching reagents so that valuable components dissolve into the liquid phase. In the slice, such tanks are operated either periodically or as a cascade of continuously working units with mechanical, pneumatic, or pneumomechanical mixing.

A cyanidation scheme in which ore pulp is charged into leaching vessels in batches, mixed for a set residence time, and then discharged for solution separation. It is less automation-friendly than continuous cyanidation but allows discrete control of leaching time and pulp handling.

A cyanidation route in which pulp flows through a series of connected agitators or tanks, with the average residence time set by total vessel volume and flow rate. It improves automation, reduces idle tank time, and is the preferred industrial mode when consistent gold dissolution and solution recovery are required.

A solid-liquid separation step in which clarified solution is poured or drawn off from a settled pulp or slurry without full filtration. In cyanidation circuits it is used to recover gold-bearing solution after leaching and to reduce downstream solids loading.

The average time that ore pulp remains in the leaching circuit or cascade before discharge, commonly expressed as ╧Д = V/Q. It determines whether dissolved reagents and oxygen can contact the gold surface long enough for complete dissolution.

term.primary: Elevated Air Pressure in Pachuca Tank

concepts.definition: Batch counter-wash operation in which pulp is mixed, settled, and decanted in the same vessel. In gold cyanidation it is used for small batches of rich concentrates and can achieve high dissolved-gold washout, but its throughput is limited by the repeated settling and washing cycles.

Continuous multi-stage washing process carried out in a cascade of thickeners, where solids move opposite to the wash water. It provides very high gold washing efficiency and is especially suitable for well-settling pulps, but it requires large installation area and can dilute the pregnant solutions.

Solid-liquid separation apparatus in which a pressure difference created by vacuum draws liquid through a porous filtering medium. In cyanide-pulp processing it produces a filtrate and a moist cake, and is used in both continuous and periodic configurations.

Continuous vacuum filter with a slowly rotating perforated drum segmented into cells and covered by filter cloth. Part of the drum is immersed in pulp, the cake forms on the outer surface, and the cake is removed by a scraper after filtration.

Continuous vacuum filter constructed from disc-shaped filtration elements operating under vacuum. It belongs to the class of vacuum filters used for granular pulps and offers high filtration area per unit footprint.

Ability of the filter cake to allow liquid to pass through during filtration. Higher cake compaction lowers permeability and slows filtration, while coarser solids and more open cake structures improve liquid flow.

Residual water content retained in the filter cake after filtration. The slice notes that flocculating additives such as polyacrylamide can increase cake moisture because of water retained inside flocs, even while they improve filtration rate.

Operating condition in which the pressure on the filtrate side is lowered to create the driving force for vacuum filtration. Lower residual pressure accelerates filtration, but it also compacts the cake and can reduce its permeability.

A batch vacuum filtration unit consisting of multiple rectangular frames suspended in a common tank and covered with filter cloth. It is used for difficult-to-filter clay slurries and cyanide pulps, allowing long washing cycles and high gold washout, but with low throughput compared with continuous drum filters.

A polymeric solid containing fixed ionic functional groups capable of selectively binding dissolved metal complexes from solution. In cyanide metallurgy, ion-exchange resins are used for sorption recovery of gold and silver from cyanide liquors.

A hydrometallurgical recovery method in which dissolved noble-metal complexes are selectively captured from solution by ion-exchange resins. In the slice, it is identified as one of the main alternatives to zinc cementation for recovering gold and silver from cyanide solutions.

A recovery method in which dissolved noble-metal cyanide complexes are adsorbed onto activated carbon from solution. The text presents it as an increasingly important alternative to zinc cementation in cyanide processing of gold and silver.

A sacrificial metallic reducing agent used to cement gold and silver from cyanide solutions. In cementation circuits, zinc acts as the anodic phase that dissolves while noble metals are reduced and deposited on its surface.

Removal of dissolved oxygen from cyanide solutions before cementation. Deaeration suppresses wasteful zinc oxidation, reduces re-dissolution of deposited gold, and improves the efficiency of metal precipitation.

Pretreatment of metallic zinc with a soluble lead salt to form a porous sponge-lead layer on the surface. The coating greatly increases specific surface area and accelerates cementation of noble metals from cyanide liquors.

A soluble zinc-containing anionic species formed during zinc oxidation in alkaline media when cyanide is insufficient. It is an intermediate product that can hydrolyze to zinc hydroxide or convert to zinc cyanide complexes depending on solution chemistry.

An insoluble white zinc compound formed by hydrolysis of zincate under low-alkali conditions or during cementation side reactions. Its precipitation contributes to the 'white precipitate' that passivates zinc surfaces and impedes noble-metal deposition.

A cementation failure mode in which zinc hydroxide and zinc cyanide precipitate on the zinc surface when free cyanide or alkali is insufficient. The deposit blocks contact between zinc and solution, lowers precipitation rate, contaminates the recovered metal product, and increases reagent consumption.

Finely divided zinc used as the cementing reagent for precipitation of gold and silver from cyanide solutions. Its high specific surface area increases cementation rate, and it is often lead-activated before use to reduce passivation and improve contact with solution.

Lead salt used to activate or lead-coat zinc dust in cyanide cementation circuits. It promotes formation of a porous lead-bearing surface layer on zinc, improving the precipitation kinetics of noble metals.

Insoluble calcium arsenate film that can form on zinc in arsenic-bearing cyanide solutions. This surface precipitate passivates zinc, blocks solution contact, and sharply worsens noble-metal cementation.

Calcium silicate film that can form when colloidal silicic acid reacts in lime-containing cyanide liquors. It creates an insulating layer on zinc and lowers the efficiency of precious-metal precipitation.

Poorly conductive calcium plumbite film that can develop on zinc when plumbite ions are present in solution. The film passivates the cementing metal and suppresses gold deposition from cyanide liquors.

Vacuum vessel used to strip dissolved oxygen and other gases from cyanide solutions before zinc cementation. It improves precipitation completeness and lowers zinc consumption by reducing re-oxidation and gas interference.

Simple clarification filter in which solution passes through a sand bed above a false bottom to remove fine suspended solids. It is suitable for small-scale plants and is used to clarify pregnant cyanide solutions before cementation.
Pressure filtration unit used to clarify cyanide solutions and to dewater gold-zinc precipitates. It produces a dense cake and clear filtrate, supporting solution recovery and downstream handling.
Cloth-based filtration unit used for fine solution clarification in auxiliary or small-capacity circuits. It removes suspended solids before zinc precipitation or other hydrometallurgical steps.

Operational KPI describing the mass of zinc required to precipitate noble metals from cyanide solution. It is reduced by effective deaeration, solution clarification, and suppression of passivating side reactions.

Failure mode in which arsenate, silicate, plumbite, or similar precipitates form insulating films on zinc during cyanide cementation. The films block solution contact, slow precious-metal deposition, and increase reagent consumption.

Failure mode in which fine suspended particles adhere to zinc surfaces or contaminate the gold-zinc precipitate. It reduces effective cementation area, worsens precipitate quality, and necessitates prior clarification of the solution.

Finely divided aluminum used as a cementing agent for precious metals from cyanide solutions. It is slower than zinc because it wets poorly, but it oxidizes to aluminate species and regenerates cyanide during metal precipitation.

Soluble anionic product formed during oxidation of aluminum in alkaline media. In cyanide cementation with aluminum, its formation accompanies precious-metal precipitation and releases cyanide back into solution.

Insoluble carbonate precipitate formed when sodium carbonate is added to lime-containing cyanide solutions. It is used to remove calcium hardness before aluminum cementation and to prevent formation of insoluble calcium aluminates.

Water-insoluble high-molecular ion-exchange material containing ionogenic groups and mobile counterions. It selectively captures ions from electrolyte solutions by reversible ion exchange and is widely used for noble-metal recovery.

A cation-exchange ionite with fixed negatively charged groups. It exchanges cations from solution for its own counterions and is typically effective across acidic, neutral, and alkaline media depending on functional-group chemistry.
An anion-exchange ionite with fixed positively charged groups. It selectively binds anions from solution and is used for recovery of anionic noble-metal complexes from cyanide liquors.

An ion-exchange resin with large pores and channels created during synthesis. Its developed internal surface and short diffusion paths give it superior ion-transport kinetics compared with conventional gel-type ionites.
An immobile charged group anchored in the ionite matrix. Fixed ions define whether the material behaves as a cationite or an anionite and provide the electrostatic basis for ion exchange.

A mobile ion that balances the charge of fixed ionic groups inside an ionite. Counterions are exchanged with ions from solution during sorption and determine the selectivity and capacity of the resin.

A dissociable functional group in an ion-exchange material that carries the exchangeable charge. Its degree of dissociation controls whether ion exchange can proceed in acidic, neutral, or alkaline media.

Uptake of dissolved substances by a solid or liquid phase through adsorption and/or absorption. In the slice, sorption is the umbrella process behind ion-exchange resin and activated-carbon recovery of precious metals from cyanide solutions.

Reversible exchange of ions between an electrolyte solution and ionogenic groups fixed in a solid phase. It is the basic mechanism of ionite-based recovery of gold, silver, and other dissolved species from process liquors.

The ratio of the swollen resin specific volume to the air-dry specific volume. It is a key structural parameter for ion-exchange resins because it controls pore accessibility, diffusion paths, and exchange kinetics; higher crosslinking generally lowers swelling.

The amount of ions that can be taken up by a unit mass of ionite. In cyanide sorption circuits it determines resin loading with gold and competing impurities, and it is reduced in real solutions by competitive adsorption of cyanide complexes and background anions.

The extent of polymer network crosslinking in a resin, typically controlled by divinylbenzene content in styrene-based ionites. Higher crosslinking improves mechanical stability but reduces swelling and can slow ion diffusion into the bead interior.

A sulfur-containing organic reagent used as an effective gold desorbent from saturated anion-exchange resins. In acidic sulfate or hydrochloric media it forms a stable cationic gold complex, enabling elution of gold and co-desorption of silver and copper.

A regeneration procedure that removes adsorbed gold and impurities from a saturated ion-exchange resin and restores its sorption performance for reuse. In the slice it is implemented by dynamic desorption in a vertical column, minimizing fresh resin consumption.

Mass transfer through the liquid boundary film adjacent to the resin surface. In ion-exchange sorption, this is often the initial rate-limiting step before the process becomes controlled by diffusion inside the bead.

Transport of ions through the internal gel phase of an ion-exchange bead. It becomes the dominant kinetic limitation after the external film resistance decreases and governs the slow approach to equilibrium in resin sorption.

A vinyl aromatic monomer used as a base component for many synthetic ion-exchange resins. In the slice it defines the polymer backbone of styrene-DVB ionites, which determines swelling and mechanical durability.
A crosslinking comonomer used in styrene-based ion-exchange resins. Its content controls the degree of network crosslinking, which in turn affects swelling, pore accessibility, and resin rigidity.

An anion-exchange resin containing functional groups of different basicity. The slice states that such resins are more selective toward gold cyanide complexes than strongly basic anionites, making them advantageous for gold sorption from complex cyanide liquors.

A quaternary-ammonium-type anion-exchange resin used for cyanide liquor treatment. It is less selective than mixed-basicity anionites in gold sorption, because it more readily binds competing cyanide complexes and background anions.

A resin-regeneration desorption step in which loaded ion-exchange material is treated with acidic thiourea solutions to strip gold, silver, and copper from the sorbent. In the slice, this operation alone is insufficient for full regeneration because many impurities remain only weakly desorbed.

An electrochemical recovery method used to precipitate gold and silver from thiourea regenerate on the cathode while using non-consumable anodes for oxygen evolution. It is presented as the most advanced precipitation route in the slice because it gives fast recovery, low reagent consumption, and cleaner final products than chemical cementation.

An electrolysis operating regime in which the deposition rate is controlled by diffusion of gold-containing complexes to the cathode surface rather than by electron-transfer kinetics. In the slice, this regime governs gold recovery from thiourea solutions and requires intensified mixing and heating to raise throughput.

A porous conductive carbon-based cathode material made of very fine fibers, used to provide a highly developed electroactive surface in gold electrowinning from thiourea solutions. The slice notes its chemical resistance in aggressive media and its large specific surface area, which improves metal deposition capacity.

An electrochemical cell used to recover dissolved precious metals from thiourea solutions by cathodic deposition and anodic water oxidation. In the slice, the apparatus is operated under controlled current, mixing, and temperature to increase deposition rate and manage gas evolution.

Electroactive cathode area per unit electrolyzer volume or mass of cathode material. In the slice, increasing this parameter is the main way to intensify gold electrowinning from thiourea regenerate because deposition is limited by mass transfer to the cathode.

A combined hydrometallurgical route in which cyanide leaching of gold-bearing pulp and simultaneous sorption of dissolved gold by ion-exchange resin are carried out in the same circuit. The process eliminates the need for separate clarification and filtration after cyanidation and increases gold recovery by lowering dissolved-gold concentration in the pulp.

An electrochemical desorption method used to strip gold and silver from loaded ion-exchange resin in an electrolytic cell. In the slice, it is applied for resin regeneration and for transferring precious metals into a cathodic deposit suitable for remelting and refining.

A corrosion-resistant metal used as an electrode substrate in aggressive electrochemical media. In the slice, titanium is mentioned as cathode material for electroelution of gold from thiourea solutions, where durability and chemical inertness are important.

A mesh-based separation device used to retain resin granules while allowing fine ore particles and solution to pass through. In sorption leaching circuits it enables countercurrent transfer of resin between Pachuca tanks and prevents loss of sorbent into the pulp stream.

Operational KPI describing the mass of activated carbon lost from the sorption circuit, including losses as fine fractions during circulation and handling. In the slice, these losses are reported as a major drawback of carbon sorption because they directly increase reagent cost and reduce process stability.

Mechanical degradation of activated carbon during transport, pumping, and cyclic column transfer, producing fine fractions that are lost with process streams. The slice identifies low mechanical strength and resulting sorbent losses as a key limitation of carbon sorption in cyanide circuits.

term.primary: Carbon Pore Plugging by Calcium Carbonate

concepts.definition: Fouling mechanism in which calcium carbonate accumulates inside the pore network of activated carbon and blocks access to the internal surface. In the slice, this is one of the main causes of sorption activity loss after carbon regeneration and repeated cyanide service.

Regeneration/desorption method in which loaded activated carbon is treated with a hot alkaline cyanide solution to strip adsorbed gold and silver complexes. In the slice, it is described as the standard industrial elution route for carbon sorption circuits, operating typically at elevated temperature to accelerate desorption.

Regeneration step in which activated carbon is treated with dilute nitric or hydrochloric acid to remove calcium carbonate deposits and part of the residual organic fouling. In the slice, acid washing is used to restore sorption activity before the carbon is returned to service.

A regeneration route in which spent activated carbon is calcined at about 600тАУ800 ┬░C for a short time in the absence of air to destroy organic fouling species and restore sorption capacity. In the slice, the regenerated carbon is cooled, screened, and returned to cyanide sorption service.

A rotating thermal-processing furnace used for calcination and regeneration operations under controlled atmosphere. In the slice, it is used to heat activated carbon without air access to remove organic contaminants and restore its sorption performance.

An acid-resistant vessel lined with sheet lead for sulfuric-acid treatment of cyanide precipitates and related leach operations. It is designed to withstand aggressive media and to handle gas evolution under agitation or air bubbling with exhaust ventilation.
A borate flux used during smelting of cyanide precipitates and gold-silver alloys. It lowers slag melting temperature and helps separate noble-metal bullion from oxide and silicate impurities.

An oxidizing nitrate flux added during smelting of cathode precipitates to oxidize metallic iron from the cathode basis and improve melt cleanup. It supports formation of a cleaner gold-silver product before refining.

An oxidizing nitrate flux used together with or instead of potassium nitrate in smelting of cathodic precipitates. It oxidizes residual metallic iron and helps produce a cleaner bullion for subsequent refinement.

An oxidizing reagent used in the chemical treatment of copper-rich cyanide precipitates before further processing. In the slice, it is combined with sulfuric acid to remove copper and zinc from the sludge.

An acidic sulfate salt used as an alternative to sulfuric acid for preliminary treatment of cyanide precipitates. It dissolves zinc and other acid-soluble impurities while reducing some of the handling issues associated with concentrated mineral acid.

A highly toxic gaseous hydride of arsenic released during acid treatment of arsenic-bearing cyanide precipitates. Its formation is a major safety hazard during leaching and requires closed vessels and strong ventilation.

A highly toxic gaseous hydride of antimony released during acid treatment of antimony-bearing cyanide precipitates. It is a dangerous byproduct of the hydrogen evolution occurring in acidic sludge leaching.

A smelting furnace in which charge is melted on the hearth under reflected heat from the roof and flame path. In the slice, it is used for smelting acid-treated cyanide precipitates and producing a gold-silver alloy or intermediate lead bullion.

A refining step in which lead-bearing bullion is oxidized so that lead is removed as slag or oxide, leaving a noble-metal residue. In the slice, cupellation is used after smelting cyanide precipitates to obtain a cleaner precious-metal product for final refining.

Operational KPI describing the mass of acid required to process a unit mass of cyanide precipitate or sludge. In the slice, sulfuric acid consumption is a key cost and safety parameter because it controls impurity removal and the amount of toxic gas evolved.

Packed or tower-type vessel used to acidify cyanide solution before regeneration. It promotes contact with sulfur dioxide or sulfuric acid so that free cyanide and complex cyanides are decomposed and hydrogen cyanide can be stripped.

Gas-stripping unit in which cyanide solution is spread over packing or trays and exposed to a strong air stream. It is used to release volatile hydrocyanic acid from the liquid phase during cyanide solution regeneration.
Gas-scrubbing unit that contacts HCN-bearing air with an alkaline solution. It captures hydrocyanic acid as cyanide or sodium/potassium hydroxide solution and closes the regeneration loop.

Oxidizing reagent added to smelting charges and acidic treatment schemes. In cyanide-precipitate processing it helps oxidize sulfur-rich and base-metal impurities, suppress matte formation, and improve bullion cleanliness.
Strong oxidizing and complexing reagent used in acidic cyanide-solution treatment. It decomposes copper cyanide complexes and releases cyanide as HCN, enabling fuller regeneration of the solution.

Sacrificial cementation metal used to precipitate dissolved precious metals from acid-treated cyanide liquors. It also removes small amounts of dissolved copper from precipitate slurries before final product upgrading.

Intermediate bullion product obtained by smelting cyanide precipitates or concentrates. Its fineness depends on the composition of the feed and the quality of slag separation, and it is typically sent for subsequent refining.

Operational KPI describing the amount of cyanide consumed per unit ore or precipitate processed. It is driven by dissolution losses, complex formation, and solution regeneration efficiency, and directly determines the cost of cyanidation circuits.

An electric melting furnace that heats metal by electromagnetic induction and is used here for refining and chlorination of precious-metal melts. The text emphasizes high-power industrial units and strong internal mixing of the bath during processing.

A refractory crucible made of graphite, used to hold molten precious metals during chlorination refining. Its purpose is to withstand high temperature and aggressive chloride-containing melts while limiting contamination of the metal.

A strong oxidizing halogen gas used to chlorinate molten crude gold and convert base metals and silver into chlorides. In the process described, chlorine selectively reacts with less noble impurities before gold and platinum-group metals.

A strong mineral acid used in silver electrorefining electrolytes together with silver nitrate. It stabilizes the electrolyte composition and supports anodic dissolution of silver while maintaining the required acidic medium.

The silver salt used as the active electrolyte component in electrolytic refining of silver. It provides dissolved silver species for cathodic deposition and is typically used in water with a small addition of nitric acid.

A refining method in which chlorine is blown through molten crude gold to oxidize and remove base metals and most of the silver as chlorides. The process produces high-purity gold but can leave some silver and platinum-group metals in the refined metal or residues.

An electrochemical refining route in which a precious-metal alloy is dissolved anodically and purified metal is deposited cathodically from solution. In the slice, it is presented as the most advanced route for high-purity gold and silver production.

An electrolytic bath used for refining silver by anodic dissolution of impure silver anodes and cathodic deposition of high-purity silver. The text describes rectangular cells with insulated linings and vertical electrodes, where current distribution, electrolyte composition, and sludge removal strongly affect product quality.

Operating condition describing the amount of free nitric acid in the silver-refining electrolyte. In the slice, it is maintained at about 10тАУ20 g/L to improve conductivity and reduce power consumption, but excessive acidity increases cathode silver dissolution, nitrate reduction, and NOx emissions.

Electrorefining operating parameter describing current per unit cathode area. The text notes that lower current density is used when palladium is present in the anode metal to limit co-deposition and stabilize electrolyte composition.

Process condition describing dissolved copper level in the silver-refining electrolyte. Elevated copper causes charge transport to be shared between Cu and Ag ions, increasing the risk of silver-copper co-deposition at the cathode and forcing frequent electrolyte replacement.

Process condition describing palladium content in the refining electrolyte. Palladium partially dissolves from the anode and can co-deposit with silver, so its concentration is tightly controlled at very low levels to avoid contamination.

Process condition describing dissolved platinum level in the silver electrolyte. Platinum is mostly transferred to slime, but any dissolved fraction can deposit with silver, so the electrolyte concentration must remain extremely low.

Feed condition describing the tellurium content of silver anodes. The text indicates that above about 0.2% Te the refining process becomes unstable, with gray spongy deposits and nitrogen oxides appearing in the cell.

Quality requirements for silver anodes used in electrorefining. The slice specifies minimum silver fineness and maximum allowable impurity levels for gold, ligature metals, and tellurium to ensure stable dissolution and acceptable cathode quality.

Anode failure mode in which excessive gold content forms a dense crust on the dissolving silver anode. This layer blocks anodic dissolution, passivates the electrode, and intensifies side reactions during silver electrorefining.

Cathodic failure mode in which silver and copper deposit together because copper accumulates in the diffusion layer and current density is too high or mixing is insufficient. It lowers cathode purity and raises electrolyte-management costs.

Operational and environmental failure mode associated with excessive nitric acid in silver electrorefining. Higher acidity increases nitrate reduction and releases nitrogen oxides, worsening workplace air quality and increasing acid loss.

Secondary cathodic reaction in silver electrorefining where nitrate ions are partially reduced to nitrite, nitric oxide, or nitrous oxide. It competes with silver deposition, lowers current efficiency, and becomes more pronounced at higher electrolyte acidity.

Insoluble residue formed during silver anode dissolution, enriched in gold, platinum-group metals, selenium, tellurium, and some hydrolized base-metal compounds. It is the main sink for noble impurities during electrorefining and a key intermediate for precious-metal recovery.

A chalcogen impurity present in silver-gold anode materials and copper-electrolytic slimes. In the slice, selenium mostly reports to anode slime as silver selenate-like species and has relatively limited influence on the electrorefining process.

A chalcogen impurity in silver anodes and silver-gold alloys that strongly disrupts electrorefining. It can form difficult-to-handle tellurium compounds, produce gray spongy deposits at low electrolyte concentrations, and must be removed before refining.

A sparingly relevant but transferable silverтАУselenium oxidized compound mentioned as a selenium-bearing slime phase in silver electrorefining. Its formation indicates that selenium leaves the anode metal and is captured in the residue rather than depositing as cathode silver.

Process KPI expressing the fraction of electrical current that actually produces cathodic silver deposition. In the slice it is reduced by nitrate reduction, silver-copper co-deposition, and other parasitic reactions, so it directly controls energy efficiency and operating cost.

An oxidizing chlorine-bearing reagent used to treat silver anode slimes after nitric-acid leaching. In the slice it helps dissolve tellurium and platinum-group metals from the insoluble residue before the remaining gold-rich fraction is sent to gold refining.

A gold chloride complex acid used as the electrolyte for gold electrorefining. It dissociates in water to form tetrachloroaurate species, enabling anodic dissolution of impure gold and cathodic deposition of high-purity gold.
The dissolved gold species present in chloroauric-acid electrolytes. It is the electrorefining feed species that forms from gold dissolution at the anode and is subsequently reduced on the cathode.

A sparingly soluble silver salt formed when residual silver is precipitated from spent electrolyte with sodium chloride. In the slice it is then reduced to metallic silver with zinc dust or iron powder.

Process parameter describing the amount of dissolved silver in the refining electrolyte. The slice cites values around 120тАУ150 g/L for high-purity silver electrolysis and about 10 g/L after preliminary electrolysis before the remaining silver is precipitated as chloride.

An intermediate electrorefining stage applied to spent silver electrolyte to further lower dissolved silver and concentrate impurities. It prepares the solution for silver chloride precipitation and downstream recovery of copper and other contaminants.

Quality characteristic expressing the mass fraction of silver in the refined product, commonly reported as assay or fineness. In the slice, cathodic silver reaches very high purity after repeated electrolysis cycles, up to 999.99 and 999.999 grade.

Electrolytic refining route for gold in chloride media that uses an asymmetric alternating-current component to prevent passivation of the anode by silver chloride. The process enables selective dissolution of gold and high-purity cathodic deposition while limiting chlorine evolution and anode crust formation.

Electrorefining medium with high chloride activity and low pH used for gold dissolution and deposition. The acidic chloride environment stabilizes gold as chloro-complexes and suppresses unwanted hydrolysis and anode passivation.

Raised operating temperature of the gold electrorefining electrolyte. Higher temperature increases electrolyte conductivity and helps suppress anode passivation, thereby lowering power consumption and improving process stability.

Current per unit anode area during electrorefining. In gold refining it strongly influences chloride concentration and electrolyte temperature requirements, and excessive values can trigger anode passivation and chlorine release.

Failure mode in gold electrorefining where silver in the anode is oxidized to insoluble AgCl that forms a thick crust on the electrode. The crust blocks gold dissolution, promotes chlorine evolution, and can cause loss of refining stability.

Monovalent gold chloro-complex formed during anodic dissolution of gold in chloride electrolyte. It coexists with tetrachloroaurate and contributes to the non-ideal electrochemical behavior of gold electrorefining, including apparent current efficiencies above 100%.

Sparingly soluble lead salt that forms in chloride electrolytes when lead dissolves from gold anodes. Its precipitation can create passivating surface films on the anode and disrupt stable gold electrorefining.

Dissolved platinum chloro-complex species formed when platinum is oxidized during gold electrorefining. It is relevant as a contaminant species that can accumulate in the electrolyte and co-deposit if its concentration becomes excessive.

Chloride species of palladium formed in gold anode dissolution under chloride electrorefining conditions. It is an electrolyte impurity that can later contaminate the cathodic gold deposit if allowed to accumulate.

A two-stage electrorefining route for silver-gold alloys in which silver is first separated by electrolysis and the gold-rich residue is then refined in a second electrolysis stage. It is used for low-gold bullion and enables sequential recovery of high-purity silver and gold.

An acid parting method for gold-silver alloys in which hot nitric acid selectively dissolves silver and many base-metal impurities while gold remains as an insoluble residue. It requires a silver-rich alloy and is used to obtain high-purity gold after recovery of the dissolved silver.

An alternative gold-silver separation method using concentrated sulfuric acid to dissolve silver and base metals from the alloy while gold remains in the residue. Its applicability is limited by alloy composition, especially copper and lead content, because dense sulfate films can hinder dissolution.

An electrolytic cell in which an anodic and a cathodic compartment are separated by a porous porcelain, clay, or ion-exchange diaphragm. In gold electrodissolution it helps control electrolyte composition and isolate the cathode from anode-side impurities and gas evolution.

Formation of needle-like metallic deposits on the cathode during electrorefining or electrolysis. In dirty or impurity-rich electrolytes, dendrites can bridge electrodes, cause short circuits, and reduce product quality and process stability.
Mass fraction of gold in a refined cathodic product or bullion. In gold electrorefining it is a primary quality indicator, and the slice reports cathodic gold of about 999.8тАУ999.9 fineness.

Gold present as liberated metallic grains rather than locked in other minerals. It is the most readily recoverable gold form and is typically amenable to gravity concentration and standard cyanidation when not coated by passivating films.

Gold occurring as intergrowths with sulfide minerals or encapsulated within sulfide matrices. This form is typically refractory to direct cyanidation and often requires flotation or oxidative pretreatment to expose the gold surface.

Gold grains covered by passivating surface films, oxidation products, or adsorbed layers that limit reagent access. In cyanidation, this coating slows dissolution and reduces extraction until the film is removed or the surface is reactivated.

The oxygen level in the roasting atmosphere that controls the rate of sulfide oxidation during calcination. Too little oxygen leaves unoxidized sulfides in the calcine, while excessive oxygen can overheat the bed and promote partial melting and loss of porosity.

A roasting failure mode in which excessive temperature causes partial melting or densification of the calcine. The resulting low-porosity product is poorly permeable to cyanide solutions, which reduces gold liberation and extraction efficiency.

A mechanized single-hearth roasting furnace used for sulfide concentrate calcination. The rabble arms move material across the hearth and along the furnace, giving long residence time and moderate mixing, but the design is difficult to control in terms of temperature and oxygen regime.

A vertical roasting furnace with multiple stacked hearths and a central shaft carrying rabble mechanisms. It enables staged contact between concentrate and gas phase, improving control of roasting temperature, oxygen access, and product porosity compared with older single-hearth furnaces.

A roasting furnace in which the charge is intensely mixed in a fluidized state by the gas stream. Strong heat exchange prevents local overheating and calcine fusion, making the process more stable than hearth roasting for sulfide concentrates.

Oxidative roasting of sulfide concentrates on a hearth with mechanical or manual material movement. The method requires careful control of particle temperature to avoid calcine overheating, partial melting, and loss of porosity needed for subsequent cyanidation.

A roasting scheme in which the first stage is carried out with limited air access to volatilize arsenic as As2O3, and the second stage uses excess oxygen to oxidize sulfur. This sequence produces a more porous calcine with lower residual arsenic and sulfur, improving downstream cyanidation.

A roasting approach in which the concentrate moves opposite to the gas flow so that the incoming material first contacts oxygen-poor gases and later encounters oxygen-rich gases. This staged gasтАУsolid contact helps remove arsenic early and complete sulfur oxidation near the furnace outlet.

Operating temperature constraint for sulfide-concentrate roasting. Keeping particle temperature below roughly 900тАУ950 ┬░C helps prevent calcine sintering and partial melting while maintaining sufficient reaction rate for porosity development and impurity removal.

A high-temperature pretreatment in which sulfide concentrates are roasted with added sodium chloride in an oxidizing atmosphere. Chlorine is generated in situ from sulfur oxides and chloride, which helps open refractory gold-bearing mineral grains and improves subsequent cyanidation.

A soluble iron(II) chloride intermediate formed during chlorinating roasting when chlorine reacts with iron-bearing sulfides or oxides. It can further oxidize to ferric chloride, regenerating chlorine and sustaining the gas-phase chlorination cycle.

A gas-solid separation unit that removes entrained dust from roasting off-gases by centrifugal separation. In roasting flowsheets, cyclones serve as the first-stage dust collector before finer gas cleaning.

A gas-cleaning device that removes fine particulate matter from flue gas using an electrostatic field. In fluidized-bed roasting circuits, it is used to capture dust that escapes cyclone separation, including condensates of toxic arsenic trioxide.

term.primary: Gold Surface Passivation by Low-Melting Films

concepts.definition: A roasting-induced failure mode in which molten or near-molten reaction products coat gold particles and block access of cyanide solutions. This passivation increases gold losses to cyanidation tailings because the metal becomes chemically inaccessible.

term.primary: Co-Smelting with Copper and Lead Concentrates

concepts.definition: A pyrometallurgical processing route in which gold-bearing sulfide concentrates are smelted together with copper or lead concentrates. Noble metals report to matte or lead bullion and are later recovered from anode slimes or silver-gold alloy products.

A sulfide concentrate rich in pyrite and arsenopyrite, commonly used as a feed for roasting prior to gold cyanidation. Its oxidation behavior governs arsenic removal, calcine porosity, and downstream gold extraction efficiency.

A high-temperature chlorination process in which gold-bearing material is mixed with sodium chloride or calcium chloride and roasted in an oxidizing atmosphere so that gold is converted into volatile chlorides. The process is used to transfer gold, silver, and base metals into the gas phase for subsequent capture from flue gases.

A volatile gold chlorination product formed during chloride volatilization at elevated temperature. It represents the gas-phase gold species that is later recovered from roasting off-gases and converted into a metal-rich residue.

A rotating high-temperature furnace used for oxidation and chlorination roasting of mineral concentrates. Continuous tumbling and gas-solid contact make it suitable for chloride volatilization and similar calcination routes.

A vertical furnace used for roasting or chlorination of agglomerated material. In chloride volatilization, it provides a high-temperature gas-solid reaction zone for converting gold into volatile chlorides.

A sealed high-pressure reactor used for oxidative leaching of sulfide gold concentrates. It maintains elevated temperature and oxygen pressure so that sulfide minerals are decomposed while gold remains in the insoluble residue.

term.primary: Autoclave Leaching of Sulfide Gold Concentrates

concepts.definition: Hydrometallurgical opening of finely disseminated gold in sulfide concentrates by oxygen-assisted pressure leaching in an autoclave. The method oxidizes pyrite and arsenopyrite under acidic or alkaline conditions, leaving the liberated gold in the solid residue for subsequent cyanidation.

Elevated temperature range used in pressure oxidation of sulfide gold concentrates. At about 120тАУ180 ┬░C, oxidation kinetics become sufficiently fast for practical leaching times while preserving the gold in the insoluble residue.

Oxidant pressure used to sustain sulfide oxidation in autoclave leaching. The reported range of roughly 0.2тАУ1 MPa provides enough dissolved oxygen for rapid decomposition of sulfide minerals and liberation of gold.

term.primary: Bacterial Leaching of Sulfide Gold Concentrates

concepts.definition: Bio-oxidative opening of sulfide gold concentrates in which microorganisms catalyze sulfide oxidation instead of using high temperature and pressure. The process relies on bacterial enzymes to accelerate oxygen-driven oxidation and prepare a gold-bearing residue for cyanidation.

Iron- and sulfur-oxidizing bacterium used as a bioleaching agent in sulfide concentrate processing. It accelerates oxidation of sulfides, ferrous iron, and elemental sulfur, enabling low-temperature hydrometallurgical opening of refractory gold feeds.

Oxidation mechanism catalyzed by microbial enzymes during bioleaching. It replaces thermal pressure oxidation by using bacterial metabolism to accelerate conversion of sulfides into oxidized products and to expose gold for later recovery.

High-temperature range required for converting metallic gold into volatile chloride species during chloride volatilization. At about 900тАУ1100 ┬░C, gold chlorination becomes effective and the volatilized products can be captured from the gas stream.

term.primary: NaCl Addition Rate for Chloride Volatilization

concepts.definition: Recommended sodium chloride dosage for chloride volatilization. Insufficient NaCl leads to incomplete chlorination and gold losses in the calcine, whereas excessive NaCl promotes sintering and coarsening of the roast product.

Residual sulfur level in pre-roasted feed used for chloride volatilization. A sulfur content of roughly 2тАУ5 % is described as favorable because it limits calcine sintering and helps maintain gold recovery while reducing NaCl consumption.

The fraction of void space in broken ore that governs permeability to leach solutions. In heap leaching, higher porosity improves percolation, capillary penetration, and access of cyanide solution to gold-bearing surfaces.

The mesophilic temperature window used for bacterial leaching of sulfide gold concentrates. It supports thiobacilli activity and accelerates sulfide oxidation while remaining below the temperatures typical of autoclave pretreatment.

The strongly acidic pulp range required for sulfide-oxidizing bacteria to remain active during bioleaching. Such acidity also favors ferric sulfate chemistry and promotes oxidation of pyrite and arsenopyrite.

The typical residence time needed for bacterial leaching of refractory sulfide concentrates. This prolonged duration reflects the slower kinetics of bio-oxidation compared with pressure oxidation, but it is still advantageous because it operates at atmospheric conditions.
A climatic site-selection condition favorable for heap leaching. A long warm period keeps leach solutions active and prevents freezing, improving percolation leaching performance over the ore stack.

A climatic condition favorable for heap leaching because it limits dilution of the lixiviant and helps maintain solution balance on the heap pad. It also reduces the risk of uncontrolled runoff from the ore stack.

The depth from the surface to the groundwater table, used as a site-selection constraint for heap leaching. A deep groundwater table reduces the risk of solution loss and groundwater contamination from cyanide irrigation.

Impermeable base area used to support heap leaching operations and collect pregnant solutions. The text describes several pad constructions, including asphalt, compacted clay, plastic liners, bentonite mixtures, and reinforced concrete, all intended to prevent solution loss and protect the base from mechanical damage.

Agglomeration of fine ore or slime fractions into porous pellets before heap leaching. In the slice, pelletization is used to restore permeability, accelerate solution percolation, and shorten cyanide leaching time, often with cement, lime, cyanide, and controlled moisture.

Agglomeration equipment used to form pellets from fine ore before heap leaching. The text specifically mentions disk and drum pelletizers as standard machines for preparing clay-rich fine fractions for improved heap permeability.

Ability of a heap of ore to transmit leach solution and air through its pore network. In the slice, permeability is a decisive factor for heap-leach performance and drops sharply when clay and fine fractions increase or when the heap is overly compacted.

Volumetric flow of leach solution through a heap per unit area and time. The text uses it as a practical indicator of heap-leach quality, showing that pelletization can raise it dramatically and that poor sizing or compaction suppresses it.

Geometric operating condition of a heap leaching stack. The slice distinguishes accelerated and long-duration heap leaching by heap height, with taller heaps used for long campaigns and lower heaps preferred for clayey or highly carbonated ores.

Degree to which ore is densified during stacking and traffic over the heap. Excess compaction reduces solution permeability, slows leaching, and lowers gold extraction, especially for clay-rich and high-carbonate feeds.
Nonuniform flow of leach solution through preferential paths in a heap. It reduces contact with ore, worsens extraction uniformity, and is promoted by poor stacking, segregation, and fines migration.

Loss of heap permeability caused by clay-rich material being compressed during stacking or equipment traffic. In the slice, this is a key reason for reduced gold recovery from clayey and high-carbonate ores and motivates lower heap heights.

Holding an ore heap after an initial leaching cycle so that leachability improves before a later re-leach. The text notes that old heaps may be left in place and treated again with a stronger cyanide solution to increase total gold recovery.

Higher-concentration cyanide lixiviant used for re-leaching aged or refractory heaps. The slice states that older heap material is leached with a stronger cyanide solution to recover residual gold more completely.

Binding additive used during pelletization of fine ore before heap leaching. It improves pellet strength and porosity retention, allowing the agglomerated material to withstand stacking and irrigation while maintaining solution permeability.

Aqueous lime slurry used to dose alkalinity during ore preparation and pelletization. In the slice it is one of the reagents applied to crushed ore before heap stacking to control pH and improve agglomerate quality.

Earthmoving machine used to place and level ore during heap construction. The text notes that bulldozers are preferred for stacking because they compact the heap less than haul trucks and help preserve permeability.

Mobile crushing unit used to reduce ore size before heap leaching. The slice mentions stationary and portable crushing installations as standard preparation equipment for accelerated heap leaching circuits.
Fixed crushing installation used to prepare ore for heap leaching. It is listed in the text as one of the standard crushing options before stacking and cyanide irrigation.
Heap leaching route using crushed ore of relatively fine size to shorten leach time. The slice gives typical particle sizes below about 20 mm and campaign durations of 7 to 70 days.

Heap leaching route using run-of-mine or coarsely blasted ore for multi-month extraction campaigns. It relies on larger heap heights and long residence times to recover gold from less finely prepared feeds.

Coarse ore size obtained directly from blasting and used in long-term heap leaching. The slice identifies run-of-mine material, typically up to about 150 mm, as suitable for large slow leaching stacks.

Pre-leach separation of fine slime fractions from coarser material before heap leaching or cyanidation. In the slice, slimes may be diverted to tank cyanidation while the coarse fraction is pelletized or stacked for heap leaching.
Fraction of very fine particles in ore. The text treats higher fines content as detrimental to heap permeability and as a key driver for pelletization or separate slime treatment.
Fraction of clay-rich material in the ore feed. In heap leaching it reduces permeability and recovery, making agglomeration or lower heap heights necessary.
Top-down delivery of leach solution onto a heap surface. The slice describes irrigation as part of the heap leaching operation and ties its effectiveness to heap permeability and uniform stacking.
Channel used to collect pregnant or drainage solutions from heap leaching pads. It is part of the solution-recovery infrastructure that directs leachate to storage and downstream recovery units.
Reservoir for distributing leach solution to heap leaching pads. The text lists it among the standard infrastructure elements of a heap leaching site.
Settling vessel used to remove suspended fines from process solutions or slurries in heap-leach infrastructure. It supports solution clarification before reuse or sorption recovery.

Transfer of irrigation or process solution through the heap leaching circuit using pumps. It is a required support operation for delivering reagent solution to the heap and returning recovered liquors.
Aqueous cyanide lixiviant used for heap leaching and ore preparation. In the slice it is applied both to wet ore during stacking and to re-leach old heaps for improved gold recovery.
Ore reduced in size before heap stacking. The slice treats crushed ore as the feed for accelerated heap leaching and notes that it is often limed and wetted with cyanide solution during transport.

Previously processed residue that may be re-agglomerated or re-leached in heap operations. The text notes that old tailings can be mixed with ore for pelletization or subjected to renewed heap leaching.
Coarse-grained fraction of ore or tailings suitable for heap leaching or physical separation. In the slice it is distinguished from slimes and may be treated separately to preserve percolation.

Fine, mud-like fraction of ore that impairs heap permeability and often needs separate cyanidation or agglomeration. The slice explicitly notes its negative impact on solution percolation and gold extraction.

Particle-sizing operation used to separate coarse and fine fractions before heap leaching or pelletization. The slice uses dry screening to narrow the size range of crushed ore and improve heap preparation.
Rotary screening device used to separate fines from agglomerated ore or crushed feed. The text describes screening after pelletization to remove newly formed fine material and recycle it.
Screening equipment used in feed preparation and pelletization circuits. The slice mentions it as part of the handling path for fine materials before heap leaching.

Operational condition requiring a protective layer between the heap and the impermeable liner or pad. The slice notes that gravel or crushed stone is used to protect the base from damage by dumped ore and machinery.
Bitumen layer used to protect or seal heap-leach base structures. The text notes that some pads use bitumen on concrete surfaces as part of the impermeable foundation.
Polymeric liner material used to make heap-leach pads impermeable. In the slice, high-density polyethylene is listed as one of the common base-sealing materials for heap leaching.
Synthetic impermeable sheet used to line heap-leach pads. The slice mentions polyethylene and polyvinyl chloride liners as standard protection against solution leakage.
Low-permeability clay layer used beneath heap leaching stacks to prevent solution loss. In the slice it is combined with sand and gravel layers to form a pad construction.
Impermeable pavement material used as a heap-leach pad surface. The slice lists asphalt pads as a common construction for solution collection and containment.
Clay additive used to improve the impermeability of heap-leach pad constructions. The text mentions old tailings mixed with bentonite as one possible pad or foundation material.
Requirement that heap leaching pads prevent lixiviant loss to the subsurface. The slice explicitly states that pad surfaces must be impermeable and sloped for solution collection.
Design requirement for heap leaching pads to support drainage of pregnant solution. The text specifies a pad inclination of about 1 to 5 degrees for collection of the drainage liquor.

Engineering requirement to protect heap-leach liners and foundations from damage by dumped ore and machinery. The slice notes that a gravel or crushed-stone layer is used as a protective cushion over the impermeable base.

Process KPI describing the time required to complete a heap leach campaign. The slice reports very different cycle times for accelerated and long-term leaching and shows that pelletization and ore preparation can shorten the cycle substantially.

Operational KPI describing the amount of ore processed through heap leaching per unit time or campaign capacity. In the text it scales with heap size and campaign duration and is tied to pad area and ore stacking strategy.

KPI representing the fraction of gold recovered from heap leaching. The slice links poor stacking, clay, and fine fractions to reduced recovery and notes that correct pelletization and heap construction improve it.

Operational KPI describing lixiviant lost through leakage, poor containment, or excessive seepage. The slice implies that impermeable pads and proper drainage are necessary to keep solution loss low in heap leaching.

Geometric property of the impermeable pad layer used under heap leaching. The text gives example thicknesses for asphalt, clay, and plastic liners, showing that liner thickness is selected to balance containment and durability.

Ability of the heap-leach foundation to remain intact under ore loading and machine traffic. The slice notes that pad integrity is preserved by protective gravel layers and by leaving a residual ore layer when unloading finished heaps.
Application of bitumen to concrete or other foundations to improve chemical resistance and impermeability. The slice mentions bitumen as a sealing layer for heap-leach pad construction.

Chelating reagent used in heap-leaching solutions to complex hardness ions, especially calcium, and suppress scale formation. In the slice it is introduced as an additive that helps prevent calcium carbonate deposition and maintain percolation and sorption performance.

Precipitation of calcium carbonate from hard or alkaline process waters onto ore surfaces, pipes, and pore spaces. In heap leaching this scaling reduces permeability, disrupts filtration, and lowers gold extraction efficiency.

Formation of jarosite-group basic iron sulfates during leaching or water-quality deterioration. These precipitates can clog heap pores and worsen solution percolation, which slows cyanide access to gold-bearing material.

Strong oxidizing reagent used in heap detoxification to destroy residual cyanide and other reactive species. In the slice it is listed together with chlorine and hydrogen peroxide as an oxidant for post-leach treatment.
