Post-leaching treatment of a heap to destroy residual cyanide and other toxic reagents before ore removal or further handling. The slice describes oxidation-based detoxification using chlorine, hydrogen peroxide, permanganate, and related oxidants.

Process parameter describing the volume of leach liquor relative to the mass of ore being treated. In heap leaching it is low compared with tank processing, and it strongly affects reagent concentration, percolation behavior, and overall throughput.

A vessel used to precipitate dissolved noble metals from solution by cementation, typically with zinc dust. In gold-recovery circuits it provides controlled mixing, solid-liquid contact, and settling of the cemented sludge before refining.

A cementation apparatus in which vibration intensifies contact between zinc granules and metal-bearing solution. It is used to accelerate precipitation of gold and silver while improving reagent utilization and slurry transport.

A vacuum or reduced-pressure vessel used to remove dissolved oxygen from precious-metal-bearing solutions before cementation. Lower oxygen content suppresses zinc oxidation and improves the efficiency of gold precipitation.

A packed column used for adsorption recovery of gold from dilute pregnant solutions on activated carbon or ion-exchange resin. Countercurrent operation and staged transfer of sorbent make it suitable for preconcentration of noble metals.

An electrochemical recovery method in which dissolved noble-metal complexes are deposited onto a cathode from solution. In the slice it is one of the routes used to recover gold and silver from eluates after sorption.

A high-temperature, high-pressure desorption route used to strip gold and silver from loaded activated carbon. It shortens elution time and reduces reagent consumption compared with atmospheric cyanide-alkali desorption.

A feed-solution condition under which zinc dust cementation remains effective. Elevated arsenic increases cementation difficulty and reagent loss, while low arsenic content allows cleaner precipitation of gold and silver.

A precipitate formed when dissolved gold and silver are reduced from cyanide solution by zinc dust or other cementing metals. It typically contains gold together with copper, zinc, lead, selenium, and silver and is routed to further refining or dor├й production.

The amount of adsorbed gold per unit mass of activated carbon. It controls when the sorbent is transferred to desorption, with the slice indicating working loadings of several kilograms of gold per ton of carbon before regeneration.

A cationic gold complex formed in thiourea-based desorption solutions. It is the soluble gold species transferred from loaded ion-exchange resin into the regenerate and is subsequently recovered by electrolysis or precipitation.

A hydrated gold precipitate obtained from thiourea-regenerate solutions by alkaline treatment. It is a recoverable intermediate that is subsequently roasted or sent to electrolysis to obtain metallic gold.

A solution-cleanup step in which air treatment is used to remove cyanide ions from a thiourea regenerate before gold precipitation. It reduces cyanide carryover into downstream alkaline precipitation or electrolysis stages.

Geometric design parameter of column-type sorption and desorption apparatus. In the slice, column equipment for activated carbon and ion-exchange resin is specified with a high H/D ratio to improve contact efficiency and countercurrent operation.

Hydrometallurgical dissolution of noble metals in a nitric-hydrochloric acid mixture. In the slice, it is used mainly for refining or reclaiming gold-bearing residues, where gold dissolves as chloro-complexes while silver remains in the chloride residue.

Non-cyanide gold dissolution route in chloride and chlorine-containing media, where chlorine acts both as oxidant and complexing agent. The method is described as a practical alternative to cyanidation for producing soluble gold chloro-complexes from ores and concentrates.

Water-treatment route for removing arsenic by converting it into insoluble compounds after oxidation to the pentavalent state or by direct sulfide precipitation. In the slice, lime, iron salts, barium salts, and sulfide reagents are all used in this role to lower arsenic concentrations in effluents.

Insoluble arsenic-bearing precipitate formed during wastewater treatment after oxidation of As(III) to As(V). It is cited as one of the few arsenic compounds with very low solubility and is therefore used for deep arsenic removal from cyanide-process effluents.

Poorly soluble arsenic sulfide precipitate that can form during sulfide or hydrogen-sulfide treatment of arsenic-containing wastewater. It is relevant because its formation removes arsenic without requiring prior oxidation to the pentavalent state.
Strong oxidizing gas used to convert trivalent arsenic into pentavalent arsenic before precipitation. In the slice, it is one of the oxidants applied for preparing wastewater for arsenate removal.

Ferromanganese alloy used as a cementing reductant for recovering gold from thiourea solutions. In the slice, it is mentioned as an alternative to zinc or aluminum dust for metal precipitation from saturated thiourea regenerates.

An oxidizing chlorine species present in alkaline hypochlorite solutions. In acidified chloride media it shifts toward hypochlorous acid and chlorine, which makes it the upstream reagent form for gold dissolution in acid hypochlorite leaching.

A weak acid and oxidant formed from hypochlorite in water. In the slice it is the intermediate chlorine species that, under acidic chloride conditions, produces molecular chlorine and supports gold dissolution.

A chlorine-bearing oxidant used in hypochlorite leaching of gold. It is the source of hypochlorous acid and chlorine in solution and, together with chloride and acid, forms an alternative to cyanidation.
A chlorine-bearing oxidizing reagent used in chloride or hypochlorite leaching systems. In the slice it is listed among oxidizers that provide the active chlorine species for gold dissolution.
A carbonaceous sorbent used to adsorb gold from chloride leach solutions. In the slice it is reported as an effective precipitating and recovering agent for dissolved gold.
A halogen oxidant and gold solvent used in iodide leaching systems. It participates with iodide in forming soluble gold iodide complexes and can be regenerated electrochemically.
A halide anion that complexes gold in iodide leaching. It stabilizes dissolved gold as an iodide complex and is regenerated during electrochemical recovery.
An alkaline additive used to raise pH in iodide leaching. The slice uses it to suppress iron dissolution from sulfide minerals and improve gold selectivity in iodine-based dissolution.
An alkaline buffer reagent used in iodide leaching to raise pH and suppress iron dissolution from sulfide minerals. It is listed alongside potassium bicarbonate as a pH-control additive.

An oxidizing anion added to iodide leaching solutions to lower reagent cost by regenerating iodine through electrochemical cycles. In the slice it participates in redox conversion back to iodine and nitrite.
A reduced nitrogen oxyanion formed during iodide-leach regeneration chemistry. It is an intermediate product in the conversion of nitrate back into iodine-forming reagents.
The neutral iodine form precipitated from iodide leach liquor during regeneration or peroxide treatment. It is a recoverable iodine phase in the process loop.

An anion-exchange resin treated with amino acid solution for sorbing gold iodide complexes from iodide leach liquors. The slice uses it in a combined sorption and regeneration route for gold recovery.
The dissolved gold species formed in iodide leaching. It is the soluble complex that is recovered by electrolysis or ion-exchange sorption in the iodide process.

Gold dissolution process using chlorine-bearing reagents to convert metallic gold into soluble chloro-complexes. In the slice, it is the classical pre-cyanide route used for polymetallic and slime-rich ores.

Gold dissolution process performed in acidified chloride media using hypochlorite as the oxidant. The active dissolving agent is molecular chlorine produced in situ from hypochlorous acid and chloride.

A chloride leaching route using sulfuric acid, sodium chloride, and manganese dioxide to generate chlorine in situ and dissolve gold. It is also able to oxidize sulfides such as pyrite and arsenopyrite, opening gold trapped in them.

Gold dissolution route based on iodine and iodide complexes. The method operates at moderate pH, can be regenerated electrochemically, and is presented as a non-cyanide alternative for gold extraction.

A gold leaching route using bromine-bearing oxidants and bromide to form soluble gold bromide complexes. It is described as a non-cyanide alternative applied to ores and scrapped materials, including telluride ores.
A hybrid bromide/cyanide gold leaching process used for telluride ores. It combines bromine chemistry with cyanide to improve dissolution of refractory gold-bearing minerals.
Gold dissolution in acidic thiourea solutions using ferric sulfate as oxidant. It is a non-cyanide leaching route whose rate depends on pH, thiourea concentration, and oxidant concentration.
An oxidation product of thiourea formed in the presence of oxygen or strong oxidants such as MnO2. In thiourea leaching it acts as a stronger oxidizing species that can promote gold dissolution.

The soluble gold species formed during thiosulfate leaching. It represents the dissolved endpoint of gold extraction in alkaline thiosulfate systems and is the species recovered in downstream sorption or electrochemical steps.

A soluble copper-thiosulfate species formed in ammoniacal thiosulfate solutions. It acts as an oxidizing/catalytic component in gold dissolution, but its accumulation also accelerates thiosulfate decomposition and reduces process economy.

A non-cyanide gold leaching route in which gold is dissolved in alkaline or ammoniacal thiosulfate solutions, often in the presence of copper ions as a catalytic oxidizer. It can provide high gold dissolution rates, but reagent instability and side reactions strongly affect economics.

Thermal degradation of thiourea in the leach solution, occurring more readily at elevated temperature. It produces cyanide and hydrogen sulfide, which consumes reagent, complicates process control, and can destabilize gold dissolution chemistry.

Breakdown of thiosulfate reagent during leaching, accelerated by higher temperature, prolonged agitation, and copper-containing catalysts. It lowers reagent efficiency, increases consumption, and is a major factor limiting the industrial attractiveness of thiosulfate gold leaching.

An aqueous alkaline medium containing dissolved sulfur species such as hydrosulfide, sulfide, thiosulfate, and polysulfides. In the slice, this solution acts as a selective lixiviant for metals and its composition strongly controls sulfur speciation, conductivity, viscosity, and metal dissolution behavior.

A parameter describing the average sulfur-chain length in polysulfide species present in alkaline sulfur solutions. The slice states that it depends on hydroxide concentration and determines the distribution and reactivity of sulfur species in the leach liquor.

A reaction pathway in which elemental sulfur in alkaline media is converted into hydrosulfide, sulfide, thiosulfate, and polysulfide species. It is the key chemical basis of sulfur dissolution in hydroxide solutions described in the slice.

A hydrometallurgical process in which sulfur is dissolved in alkaline hydroxide solutions to generate active sulfur species for selective metal dissolution. The slice describes this route as applicable to purification of process liquors and wastewater and to selective leaching of metals such as gold, silver, copper, lead, and zinc.

A petroleum-derived organic sulfide phase used as a selective solvent for noble-metal dissolution. It forms stable solvates and complexes with dissolved metals and serves as the working medium in the sulfur-organic leaching route described in the slice.

An oxidizing copper chloride used in organic sulfide leaching as a weak oxidant for dissolving noble metals. In the slice it is reduced to copper(I) chloride during metal extraction and participates in forming stable metal-containing complexes in the organic phase.

A reduced copper chloride species formed from copper(II) chloride during sulfur-organic leaching. The slice describes it as a complex-forming intermediate in the organic phase that can disproportionate to regenerate copper(II) chloride and elemental copper.

A leaching mechanism in which organic sulfide molecules coordinate dissolved metal species and stabilize them as soluble solvates or complexes in the organic phase. In the slice this mechanism underpins selective extraction of noble metals from ore and concentrate feeds.

A hydrometallurgical extraction route in which noble metals are selectively dissolved into petroleum-derived organic sulfide solvents using copper chloride as the oxidant. The process is highlighted as reversible through metal recovery from the organic phase and solvent recycle.

A thermodynamic parameter describing the stability of a dissolved metal complex in solution. In the slice it is used to compare gold complexes formed with cyanide, sulfide, thiosulfate, thiourea, iodide, bromide, and chloride, and it largely determines whether an alternative lixiviant can achieve practical dissolution rates.

Aqueous process stream formed in gold recovery circuits that contains free cyanides, thiocyanates, metal-cyanide complexes, and dissolved metal ions. It requires detoxification or regeneration before discharge or recycle because of toxicity and the risk of groundwater and air contamination.

Containment and settling infrastructure used to receive flotation or cyanidation tailings and associated process water. In cyanide circuits, it can act as a location for natural attenuation, but it also creates leakage and volatile-emission risks if the liquor becomes acidic.

Spontaneous attenuation route for cyanide-bearing effluents in tailings ponds driven by HCN volatilization, solar exposure, and biological activity. It is a low-cost but climate-dependent detoxification pathway that can reduce cyanide concentration over time.

Photochemical treatment used to decompose stable cyanide complexes, especially complexes of iron, gold, and silver in wastewater. The slice identifies ultraviolet irradiation as necessary where ordinary chemical destruction is insufficient.

Volatile release of hydrocyanic acid from acidified cyanide liquors or tailings ponds. It creates an acute air-pollution and occupational-safety hazard and is one of the main reasons cyanide effluents must be neutralized before storage or disposal.

Leakage of cyanide-bearing solutions through the pond bed or dam into groundwater and surface waters. This is a critical environmental failure mode for cyanide tailings storage and drives the need for impermeable liners and detoxification.

Geometric parameter of a solution or pond that controls the relative extent of the exposed liquid surface. In cyanide detoxification, a higher surface-to-volume ratio accelerates volatilization and photochemical degradation of cyanide species.

Regulatory limit on contaminant concentration in environmental media such as water bodies. In the slice, it is used for cyanide, thiocyanate, and arsenic species to define acceptable discharge levels for gold-plant wastewater.

Process KPI describing the cyanide content remaining in treated wastewater or tailings liquor after detoxification. It is a direct measure of treatment completeness and environmental compliance, with lower values indicating more effective destruction or removal of cyanide species.

Operational KPI describing the amount of chlorine reagent required per unit of cyanide-bearing effluent treated. In chlorination of cyanide wastewater, it increases sharply in the presence of ammonia, copper, nickel, and poorly mixed streams because of side reactions and chloramine formation.

Electrochemical potential of a wastewater or slurry that reflects its oxidizing or reducing state. In chlorination-based cyanide destruction, it is used as a control parameter to indicate when oxidation has reached the target regime, such as the reported stable value near 600 mV at alkaline pH.

Chlorinated nitrogen species formed when active chlorine reacts with ammonia-containing effluents. In cyanide-wastewater treatment it is an undesirable byproduct because it consumes chlorine, raises reagent demand, and complicates complete oxidation of cyanide species.

Hazardous byproduct formation during chlorination of cyanide-bearing liquors when pH control is insufficient or cyanide concentration is too high. Cyanogen chloride is volatile and highly toxic, making this side reaction a key safety and operating constraint in cyanide detoxification.

Water-soluble polymeric reagent carrying anionic functional groups and used to flocculate fine suspended solids. In cyanide-effluent treatment, it helps aggregate the precipitates formed after oxidation so they can be separated by settling or filtration.

A precipitated iron sulfide reagent used to destroy free and dissolved cyanides in wastewater treatment. It is prepared by combining ferrous sulfate with a soluble sulfide and is applied either as a suspension or as a percolation bed.

A cyanide-destruction method in which cyanides in free and dissolved form are decomposed by contact with iron sulfide. The process is carried out for 15тАУ60 minutes and can be implemented by direct slurry addition or by percolation through an iron-sulfide bed.

Operating pH window used for iron-sulfide cyanide treatment. In this range the added sulfide must exceed the total cyanide concentration by roughly a factor of three to achieve effective decomposition.

Oxidative wastewater treatment using ozone generated from air or oxygen by electric discharge. In cyanide effluents it oxidizes cyanide and thiocyanate species, but it is comparatively expensive in both capital and energy costs.

Process KPI describing the fraction of cyanide species converted to less toxic products during oxidation-based detoxification. In the INCO process described in the slice, the oxidation degree reaches about 99.9%.

Operational KPI expressing the mass of sulfur dioxide required per unit mass of cyanide treated. The slice reports an average demand of about 3.1 kg SO2 per 1 kg cyanide in the INCO cyanide-destruction process.
Process KPI describing the fraction of supplied sulfur dioxide that is effectively consumed in cyanide oxidation. The slice reports utilization of about 80% for the SO2/air detoxification route.

A cyanide-removal method based on converting CN- to ferrocyanide and precipitating ferric hexacyanoferrate(III) as Prussian blue. It can reduce cyanide to very low levels in synthetic solutions, but it is ineffective for industrial liquors with high thiocyanate content.

A two-stage biological treatment route for cyanide wastewater in which adapted microorganisms oxidize cyanide and thiocyanate, followed by nitrifying bacteria converting ammonia to nitrate. The method can reduce cyanide to near-zero levels under mild operating conditions.

A rotating biological reactor used for cyanide wastewater treatment. In the slice it consists of a plastic housing with multiple driven discs that support biomass attachment and provide aeration and mixing during biological oxidation.

An oxidative cyanide-destruction process in which a gas-air mixture containing sulfur dioxide is bubbled through wastewater in the presence of lime and a copper catalyst. Cyanide is converted mainly to cyanate, while thiocyanate removal is more selective than in chlorination or ozonation.

Operating pH range used for the SO2/air oxidation process. The mildly alkaline medium supports cyanide oxidation, enables lime control of acidity, and helps precipitate metals as hydroxides after treatment.

A cyanide-regeneration method in which cyanide solutions are acidified with sulfuric acid and the released hydrogen cyanide is captured in absorbers for recycle. The process can remove more than 90% of cyanide, but ferrocyanides and thiocyanates are not fully decomposed.

Acidic operating window used in Mills-Crowe cyanide solution acidification. At this pH the target discharge concentration can be achieved within a few hours, but filtration before aeration may be required to avoid apparatus fouling by precipitates.

A much less toxic oxyanion formed during oxidative destruction of cyanide. In the slice it is the main product of SO2/air treatment and an intermediate species in subsequent oxidation to nitrogen and bicarbonate.
A sodium sulfite-derived reagent used as a carrier of sulfur dioxide in cyanide detoxification. It supplies both sulfite species and alkalinity for neutralization in SO2-based wastewater treatment.
Electrochemical destruction or transformation of cyanide compounds in wastewater, excluding ferrocyanides. The slice notes electrowinning of metal-cyanide complexes as one variant of this route.

Electrochemical cyanide-destruction route in which cyanide is oxidized directly at the anode without added chloride. It is used for wastewater detoxification and is characterized in the text by graphite, lead, or magnetite anodes, high current density, and relatively long treatment times.

Electrochemical detoxification method in which chloride ions are oxidized at the anode to chlorine, which then reacts with cyanides in solution. In the slice, it is applied only when chlorides are present in the feed and is used industrially as a more effective cyanide-removal variant than direct anodic oxidation for some wastewaters.

Electrochemical process in which complex cyanides dissociate under reductive conditions, metals are precipitated on the cathode, and cyanide is regenerated in the liquor. The text presents this as a practical cyanide-regeneration route for metal-bearing solutions.

Commercial strong-base anion-exchange resin used in cyanide-bearing wastewater treatment. In the slice, it sorbs cyanide and thiocyanate ions to very low residual concentrations and serves as the anion-exchange stage in pilot detoxification flowsheets.

Commercial cation-exchange resin used to recover dissolved base metals from cyanide solutions after anion-exchange treatment. The text reports high sorption of copper, nickel, and zinc on this resin and uses it as the cationic stage in pilot wastewater-cleanup circuits.

term.primary: State Educational Standard of Higher Professional Education

concepts.definition: Industrial processing domain focused on upgrading coal by removing mineral matter and improving fuel quality. It includes gravity separation, flotation, briquetting, and thermal treatment routes mentioned in the study guide.

The fraction of combustible components released from coal during heating in the absence of air. It is a key coal-quality parameter used to classify coal ranks and evaluate processing and combustion behavior.
The heat released by complete combustion of a unit mass of fuel. In coal technology, it is a core quality indicator because it determines fuel value and the economic attractiveness of beneficiation.
Self-heating and ignition of coal caused by slow oxidation during storage or handling. It is a major safety hazard for coal stockpiles, transport, and processing sites.

Rapid combustion of suspended coal dust in air, producing a pressure wave and severe industrial hazard. The topic list explicitly highlights coal dust explosiveness as a key safety issue in coal processing.

Agglomeration method in which fine coal is compacted into larger mechanically stable briquettes. It is used to improve handling, reduce dusting, and create commercial fuel products from fine or low-grade coal.

Beneficiation method that separates particles according to differences in electrical conductivity, surface charging, and response to an electric field. The study guide mentions it for vermiculite and coal-related processing routes.

The ease with which a coal or ore feed can be upgraded by physical separation methods such as gravity, flotation, or screening. It is used to classify coals and to select the most effective beneficiation route.

A coal type formed predominantly from aquatic organic matter and sapropelic deposits. It differs from humic coal in origin and composition, which affects beneficiation behavior and end-use properties.
A coal type formed mainly from terrestrial plant material. It is the classical coal family processed in coal beneficiation and is commonly classified by rank, ash content, and washability.

A fibrous silicate mineral group used industrially for heat- and chemical-resistant products. In beneficiation, asbestos ores are characterized by asbestos content and fiber length, which determine product quality and processing route.
The fraction of asbestos-bearing material in an ore. It is a key classification parameter for asbestos deposits because it governs ore type, processing strategy, and the quality of asbestos products.
Characteristic length of fibrous mineral particles, especially asbestos fibers. It is an important quality and classification parameter because it directly affects product grade and separability.

Layered hydrated magnesium-aluminum silicate mineral processed as an industrial nonmetallic raw material. The study guide mentions its beneficiation by form-based separation, gravity methods, and electrostatic separation.

Graphite variety consisting of discrete flaky crystals. It is typically recovered by selective grinding and flotation and is important because its morphology strongly affects beneficiation response and product quality.

Graphite variety with compact crystalline structure and lower natural liberation than flake graphite. It requires different comminution and beneficiation strategies because of its distinct texture and intergrowth behavior.

Fine-grained graphite variety with very small crystallites. It is generally processed by different beneficiation routes than flake graphite because its liberation and flotation behavior are strongly controlled by fine size.

Comminution strategy that preferentially breaks softer or more brittle components while minimizing overgrinding of the valuable mineral. In graphite and other nonmetallic ores, it is used to improve liberation before downstream separation.

Mineral-processing domain focused on recovering diamonds from placer and kimberlite feeds. It typically combines disintegration, screening, gravity separation, optical sorting, luminescent sorting, grease-based separation, electrical separation, and hand sorting to produce diamond concentrates.

Volcanic ultrabasic rock that hosts most primary diamond deposits. Kimberlites are the main geological matrix for diamond-bearing ore and commonly contain olivine, pyroxenes, phlogopite, calcite, serpentine, garnet, and spinel.

Polycrystalline black diamond aggregate with a porous, irregular structure. It is an industrial diamond variety rather than a typical gem-quality crystal and is relevant to diamond sorting and beneficiation.

Industrial-grade diamond material of lower transparency and irregular habit than gem-quality stones. Bort is used in abrasive and technical applications and appears as one of the diamond varieties addressed in beneficiation practice.

Polycrystalline diamond variety with radial or spherulitic internal structure. It is an industrial diamond type distinguished from transparent single-crystal diamonds and is relevant for sorting and cleaning of rough diamond concentrates.

Preparatory ore treatment used to break down clay-bound, cemented, or weakly consolidated material before diamond recovery. Its purpose is to liberate diamond particles while minimizing breakage and loss of valuable crystals.

Optical sorting method that separates particles by differences in reflected or transmitted light response. In diamond processing it is used to identify and reject or recover diamond-bearing particles based on optical contrast.

Sorting method that exploits diamond luminescence under excitation such as ultraviolet or other radiation. It is used to detect and separate diamond grains from non-luminescent gangue or concentrate fractions.

Diamond recovery method based on the preferential adhesion of diamond grains to a greasy surface. It exploits the strong hydrophobicity and surface affinity of diamonds to retain them while gangue particles are washed away.

Manual separation method used to recover diamonds based on visible optical properties such as transparency, luster, and morphology. It is typically applied at an early or finishing stage when the material stream is already enriched.

Sorting method that separates material by natural or induced radiation response. In mineral beneficiation it is applied to selected ores, including some barite feeds, where a radiometric signal can distinguish valuable material from gangue.
Finishing operation used to remove adhering gangue, coatings, and low-value particles from rough diamond concentrates. It improves concentrate purity before final sorting, valuation, or sale.

Mineral-processing domain aimed at upgrading barite ores and removing gangue and harmful impurities. Depending on ore type, it can use washing, classification, jigging, table separation, radiometric sorting, chemical treatment, and flotation.

Mineral-processing domain focused on recovering and upgrading talc-bearing ores. The flowsheets usually exploit talc's natural hydrophobicity and may include photometric separation, flotation, and selective grinding.

Mineral-processing domain devoted to separation and upgrading of mica ores such as muscovite and phlogopite. It typically uses friction-based, shape-based, gravity, and flotation methods to recover sheet-like mica products.

Mineral-processing domain focused on recovering asbestos fibers and separating them from associated rock-forming minerals. The process commonly relies on liberation, air and centrifugal classification, gravity separation, and vibrational or pneumatic sorting.

A combined beneficiation route that couples flotation with gravity separation to exploit both surface properties and density differences. In phosphorite and other ore processing, it is used when neither flotation nor gravity alone gives sufficient selectivity or recovery.

Naturally occurring elemental sulfur present in ore bodies as a recoverable mineral commodity. It is the principal feed material in sulfur ore beneficiation and is processed by gravity, flotation, thermal, and extraction routes.

A phosphorite ore type in which silica-bearing gangue is dominant or abundant. Such ores typically require collectors and depressants tuned to quartz and silicate minerals to achieve selective phosphate recovery.

A phosphorite ore type containing substantial carbonate gangue, commonly calcite and dolomite. Its beneficiation is complicated by the close surface chemistry of carbonate minerals and phosphate minerals, so selective depression and pH control are critical.

A separation process in which hydrophobic particles are selectively wetted by oil and bind into larger agglomerates. It is used to concentrate naturally hydrophobic or surface-modified minerals when conventional flotation is inefficient.

A concentration device that combines table-based stratification with magnetic action to separate particles by density and magnetic response. It is used in beneficiation circuits where heavy, weakly magnetic, or magnetically conditioned particles must be recovered with high selectivity.

A mineral-processing domain focused on upgrading sulfur-bearing ores and separating native sulfur from gangue and harmful impurities. It includes flotation, electrical separation, thermal routes, and underground or autoclave melting depending on ore type and sulfur distribution.

A lecture-note source on mineral beneficiation referenced in the course bibliography. It provides the foundational theoretical and practical material for flotation, gravity, magnetic, and related separation methods.

term.primary: Processing and Beneficiation of Nonferrous Metal Ores, Book 2, Volume 3 (2005)

concepts.definition: A textbook source on the processing and beneficiation of nonferrous metal ores. It is cited as a reference base for ore-dressing flowsheets, reagent schemes, and industrial beneficiation practice.
A software documentation source for the UniTest testing system used in the course. It describes the computerized test delivery and knowledge-checking workflow referenced in the educational materials.
A university textbook volume devoted to flotation-based beneficiation methods. It serves as a foundational source for flotation theory, reagent practice, and industrial flowsheets.

term.primary: Technology of Beneficiation and Processing of Nonmetallic Minerals (2009)

concepts.definition: An educational source on beneficiation and processing of nonmetallic mineral raw materials. It is relevant for coal, graphite, diamond, phosphates, potash salts, and other nonmetallic ore systems.

term.primary: Technology of Beneficiation and Processing of Mining-Chemical Raw Materials (2009)

concepts.definition: An educational source describing beneficiation and processing routes for mining-chemical raw materials. It supports the sections on phosphorites, potash ores, sulfur, and related industrial mineral feeds.
A textbook source on the extraction, processing, and refining of precious metals. It is relevant to gold, silver, platinum-group metals, and their beneficiation and refining routes.

term.primary: Phosphate Ores of the Krasnoyarsk Territory (2006)

concepts.definition: A regional technical source on phosphate ores and their beneficiation. It is relevant to phosphate-ore classification, local ore types, and processing challenges.

A technical source on the beneficiation of phosphate ores containing rare metals. It is relevant to complex phosphate feeds where flotation, selective depression, and multi-stage flowsheets are required.
A handbook on flotation reagents and their industrial use in mineral processing. It is a key source for collector, frother, regulator, and depressant chemistry.
A textbook source focused on gold beneficiation. It is relevant to gravity concentration, flotation of gold-bearing ores, and preconcentration before cyanidation.

term.primary: Technology of Gold and Silver Recovery from Refractory Ores (1999)

concepts.definition: A technical source on recovering gold and silver from refractory ores. It is relevant to oxidative pretreatment, flotation, cyanidation, and combined hydrometallurgical flowsheets.
A textbook source on diamond beneficiation. It is relevant to disintegration, screening, gravity separation, optical sorting, grease separation, and diamond cleaning.

term.primary: Theory and Practice of Integrated Mineral Processing in Asia, Africa, and Latin America (1989)

concepts.definition: A source on integrated mineral-processing practice across different mining regions. It is relevant to complex ore treatment strategies and combined beneficiation flowsheets.

term.primary: Handbook on Ore Beneficiation: Concentrating Plants (1984)

concepts.definition: A handbook source covering ore-beneficiation plants and industrial flowsheets. It provides reference practice for plant layout, equipment selection, and process routing.

term.primary: Mineral Beneficiation Course Program and Assignment Guidelines (2008)

concepts.definition: A teaching-methodical source for the mineral beneficiation course. It is relevant as an educational reference describing coursework structure, exercises, and assessment materials.
A periodical information source cited in the bibliography. It provides market and commercial information relevant to mineral raw materials and industrial processing.

term.primary: World Mineral Raw Materials Market Conjuncture (2000)

concepts.definition: An online market-information source on mineral raw materials. It is relevant to industrial demand, pricing context, and market conditions for mineral beneficiation products.

term.primary: Electronic Educational Complex for Mineral Beneficiation

concepts.definition: An electronic educational resource for the mineral beneficiation discipline. It is relevant as a digital source of course materials, presentations, and self-study content.

A complex ore feed containing phosphate minerals together with niobium-bearing phases such as pyrochlore. It is typically processed by selective flotation schemes that separate apatite/phosphate values from niobium minerals and silicate gangue.

A beneficiation domain for phosphate-niobium ores in which phosphate minerals and niobium-bearing minerals are selectively recovered using anionic or cationic collectors, depressants, and pH control. The process is used to produce separate phosphate and niobium concentrates from complex mixed feeds.

A flotation application focused on recovering fluorite from ores containing calcite, quartz, barite, or other carbonate and silicate gangue. It usually relies on selective depression of gangue minerals and carefully chosen anionic collectors.

A beneficiation application for chromite-bearing ores, typically performed to separate chromite from serpentine, olivine, and other silicate gangue. The process may use either direct anionic flotation or reverse cationic flotation depending on gangue mineralogy.

A flotation domain for manganese-bearing ores, often used for fine or slime fractions obtained after gravity concentration. It targets manganese minerals while rejecting quartz, feldspar, clays, and carbonate gangue through controlled reagent schemes.

A mineral beneficiation application for recovering ilmenite from titanium-bearing ores. It is commonly used to separate ilmenite from quartz and other silicate or oxide gangue using selective collectors and pH regulation.

A flotation process for niobium-bearing pyrochlore ores, often performed in phosphate-niobium ore circuits. Selective collectors and depressants are used to separate pyrochlore from apatite, carbonates, and silicate gangue.

The mass fraction of final concentrate obtained from the feed in a beneficiation or flotation circuit. It is a core process KPI because it determines product quantity, influences concentrate grade, and is used together with recovery to evaluate flowsheet performance.

aliases: Technology of gold and silver extraction from refractory gold-arsenic flotation concentrate of Ikkijelon deposit

concepts.definition: Bibliographic source for the reported study on processing refractory gold-arsenic flotation concentrate by arsenatizing roasting and sorption cyanidation. It identifies the specific publication and links the reported extraction results to a citable article record.

A sulfide flotation concentrate containing gold and elevated arsenic, typically refractory to direct cyanidation because gold is finely disseminated and associated with arsenic-bearing sulfides. Such concentrates usually require oxidative pretreatment before leaching.

Thermochemical pretreatment in which arsenic-bearing sulfide concentrates are roasted below the melting point of gold-bearing components to convert refractory sulfides into more leachable calcine. The process improves gold accessibility by oxidizing arsenic and sulfur-bearing phases.

A combined hydrometallurgical route in which cyanide leaching and simultaneous adsorption of dissolved precious metals on a sorbent occur in the same agitated circuit. In the slice, it is used to recover gold and silver from the flotation concentrate and from the calcine after roasting.

Mass fraction of arsenic in ore, concentrate, or calcine. Elevated arsenic content is a key indicator of refractory behavior because it is associated with sulfide encapsulation, higher roasting demand, and reduced direct cyanidation response.

The tendency of an ore or concentrate to resist gold and silver dissolution in cyanide solution because the precious metals are finely disseminated or locked in sulfide/arsenic minerals. It is a practical descriptor of whether oxidative pretreatment is needed before leaching.

Process KPI representing the fraction of silver transferred from the feed into the leachate or final recovered product. In the reported study it is used alongside gold recovery to compare direct cyanidation with the roastingтАУcyanidation route.

term.primary: Inductively Coupled Plasma Optical Emission Spectrometry

concepts.definition: Elemental analysis technique in which an argon plasma excites atoms and ions, and their emission lines are measured to determine composition. It is suitable for multi-element quantification in ores, concentrates, and calcines.

Analytical method that quantifies elements by measuring absorption of element-specific radiation by free atoms in the vapor phase. In the slice it is used for gold, silver, and general compositional analysis of sample and process products.

Diffraction-based method used to identify crystalline phases in ore, concentrate, and roast products. It reveals mineral transformations caused by roasting and is therefore useful for evaluating calcine formation and phase changes.

Vibrational spectroscopic method used to identify functional groups and molecular bonding environments in solids or extracts. In the slice it supports chemical-state analysis of the concentrate and roasting products.

Combined precious-metal assay in which gold and silver are first concentrated by fire assay and then quantified by atomic absorption. It is a standard high-sensitivity method for determining noble-metal content in ores and concentrates.

Classical quantitative analytical method based on measuring mass after selective precipitation, filtration, drying, or ignition. It is used to determine composition and mass fractions in mineral-processing samples.

Volumetric analytical method that determines analyte concentration from the amount of standard reagent consumed in a reaction. In ore-processing studies it is used for compositional and solution-chemistry measurements.

Analytical method that determines composition from the intensity of light absorption or transmission by a colored or derivatized sample. It is suitable for solution assays and compositional control in metallurgical experiments.

An inorganic chloride additive used in arsenatizing roasting of sulfide flotation concentrate. In the described process it supplies chlorine to promote thermochemical breakdown of iron sulfide/arsenopyrite minerals and to increase the formation of reactive iron chloride intermediates.

An electrically heated chamber furnace used for laboratory or pilot roasting of mineral charges. In the slice it is equipped with silicon-carbide heaters and used to roast flotation concentrate at controlled temperatures in the 650тАУ750 ┬░C range.

The solid product obtained after roasting ore or concentrate under oxidizing or chlorinating conditions. In this slice the calcine is a porous, partially agglomerated arsenatizing-roast product that is subsequently subjected to cyanidation to recover gold and silver.

Cyanide leaching of a roasted calcine product to recover precious metals after thermal pretreatment. In the reported process it follows arsenatizing roasting and is used to exploit the increased chemical accessibility of gold and silver in the roasted material.
